When one who is close to Allah commits an offense, even if that offense is forgiven, its effect remains. As long as the effect and the suspicion persist, there is fear, not fear of punishment, but fear of the Majesty. The accused before the ruler finds in the accusation a sore spot that leads him to cloud the clarity of trust. Musa (peace be upon him) committed the offense against that Pharaonic man, then he sought forgiveness and acknowledged the wrong against himself, then he was forgiven. Then after forgiveness he said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals" (28:17). Then the next day he was tested with the other Pharaonic man, and he intended to strike him, and this intention became another offense. He was tested the next day because of his saying "I will never be a supporter of the criminals," which is an expression of ability (iqtidar) in the sense of "I will never do." So he was punished through the intention when he wanted to strike and did not do it. Then the Israelite was empowered over him until he revealed his secret, because when the Israelite saw him rolling up his sleeves to strike, he thought he meant him, so he informed on him, and said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" (28:19). The Pharaonic man fled and informed Pharaoh of what the Israelite had revealed about Musa. The killing of the previous day had been kept secret, and no one knew who had killed. When Pharaoh learned of this, he sent to seek Musa in order to kill him, and the search intensified and they seized the main roads. A man came running and said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you" (28:20), and the rest of the verse. So he left as Allah had informed. Thus Musa's fear was only because of this offense. Even though his Lord brought him near, honored him, chose him, and spoke to him, the lingering suspicion went away from him and did not return.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease" (27:12). The discussion of this has already been given in Ta-Ha. [[See vol. 11, p. 191, first or second edition.]]

"Among nine signs" (fi tis'i ayat): Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about it is that the meaning is: this verse is included among nine signs. Al-Mahdawi said: The meaning is "Throw down your staff" and "insert your hand into your bosom," so these are two of the nine signs. Al-Qushayri said its meaning is like your saying "I went out among ten men, and you were one of them," meaning "I went out as the tenth of ten." So fi (among) here means min (from), because of its closeness to it, as you say "Take for me ten of the camels, among them two stallions," meaning "from them." Al-Asma'i, regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who has spent thirty months, in three states, ever be content?" [[In another narration: "Will he ever be content (ya'mun)?"]]

He said fi means min. It has also been said that fi means ma'a (with), so the signs are ten, among them the hand, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the staff, the locusts, the lice, the flood, the blood, the frogs, the years of famine, and the obliteration (tamas) [[Tamas: to remove a thing from its form. Allah turned their wealth and money into stones. See vol. 8, p. 374.]]. The explanation of all of them has already been given.

"To Pharaoh and his people": Al-Farra' said: There is an implied element in the speech, indicated by the context, meaning: you are sent (mab'uth) or dispatched (mursal) to Pharaoh and his people.

"Indeed, they were a people of defiant wickedness" (27:12): meaning they were outside obedience to Allah. This has already been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: "So when Our signs came to them, clear" (27:13): meaning clear and evident. Al-Akhfash said: It may also be mubsara (with the meaning of a verbal noun), as one says "al-walad majbana" (a child is a source of cowardice).

"They said, 'This is obvious magic'" (27:13): They continued in their habit of denial. Therefore He said: "And they rejected them while their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance" (27:14). That is, they were certain that they were from Allah and were not magic, but they disbelieved in them and were too proud to believe in Musa. This shows that they were obstinate. "Zulman" (in wrongdoing) and "uluwwan" (in arrogance) are in the accusative as qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: they rejected them with a rejection that was wrongful and arrogant. The ba' (with) is extra, meaning "they rejected them," as Abu 'Ubayda said.

"So look," O Muhammad, "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (27:14): meaning the final fate of the disbelieving tyrants. Look at that with the eye of your heart and reflect upon it. The address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 7–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When Musa said to his family﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "remember." It is as if He said, following His words "And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing": "Take, O Muhammad, from the traces of His wisdom and knowledge the story of Musa, when he said to his family."

(﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾) That is, I saw it from afar. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:
"He perceived a faint sound, and the hunter startled him, at afternoon, when evening had drawn near."
[[Anasat: he sensed. Al-nabʾa: a faint sound.]]

(﴿I will bring you from it news, or bring you a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves﴾) Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-shihabin qabasin" with tanwin on "shihab." The rest read it without tanwin, as an idafa (construct), meaning "with a flame of fire," and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Al-Farra' claimed that omitting the tanwin is like the expressions "wa-dar al-akhirah" (and the abode of the Hereafter) and "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque) and "salat al-ula" (the first prayer), where a thing is annexed to itself when its names differ. Al-Nahhas said: the annexation of a thing to itself is impossible according to the Basrans, because the meaning of idafa in language is the joining of one thing to another; it is impossible for a thing to be joined to itself. A thing is annexed to another only so that the meaning of possession or kind may be made clear, and it is impossible for it to be shown to be the possessor of itself or of its own kind. "Shihab qabas" is an idafa of kind and genus, as you say, "this is a garment of silk" and "a ring of iron" and the like. "Shihab" is any bearer of light, such as a star or a lit stick. "Qabas" is the name of what is taken (uqtubisa) from an ember and the like, so the meaning is "a shihab of qabas" (a brand from a flame). It is said: "aqbastu qabsan," and the noun is "qabas," as you say: "qabadtu qabdan," and the noun is "qabd." Whoever reads "bi-shihabin qabasin" makes it a substitute (badal) for it. Al-Mahdawi said: or it is an attribute (sifah) of it, because "qabas" may be a noun that is not an attribute, and it may be an attribute. As for it not being an attribute, it is because they say "qabastuhu aqbasuhu qabsan," and "qabas" means "that which is taken." When it is an attribute, the better is that it be a descriptive (na't). The idafa is better when it is not an attribute, and it is the idafa of kind to its genus, like "a ring of silver" and the like. If it were read with the accusative of "qabas," as a specification (bayan) or a state (hal), it would be better. In other than the Qur'an it is permitted to say "bi-shihabin qabasan," as a verbal noun (masdar), or a specification, or a state. ﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: the original of the "ta'" (t) is "ta'," and it was changed here to "ta'" (t-to-t form) ... [translation note: the original reads "أَصْلُ الطَّاءِ تَاءٌ فَأُبْدِلَ مِنْهَا هُنَا طَاءً" meaning the ta' in "tasṭalūna" is originally "ta'" (ت) that was changed to "ta'" (ط)], because the ta' is emphatic (mutbaqah) and the sad is emphatic, so their combination is good. Its meaning is "they seek warmth from the cold." It is said: "istalā yaṣṭalī" when one seeks warmth. The poet said:
"Fire is the fruit of winter, so whoever wants to eat the fruits in winter, let him seek warmth."
Al-Zajjaj: every white thing that has light is a shihab. Abu 'Ubaydah: the shihab is fire. Abu al-Najm said:
"As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light and then became extinguished."
Ahmad ibn Yahya: the origin of the shihab is a stick with an ember at one end and no fire at the other. The saying of al-Nahhas on it is good: the shihab is a far-reaching ray, and from it comes the star that extends its light in the sky. The poet said:
"In his hand is a straight spear, well-shaped, in which is a point like the flame of a brand."
[[al-sa'dah: a spear-shaft that grows straight.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when Musa came to the one he thought was fire while it was light. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. When Musa saw the fire he stood near it, and he saw it coming out of the branch of a green tree, very intensely green, called al-'Ulayq. The fire does not increase except in size and blaze, and the tree does not increase except in greenness and beauty. He was amazed by it and reached toward it with a bundle of sticks in his hand to take a brand from it, but it inclined toward him, so he feared it and drew back. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, until its matter became clear: that it was commanded and he did not know who had commanded it, until "he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it." This meaning has already passed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11 p. 172 onward and p. 113]].

(﴿was called﴾) That is, God called him, as He said: "And We called him from the right side of the mount."

(﴿that blessed﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: "anna" is in the place of the accusative, meaning "that it was blessed." He said: it may also be in the place of the nominative, making it the subject of what has no named agent. Abu Hatim related that in the reading of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid it is "that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it." Al-Nahhas said: the like of this is not found with a sound chain, and even if it were sound it would be explanatory, so the blessing returns to the fire and to those around it, the angels and Musa. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah" and "barak Allah fika." Al-Tha'labi: the Arabs say "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak Allah 'alayka," and "barak Allah laka," four dialects. The poet said:
"So you were blessed as a newborn, and blessed as a growing youth, and blessed in gray hair when you became white-haired."
Al-Tabari: He said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and did not say "blessed is in the fire" according to the dialect of one who says "barakaka Allah." It is said "barakahu Allah," "barak lahu," "barak 'alayhi," and "barak fihi," with the same meaning, that is, blessing was upon whoever was in the fire, namely Musa, or upon whoever was near the fire, not that he was in its middle. Al-Suddi said: there were angels in the fire, so the blessing returns to Musa and the angels, that is, "blessed are you, O Musa, and the angels who are around it." This is a greeting from God to Musa and an honouring of him, just as He greeted Abraham through the tongues of the angels when they entered upon him, saying: "The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house" [[See vol. 9 p. 70]]. A third view was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "sanctified is whoever is in the fire," and he is God, glorified and exalted, meaning Himself, may He be sanctified and exalted. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fire is the light of God, the Mighty and Majestic; God called Musa while he was in the light, and the interpretation of this is that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a great light and thought it was fire, because God appeared to Musa through His signs and His speech from the fire, not that He is located in a direction, "He who is in the heaven is God, and in the earth is God" [[See vol. 16 p. 121]], not that He is contained in them, but He manifests Himself in every act, so that by it the existence of the Doer is known. It was also said in this regard: "blessed is whoever is in the fire," meaning His authority and power. And it was said: "blessed is what is in the fire of the command of God, which He made a sign."

I say: Among what indicates the soundness of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is what Muslim in his Sahih and Ibn Majah in his Sunan related, and the wording is his, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn every creature that His sight reaches." [[Perhaps the feminine pronoun is by way of the lights as "anwar."
(Footnote of Ibn Majah).]] Then Abu 'Ubaydah recited: "that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to God, Lord of the worlds." Al-Bayhaqi also related it. The wording of Muslim from Abu Musa: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood among us and spoke five words, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light, in another narration of Abu Bakr, fire. If He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn whatever of His creation His sight reaches." Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said that the subuhat (glories) are the majesty of His Face, and from it is said: "Subhan Allah" is only glorification and exaltation of Him. His saying "if He were to uncover it" means: if He lifted the veil from their eyes and did not strengthen them to see Him, they would burn and would not be able to bear it. Ibn Jurayj said: the fire is one of the veils, and they are seven veils: the veil of might, the veil of kingdom, the veil of sovereignty, the veil of fire, the veil of light, the veil of cloud, and the veil of water. In truth the created thing is veiled, and God is not veiled by anything. So the fire was light, and He mentioned it by the word "fire" because Musa supposed it to be fire, and the Arabs place one of the two in the place of the other. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fire was indeed the fire itself, and He made him hear His speech from its direction, and manifested His lordship to him from its side. This is as it is related that it is written in the Torah: "God came from Sinai, and shone forth from Se'ir, and was exalted from the mountains of Paran." So His coming from Sinai is His sending Musa from it; His shining from Se'ir is His sending Jesus the Messiah from it; and His being exalted from Paran is His sending Muhammad ﷺ; and Paran is Mecca. In "al-Qasas" there will come, God willing, further explanation of His making him hear His speech from the tree.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: a declaration of God, Lord of the worlds, as far removed from imperfection and as sanctified. It has already been mentioned in more than one place. The meaning: those around it say "and glory be to God," and the verb is omitted. It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, said it when he finished hearing the call, seeking help from God and declaring Him free of imperfection; al-Suddi said this. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Its meaning: "and blessed is whoever glorifies God, the Lord of the worlds," related by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, God, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾: the "hu" (he) is a support pronoun (imad) and not a pronoun referring back, according to the Kufans. The correct view is that it refers to the matter and the affair. ("I am God, the Almighty") the Dominant, having none like Him. "The All-Wise" in His command and His action. It was said: Musa said, "O Lord, who is it that called?" He said to him: "Indeed, it" (that is, I am the one calling you) "I am God."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa thought that God had commanded him to let it go, so he let it go. It was also said: He said this to him only so that Musa would know that the One speaking to him is God, and that Musa is His messenger, and every prophet needs a sign within himself by which he knows his prophethood. In the verse there is an ellipsis: that is, "and throw down your staff," so he threw it from his hand, and it became a snake moving quickly as if it were a jann, which is a small, light snake. Al-Kalbi said: neither small nor large. It was also said: it was first turned into a small snake for him, and when he became at ease with it, it was turned into a large snake. It was also said: it turned at one time into a small snake, and at another into a moving serpent, which is the female, and at another into a thu'ban, which is the large male of snakes. It was also said: the meaning is that it turned into a thu'ban moving like a jann, having the bulk of the thu'ban and the lightness and quickness of the jann, and it is a snake that moves. The plural of jann is jinnan, and from it comes the hadith: "He forbade killing the jinnan which are in houses."

(﴿He turned back fleeing﴾) in fear, according to the habit of humans. (﴿and did not look back﴾): that is, he did not return. Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: he did not turn his head.

(﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾): that is, of the snake and its harm.

(﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾). The sentence is complete, then He made an exception of a disconnected kind, saying: (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾). It was also said: it is an exception from an omitted element, and the meaning is: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have done wrong (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾), then substituted good after evil," for he does not fear, as al-Farra' said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 7–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: An exception (istithna', grammatical exception) from an omitted antecedent is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned. If this were permitted, one could say "Inni la adribu al-qawma illa Zaydan" with the meaning "I do not strike the people, but I strike others, except Zayd." This is the opposite of clarity, and it brings in something whose meaning is not understood.

Al-Farra' also claimed that some grammarians make illa (except) mean waw (and), so that the meaning is "and not those who did wrong." He cited the verse:

"And every brother is parted from his brother, by your father's life, except the two Farqadan (stars)."

Al-Nahhas said: That illa should mean waw has no basis, and it is not permissible in any speech. The meaning of illa is the opposite of waw, because when you say "Your brothers came, except Zayd," you exclude Zayd from what the brothers included, so there is no relation or closeness between them.

There is another view on the verse: that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the meaning is "except those among the messengers who did wrong by committing minor sins from which no one is free." This is with the exception of what is related about Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him), and what Allah the Exalted mentioned about our Prophet (peace be upon him) in His saying: "That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows" (48:2). Al-Mahdawi mentioned this, and al-Nahhas preferred it, and said: Allah knew who among them would disobey, [[The addition is from al-Nahhas's "I'rab al-Quran."]] so He made an exception, saying: "except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil" (27:11), for he fears even though I have forgiven him.

Al-Dahhak said: It means Adam and Dawud (peace be upon them both).

Al-Zamakhshari said: Like what proceeded from Adam, Yunus, Dawud, Sulayman, and the brothers of Yusuf, and from Musa (peace be upon him) in striking the Coptic man.

If someone says: What is the meaning of fear after repentance and forgiveness? It is said to him: This is the way of the scholars of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that they are fearful and anxious about their disobedience. They also do not feel safe that some of the conditions of repentance may remain unfulfilled, so they fear being held accountable for it.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij said: Allah said to Musa, "I made you fear because you killed a soul." Al-Hasan said: The prophets would sin and then be punished.

Al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri, al-Mawardi, and others said: The exception on this view is sound, meaning: except one of the prophets and messengers who wronged himself in a minor sin committed before prophethood. Musa feared because of killing the Copt, and he repented from it. It has also been said that after prophethood they are protected (ma'sum) from minor and major sins. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 1, pp. 308 onward, second and third editions.]]

I say: The first view is more sound, because of their disowning of such things on the Day of Resurrection, as in the hadith of intercession. When one who is close to Allah commits an offense, even if that offense is forgiven, its effect remains. As long as the effect and the suspicion persist, there is fear, not fear of punishment, but fear of the Majesty. The accused before the ruler finds in the accusation a sore spot that leads him to cloud the clarity of trust. Musa (peace be upon him) committed the offense against that Pharaonic man, then he sought forgiveness and acknowledged the wrong against himself, then he was forgiven. Then after forgiveness he said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals" (28:17). Then the next day he was tested with the other Pharaonic man, and he intended to strike him, and this intention became another offense. He was tested the next day because of his saying "I will never be a supporter of the criminals," which is an expression of ability (iqtidar) in the sense of "I will never do." So he was punished through the intention when he wanted to strike and did not do it. Then the Israelite was empowered over him until he revealed his secret, because when the Israelite saw him rolling up his sleeves to strike, he thought he meant him, so he informed on him, and said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" (28:19). The Pharaonic man fled and informed Pharaoh of what the Israelite had revealed about Musa. The killing of the previous day had been kept secret, and no one knew who had killed. When Pharaoh learned of this, he sent to seek Musa in order to kill him, and the search intensified and they seized the main roads. A man came running and said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you" (28:20), and the rest of the verse. So he left as Allah had informed. Thus Musa's fear was only because of this offense. Even though his Lord brought him near, honored him, chose him, and spoke to him, the lingering suspicion went away from him and did not return.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease" (27:12). The discussion of this has already been given in Ta-Ha. [[See vol. 11, p. 191, first or second edition.]]

"Among nine signs" (fi tis'i ayat): Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about it is that the meaning is: this verse is included among nine signs. Al-Mahdawi said: The meaning is "Throw down your staff" and "insert your hand into your bosom," so these are two of the nine signs. Al-Qushayri said its meaning is like your saying "I went out among ten men, and you were one of them," meaning "I went out as the tenth of ten." So fi (among) here means min (from), because of its closeness to it, as you say "Take for me ten of the camels, among them two stallions," meaning "from them." Al-Asma'i, regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who has spent thirty months, in three states, ever be content?" [[In another narration: "Will he ever be content (ya'mun)?"]]

He said fi means min. It has also been said that fi means ma'a (with), so the signs are ten, among them the hand, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the staff, the locusts, the lice, the flood, the blood, the frogs, the years of famine, and the obliteration (tamas) [[Tamas: to remove a thing from its form. Allah turned their wealth and money into stones. See vol. 8, p. 374.]]. The explanation of all of them has already been given.

"To Pharaoh and his people": Al-Farra' said: There is an implied element in the speech, indicated by the context, meaning: you are sent (mab'uth) or dispatched (mursal) to Pharaoh and his people.

"Indeed, they were a people of defiant wickedness" (27:12): meaning they were outside obedience to Allah. This has already been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: "So when Our signs came to them, clear" (27:13): meaning clear and evident. Al-Akhfash said: It may also be mubsara (with the meaning of a verbal noun), as one says "al-walad majbana" (a child is a source of cowardice).

"They said, 'This is obvious magic'" (27:13): They continued in their habit of denial. Therefore He said: "And they rejected them while their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance" (27:14). That is, they were certain that they were from Allah and were not magic, but they disbelieved in them and were too proud to believe in Musa. This shows that they were obstinate. "Zulman" (in wrongdoing) and "uluwwan" (in arrogance) are in the accusative as qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: they rejected them with a rejection that was wrongful and arrogant. The ba' (with) is extra, meaning "they rejected them," as Abu 'Ubayda said.

"So look," O Muhammad, "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (27:14): meaning the final fate of the disbelieving tyrants. Look at that with the eye of your heart and reflect upon it. The address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

When Musa saw the fire he stood near it, and he saw it coming out of the branch of a green tree, very intensely green, called al-'Ulayq. The fire does not increase except in size and blaze, and the tree does not increase except in greenness and beauty. He was amazed by it and reached toward it with a bundle of sticks in his hand to take a brand from it, but it inclined toward him, so he feared it and drew back. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, until its matter became clear: that it was commanded and he did not know who had commanded it, until "he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it." This meaning has already passed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11 p. 172 onward and p. 113]].

(﴿was called﴾) That is, God called him, as He said: "And We called him from the right side of the mount."

(﴿that blessed﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: "anna" is in the place of the accusative, meaning "that it was blessed." He said: it may also be in the place of the nominative, making it the subject of what has no named agent. Abu Hatim related that in the reading of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid it is "that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it." Al-Nahhas said: the like of this is not found with a sound chain, and even if it were sound it would be explanatory, so the blessing returns to the fire and to those around it, the angels and Musa. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah" and "barak Allah fika." Al-Tha'labi: the Arabs say "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak Allah 'alayka," and "barak Allah laka," four dialects. The poet said:
"So you were blessed as a newborn, and blessed as a growing youth, and blessed in gray hair when you became white-haired."
Al-Tabari: He said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and did not say "blessed is in the fire" according to the dialect of one who says "barakaka Allah." It is said "barakahu Allah," "barak lahu," "barak 'alayhi," and "barak fihi," with the same meaning, that is, blessing was upon whoever was in the fire, namely Musa, or upon whoever was near the fire, not that he was in its middle. Al-Suddi said: there were angels in the fire, so the blessing returns to Musa and the angels, that is, "blessed are you, O Musa, and the angels who are around it." This is a greeting from God to Musa and an honouring of him, just as He greeted Abraham through the tongues of the angels when they entered upon him, saying: "The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house" [[See vol. 9 p. 70]]. A third view was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "sanctified is whoever is in the fire," and he is God, glorified and exalted, meaning Himself, may He be sanctified and exalted. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fire is the light of God, the Mighty and Majestic; God called Musa while he was in the light, and the interpretation of this is that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a great light and thought it was fire, because God appeared to Musa through His signs and His speech from the fire, not that He is located in a direction, "He who is in the heaven is God, and in the earth is God" [[See vol. 16 p. 121]], not that He is contained in them, but He manifests Himself in every act, so that by it the existence of the Doer is known. It was also said in this regard: "blessed is whoever is in the fire," meaning His authority and power. And it was said: "blessed is what is in the fire of the command of God, which He made a sign."

I say: Among what indicates the soundness of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is what Muslim in his Sahih and Ibn Majah in his Sunan related, and the wording is his, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn every creature that His sight reaches." [[Perhaps the feminine pronoun is by way of the lights as "anwar."
(Footnote of Ibn Majah).]] Then Abu 'Ubaydah recited: "that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to God, Lord of the worlds." Al-Bayhaqi also related it. The wording of Muslim from Abu Musa: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood among us and spoke five words, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light, in another narration of Abu Bakr, fire. If He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn whatever of His creation His sight reaches." Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said that the subuhat (glories) are the majesty of His Face, and from it is said: "Subhan Allah" is only glorification and exaltation of Him. His saying "if He were to uncover it" means: if He lifted the veil from their eyes and did not strengthen them to see Him, they would burn and would not be able to bear it. Ibn Jurayj said: the fire is one of the veils, and they are seven veils: the veil of might, the veil of kingdom, the veil of sovereignty, the veil of fire, the veil of light, the veil of cloud, and the veil of water. In truth the created thing is veiled, and God is not veiled by anything. So the fire was light, and He mentioned it by the word "fire" because Musa supposed it to be fire, and the Arabs place one of the two in the place of the other. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fire was indeed the fire itself, and He made him hear His speech from its direction, and manifested His lordship to him from its side. This is as it is related that it is written in the Torah: "God came from Sinai, and shone forth from Se'ir, and was exalted from the mountains of Paran." So His coming from Sinai is His sending Musa from it; His shining from Se'ir is His sending Jesus the Messiah from it; and His being exalted from Paran is His sending Muhammad ﷺ; and Paran is Mecca. In "al-Qasas" there will come, God willing, further explanation of His making him hear His speech from the tree.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: a declaration of God, Lord of the worlds, as far removed from imperfection and as sanctified. It has already been mentioned in more than one place. The meaning: those around it say "and glory be to God," and the verb is omitted. It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, said it when he finished hearing the call, seeking help from God and declaring Him free of imperfection; al-Suddi said this. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Its meaning: "and blessed is whoever glorifies God, the Lord of the worlds," related by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, God, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾: the "hu" (he) is a support pronoun (imad) and not a pronoun referring back, according to the Kufans. The correct view is that it refers to the matter and the affair. ("I am God, the Almighty") the Dominant, having none like Him. "The All-Wise" in His command and His action. It was said: Musa said, "O Lord, who is it that called?" He said to him: "Indeed, it" (that is, I am the one calling you) "I am God."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa thought that God had commanded him to let it go, so he let it go. It was also said: He said this to him only so that Musa would know that the One speaking to him is God, and that Musa is His messenger, and every prophet needs a sign within himself by which he knows his prophethood. In the verse there is an ellipsis: that is, "and throw down your staff," so he threw it from his hand, and it became a snake moving quickly as if it were a jann, which is a small, light snake. Al-Kalbi said: neither small nor large. It was also said: it was first turned into a small snake for him, and when he became at ease with it, it was turned into a large snake. It was also said: it turned at one time into a small snake, and at another into a moving serpent, which is the female, and at another into a thu'ban, which is the large male of snakes. It was also said: the meaning is that it turned into a thu'ban moving like a jann, having the bulk of the thu'ban and the lightness and quickness of the jann, and it is a snake that moves. The plural of jann is jinnan, and from it comes the hadith: "He forbade killing the jinnan which are in houses."

(﴿He turned back fleeing﴾) in fear, according to the habit of humans. (﴿and did not look back﴾): that is, he did not return. Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: he did not turn his head.

(﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾): that is, of the snake and its harm.

(﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾). The sentence is complete, then He made an exception of a disconnected kind, saying: (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾). It was also said: it is an exception from an omitted element, and the meaning is: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have done wrong (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾), then substituted good after evil," for he does not fear, as al-Farra' said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 7–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: An exception (istithna', grammatical exception) from an omitted antecedent is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned. If this were permitted, one could say "Inni la adribu al-qawma illa Zaydan" with the meaning "I do not strike the people, but I strike others, except Zayd." This is the opposite of clarity, and it brings in something whose meaning is not understood.

Al-Farra' also claimed that some grammarians make illa (except) mean waw (and), so that the meaning is "and not those who did wrong." He cited the verse:

"And every brother is parted from his brother, by your father's life, except the two Farqadan (stars)."

Al-Nahhas said: That illa should mean waw has no basis, and it is not permissible in any speech. The meaning of illa is the opposite of waw, because when you say "Your brothers came, except Zayd," you exclude Zayd from what the brothers included, so there is no relation or closeness between them.

There is another view on the verse: that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the meaning is "except those among the messengers who did wrong by committing minor sins from which no one is free." This is with the exception of what is related about Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him), and what Allah the Exalted mentioned about our Prophet (peace be upon him) in His saying: "That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows" (48:2). Al-Mahdawi mentioned this, and al-Nahhas preferred it, and said: Allah knew who among them would disobey, [[The addition is from al-Nahhas's "I'rab al-Quran."]] so He made an exception, saying: "except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil" (27:11), for he fears even though I have forgiven him.

Al-Dahhak said: It means Adam and Dawud (peace be upon them both).

Al-Zamakhshari said: Like what proceeded from Adam, Yunus, Dawud, Sulayman, and the brothers of Yusuf, and from Musa (peace be upon him) in striking the Coptic man.

If someone says: What is the meaning of fear after repentance and forgiveness? It is said to him: This is the way of the scholars of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that they are fearful and anxious about their disobedience. They also do not feel safe that some of the conditions of repentance may remain unfulfilled, so they fear being held accountable for it.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij said: Allah said to Musa, "I made you fear because you killed a soul." Al-Hasan said: The prophets would sin and then be punished.

Al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri, al-Mawardi, and others said: The exception on this view is sound, meaning: except one of the prophets and messengers who wronged himself in a minor sin committed before prophethood. Musa feared because of killing the Copt, and he repented from it. It has also been said that after prophethood they are protected (ma'sum) from minor and major sins. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 1, pp. 308 onward, second and third editions.]]

I say: The first view is more sound, because of their disowning of such things on the Day of Resurrection, as in the hadith of intercession. When one who is close to Allah commits an offense, even if that offense is forgiven, its effect remains. As long as the effect and the suspicion persist, there is fear, not fear of punishment, but fear of the Majesty. The accused before the ruler finds in the accusation a sore spot that leads him to cloud the clarity of trust. Musa (peace be upon him) committed the offense against that Pharaonic man, then he sought forgiveness and acknowledged the wrong against himself, then he was forgiven. Then after forgiveness he said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals" (28:17). Then the next day he was tested with the other Pharaonic man, and he intended to strike him, and this intention became another offense. He was tested the next day because of his saying "I will never be a supporter of the criminals," which is an expression of ability (iqtidar) in the sense of "I will never do." So he was punished through the intention when he wanted to strike and did not do it. Then the Israelite was empowered over him until he revealed his secret, because when the Israelite saw him rolling up his sleeves to strike, he thought he meant him, so he informed on him, and said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" (28:19). The Pharaonic man fled and informed Pharaoh of what the Israelite had revealed about Musa. The killing of the previous day had been kept secret, and no one knew who had killed. When Pharaoh learned of this, he sent to seek Musa in order to kill him, and the search intensified and they seized the main roads. A man came running and said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you" (28:20), and the rest of the verse. So he left as Allah had informed. Thus Musa's fear was only because of this offense. Even though his Lord brought him near, honored him, chose him, and spoke to him, the lingering suspicion went away from him and did not return.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease" (27:12). The discussion of this has already been given in Ta-Ha. [[See vol. 11, p. 191, first or second edition.]]

"Among nine signs" (fi tis'i ayat): Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about it is that the meaning is: this verse is included among nine signs. Al-Mahdawi said: The meaning is "Throw down your staff" and "insert your hand into your bosom," so these are two of the nine signs. Al-Qushayri said its meaning is like your saying "I went out among ten men, and you were one of them," meaning "I went out as the tenth of ten." So fi (among) here means min (from), because of its closeness to it, as you say "Take for me ten of the camels, among them two stallions," meaning "from them." Al-Asma'i, regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who has spent thirty months, in three states, ever be content?" [[In another narration: "Will he ever be content (ya'mun)?"]]

He said fi means min. It has also been said that fi means ma'a (with), so the signs are ten, among them the hand, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the staff, the locusts, the lice, the flood, the blood, the frogs, the years of famine, and the obliteration (tamas) [[Tamas: to remove a thing from its form. Allah turned their wealth and money into stones. See vol. 8, p. 374.]]. The explanation of all of them has already been given.

"To Pharaoh and his people": Al-Farra' said: There is an implied element in the speech, indicated by the context, meaning: you are sent (mab'uth) or dispatched (mursal) to Pharaoh and his people.

"Indeed, they were a people of defiant wickedness" (27:12): meaning they were outside obedience to Allah. This has already been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: "So when Our signs came to them, clear" (27:13): meaning clear and evident. Al-Akhfash said: It may also be mubsara (with the meaning of a verbal noun), as one says "al-walad majbana" (a child is a source of cowardice).

"They said, 'This is obvious magic'" (27:13): They continued in their habit of denial. Therefore He said: "And they rejected them while their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance" (27:14). That is, they were certain that they were from Allah and were not magic, but they disbelieved in them and were too proud to believe in Musa. This shows that they were obstinate. "Zulman" (in wrongdoing) and "uluwwan" (in arrogance) are in the accusative as qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: they rejected them with a rejection that was wrongful and arrogant. The ba' (with) is extra, meaning "they rejected them," as Abu 'Ubayda said.

"So look," O Muhammad, "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (27:14): meaning the final fate of the disbelieving tyrants. Look at that with the eye of your heart and reflect upon it. The address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 7–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When Musa said to his family﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "remember." It is as if He said, following His words "And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing": "Take, O Muhammad, from the traces of His wisdom and knowledge the story of Musa, when he said to his family."

(﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾) That is, I saw it from afar. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:
"He perceived a faint sound, and the hunter startled him, at afternoon, when evening had drawn near."
[[Anasat: he sensed. Al-nabʾa: a faint sound.]]

(﴿I will bring you from it news, or bring you a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves﴾) Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-shihabin qabasin" with tanwin on "shihab." The rest read it without tanwin, as an idafa (construct), meaning "with a flame of fire," and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Al-Farra' claimed that omitting the tanwin is like the expressions "wa-dar al-akhirah" (and the abode of the Hereafter) and "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque) and "salat al-ula" (the first prayer), where a thing is annexed to itself when its names differ. Al-Nahhas said: the annexation of a thing to itself is impossible according to the Basrans, because the meaning of idafa in language is the joining of one thing to another; it is impossible for a thing to be joined to itself. A thing is annexed to another only so that the meaning of possession or kind may be made clear, and it is impossible for it to be shown to be the possessor of itself or of its own kind. "Shihab qabas" is an idafa of kind and genus, as you say, "this is a garment of silk" and "a ring of iron" and the like. "Shihab" is any bearer of light, such as a star or a lit stick. "Qabas" is the name of what is taken (uqtubisa) from an ember and the like, so the meaning is "a shihab of qabas" (a brand from a flame). It is said: "aqbastu qabsan," and the noun is "qabas," as you say: "qabadtu qabdan," and the noun is "qabd." Whoever reads "bi-shihabin qabasin" makes it a substitute (badal) for it. Al-Mahdawi said: or it is an attribute (sifah) of it, because "qabas" may be a noun that is not an attribute, and it may be an attribute. As for it not being an attribute, it is because they say "qabastuhu aqbasuhu qabsan," and "qabas" means "that which is taken." When it is an attribute, the better is that it be a descriptive (na't). The idafa is better when it is not an attribute, and it is the idafa of kind to its genus, like "a ring of silver" and the like. If it were read with the accusative of "qabas," as a specification (bayan) or a state (hal), it would be better. In other than the Qur'an it is permitted to say "bi-shihabin qabasan," as a verbal noun (masdar), or a specification, or a state. ﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: the original of the "ta'" (t) is "ta'," and it was changed here to "ta'" (t-to-t form) ... [translation note: the original reads "أَصْلُ الطَّاءِ تَاءٌ فَأُبْدِلَ مِنْهَا هُنَا طَاءً" meaning the ta' in "tasṭalūna" is originally "ta'" (ت) that was changed to "ta'" (ط)], because the ta' is emphatic (mutbaqah) and the sad is emphatic, so their combination is good. Its meaning is "they seek warmth from the cold." It is said: "istalā yaṣṭalī" when one seeks warmth. The poet said:
"Fire is the fruit of winter, so whoever wants to eat the fruits in winter, let him seek warmth."
Al-Zajjaj: every white thing that has light is a shihab. Abu 'Ubaydah: the shihab is fire. Abu al-Najm said:
"As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light and then became extinguished."
Ahmad ibn Yahya: the origin of the shihab is a stick with an ember at one end and no fire at the other. The saying of al-Nahhas on it is good: the shihab is a far-reaching ray, and from it comes the star that extends its light in the sky. The poet said:
"In his hand is a straight spear, well-shaped, in which is a point like the flame of a brand."
[[al-sa'dah: a spear-shaft that grows straight.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when Musa came to the one he thought was fire while it was light. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. When Musa saw the fire he stood near it, and he saw it coming out of the branch of a green tree, very intensely green, called al-'Ulayq. The fire does not increase except in size and blaze, and the tree does not increase except in greenness and beauty. He was amazed by it and reached toward it with a bundle of sticks in his hand to take a brand from it, but it inclined toward him, so he feared it and drew back. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, until its matter became clear: that it was commanded and he did not know who had commanded it, until "he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it." This meaning has already passed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11 p. 172 onward and p. 113]].

(﴿was called﴾) That is, God called him, as He said: "And We called him from the right side of the mount."

(﴿that blessed﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: "anna" is in the place of the accusative, meaning "that it was blessed." He said: it may also be in the place of the nominative, making it the subject of what has no named agent. Abu Hatim related that in the reading of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid it is "that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it." Al-Nahhas said: the like of this is not found with a sound chain, and even if it were sound it would be explanatory, so the blessing returns to the fire and to those around it, the angels and Musa. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah" and "barak Allah fika." Al-Tha'labi: the Arabs say "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak Allah 'alayka," and "barak Allah laka," four dialects. The poet said:
"So you were blessed as a newborn, and blessed as a growing youth, and blessed in gray hair when you became white-haired."
Al-Tabari: He said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and did not say "blessed is in the fire" according to the dialect of one who says "barakaka Allah." It is said "barakahu Allah," "barak lahu," "barak 'alayhi," and "barak fihi," with the same meaning, that is, blessing was upon whoever was in the fire, namely Musa, or upon whoever was near the fire, not that he was in its middle. Al-Suddi said: there were angels in the fire, so the blessing returns to Musa and the angels, that is, "blessed are you, O Musa, and the angels who are around it." This is a greeting from God to Musa and an honouring of him, just as He greeted Abraham through the tongues of the angels when they entered upon him, saying: "The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house" [[See vol. 9 p. 70]]. A third view was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "sanctified is whoever is in the fire," and he is God, glorified and exalted, meaning Himself, may He be sanctified and exalted. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fire is the light of God, the Mighty and Majestic; God called Musa while he was in the light, and the interpretation of this is that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a great light and thought it was fire, because God appeared to Musa through His signs and His speech from the fire, not that He is located in a direction, "He who is in the heaven is God, and in the earth is God" [[See vol. 16 p. 121]], not that He is contained in them, but He manifests Himself in every act, so that by it the existence of the Doer is known. It was also said in this regard: "blessed is whoever is in the fire," meaning His authority and power. And it was said: "blessed is what is in the fire of the command of God, which He made a sign."

I say: Among what indicates the soundness of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is what Muslim in his Sahih and Ibn Majah in his Sunan related, and the wording is his, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn every creature that His sight reaches." [[Perhaps the feminine pronoun is by way of the lights as "anwar."
(Footnote of Ibn Majah).]] Then Abu 'Ubaydah recited: "that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to God, Lord of the worlds." Al-Bayhaqi also related it. The wording of Muslim from Abu Musa: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood among us and spoke five words, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light, in another narration of Abu Bakr, fire. If He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn whatever of His creation His sight reaches." Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said that the subuhat (glories) are the majesty of His Face, and from it is said: "Subhan Allah" is only glorification and exaltation of Him. His saying "if He were to uncover it" means: if He lifted the veil from their eyes and did not strengthen them to see Him, they would burn and would not be able to bear it. Ibn Jurayj said: the fire is one of the veils, and they are seven veils: the veil of might, the veil of kingdom, the veil of sovereignty, the veil of fire, the veil of light, the veil of cloud, and the veil of water. In truth the created thing is veiled, and God is not veiled by anything. So the fire was light, and He mentioned it by the word "fire" because Musa supposed it to be fire, and the Arabs place one of the two in the place of the other. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fire was indeed the fire itself, and He made him hear His speech from its direction, and manifested His lordship to him from its side. This is as it is related that it is written in the Torah: "God came from Sinai, and shone forth from Se'ir, and was exalted from the mountains of Paran." So His coming from Sinai is His sending Musa from it; His shining from Se'ir is His sending Jesus the Messiah from it; and His being exalted from Paran is His sending Muhammad ﷺ; and Paran is Mecca. In "al-Qasas" there will come, God willing, further explanation of His making him hear His speech from the tree.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: a declaration of God, Lord of the worlds, as far removed from imperfection and as sanctified. It has already been mentioned in more than one place. The meaning: those around it say "and glory be to God," and the verb is omitted. It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, said it when he finished hearing the call, seeking help from God and declaring Him free of imperfection; al-Suddi said this. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Its meaning: "and blessed is whoever glorifies God, the Lord of the worlds," related by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, God, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾: the "hu" (he) is a support pronoun (imad) and not a pronoun referring back, according to the Kufans. The correct view is that it refers to the matter and the affair. ("I am God, the Almighty") the Dominant, having none like Him. "The All-Wise" in His command and His action. It was said: Musa said, "O Lord, who is it that called?" He said to him: "Indeed, it" (that is, I am the one calling you) "I am God."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa thought that God had commanded him to let it go, so he let it go. It was also said: He said this to him only so that Musa would know that the One speaking to him is God, and that Musa is His messenger, and every prophet needs a sign within himself by which he knows his prophethood. In the verse there is an ellipsis: that is, "and throw down your staff," so he threw it from his hand, and it became a snake moving quickly as if it were a jann, which is a small, light snake. Al-Kalbi said: neither small nor large. It was also said: it was first turned into a small snake for him, and when he became at ease with it, it was turned into a large snake. It was also said: it turned at one time into a small snake, and at another into a moving serpent, which is the female, and at another into a thu'ban, which is the large male of snakes. It was also said: the meaning is that it turned into a thu'ban moving like a jann, having the bulk of the thu'ban and the lightness and quickness of the jann, and it is a snake that moves. The plural of jann is jinnan, and from it comes the hadith: "He forbade killing the jinnan which are in houses."

(﴿He turned back fleeing﴾) in fear, according to the habit of humans. (﴿and did not look back﴾): that is, he did not return. Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: he did not turn his head.

(﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾): that is, of the snake and its harm.

(﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾). The sentence is complete, then He made an exception of a disconnected kind, saying: (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾). It was also said: it is an exception from an omitted element, and the meaning is: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have done wrong (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾), then substituted good after evil," for he does not fear, as al-Farra' said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 7–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: An exception (istithna', grammatical exception) from an omitted antecedent is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned. If this were permitted, one could say "Inni la adribu al-qawma illa Zaydan" with the meaning "I do not strike the people, but I strike others, except Zayd." This is the opposite of clarity, and it brings in something whose meaning is not understood.

Al-Farra' also claimed that some grammarians make illa (except) mean waw (and), so that the meaning is "and not those who did wrong." He cited the verse:

"And every brother is parted from his brother, by your father's life, except the two Farqadan (stars)."

Al-Nahhas said: That illa should mean waw has no basis, and it is not permissible in any speech. The meaning of illa is the opposite of waw, because when you say "Your brothers came, except Zayd," you exclude Zayd from what the brothers included, so there is no relation or closeness between them.

There is another view on the verse: that the exception is connected (muttasil), and the meaning is "except those among the messengers who did wrong by committing minor sins from which no one is free." This is with the exception of what is related about Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him), and what Allah the Exalted mentioned about our Prophet (peace be upon him) in His saying: "That Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what follows" (48:2). Al-Mahdawi mentioned this, and al-Nahhas preferred it, and said: Allah knew who among them would disobey, [[The addition is from al-Nahhas's "I'rab al-Quran."]] so He made an exception, saying: "except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil" (27:11), for he fears even though I have forgiven him.

Al-Dahhak said: It means Adam and Dawud (peace be upon them both).

Al-Zamakhshari said: Like what proceeded from Adam, Yunus, Dawud, Sulayman, and the brothers of Yusuf, and from Musa (peace be upon him) in striking the Coptic man.

If someone says: What is the meaning of fear after repentance and forgiveness? It is said to him: This is the way of the scholars of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that they are fearful and anxious about their disobedience. They also do not feel safe that some of the conditions of repentance may remain unfulfilled, so they fear being held accountable for it.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij said: Allah said to Musa, "I made you fear because you killed a soul." Al-Hasan said: The prophets would sin and then be punished.

Al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri, al-Mawardi, and others said: The exception on this view is sound, meaning: except one of the prophets and messengers who wronged himself in a minor sin committed before prophethood. Musa feared because of killing the Copt, and he repented from it. It has also been said that after prophethood they are protected (ma'sum) from minor and major sins. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [[See vol. 1, pp. 308 onward, second and third editions.]]

I say: The first view is more sound, because of their disowning of such things on the Day of Resurrection, as in the hadith of intercession. When one who is close to Allah commits an offense, even if that offense is forgiven, its effect remains. As long as the effect and the suspicion persist, there is fear, not fear of punishment, but fear of the Majesty. The accused before the ruler finds in the accusation a sore spot that leads him to cloud the clarity of trust. Musa (peace be upon him) committed the offense against that Pharaonic man, then he sought forgiveness and acknowledged the wrong against himself, then he was forgiven. Then after forgiveness he said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals" (28:17). Then the next day he was tested with the other Pharaonic man, and he intended to strike him, and this intention became another offense. He was tested the next day because of his saying "I will never be a supporter of the criminals," which is an expression of ability (iqtidar) in the sense of "I will never do." So he was punished through the intention when he wanted to strike and did not do it. Then the Israelite was empowered over him until he revealed his secret, because when the Israelite saw him rolling up his sleeves to strike, he thought he meant him, so he informed on him, and said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" (28:19). The Pharaonic man fled and informed Pharaoh of what the Israelite had revealed about Musa. The killing of the previous day had been kept secret, and no one knew who had killed. When Pharaoh learned of this, he sent to seek Musa in order to kill him, and the search intensified and they seized the main roads. A man came running and said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you" (28:20), and the rest of the verse. So he left as Allah had informed. Thus Musa's fear was only because of this offense. Even though his Lord brought him near, honored him, chose him, and spoke to him, the lingering suspicion went away from him and did not return.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease" (27:12). The discussion of this has already been given in Ta-Ha. [[See vol. 11, p. 191, first or second edition.]]

"Among nine signs" (fi tis'i ayat): Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about it is that the meaning is: this verse is included among nine signs. Al-Mahdawi said: The meaning is "Throw down your staff" and "insert your hand into your bosom," so these are two of the nine signs. Al-Qushayri said its meaning is like your saying "I went out among ten men, and you were one of them," meaning "I went out as the tenth of ten." So fi (among) here means min (from), because of its closeness to it, as you say "Take for me ten of the camels, among them two stallions," meaning "from them." Al-Asma'i, regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who has spent thirty months, in three states, ever be content?" [[In another narration: "Will he ever be content (ya'mun)?"]]

He said fi means min. It has also been said that fi means ma'a (with), so the signs are ten, among them the hand, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the staff, the locusts, the lice, the flood, the blood, the frogs, the years of famine, and the obliteration (tamas) [[Tamas: to remove a thing from its form. Allah turned their wealth and money into stones. See vol. 8, p. 374.]]. The explanation of all of them has already been given.

"To Pharaoh and his people": Al-Farra' said: There is an implied element in the speech, indicated by the context, meaning: you are sent (mab'uth) or dispatched (mursal) to Pharaoh and his people.

"Indeed, they were a people of defiant wickedness" (27:12): meaning they were outside obedience to Allah. This has already been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: "So when Our signs came to them, clear" (27:13): meaning clear and evident. Al-Akhfash said: It may also be mubsara (with the meaning of a verbal noun), as one says "al-walad majbana" (a child is a source of cowardice).

"They said, 'This is obvious magic'" (27:13): They continued in their habit of denial. Therefore He said: "And they rejected them while their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance" (27:14). That is, they were certain that they were from Allah and were not magic, but they disbelieved in them and were too proud to believe in Musa. This shows that they were obstinate. "Zulman" (in wrongdoing) and "uluwwan" (in arrogance) are in the accusative as qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: they rejected them with a rejection that was wrongful and arrogant. The ba' (with) is extra, meaning "they rejected them," as Abu 'Ubayda said.

"So look," O Muhammad, "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (27:14): meaning the final fate of the disbelieving tyrants. Look at that with the eye of your heart and reflect upon it. The address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 7–14 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When Musa said to his family﴾. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "remember." It is as if He said, following His words "And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and All-Knowing": "Take, O Muhammad, from the traces of His wisdom and knowledge the story of Musa, when he said to his family."

(﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾) That is, I saw it from afar. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:
"He perceived a faint sound, and the hunter startled him, at afternoon, when evening had drawn near."
[[Anasat: he sensed. Al-nabʾa: a faint sound.]]

(﴿I will bring you from it news, or bring you a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves﴾) Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-shihabin qabasin" with tanwin on "shihab." The rest read it without tanwin, as an idafa (construct), meaning "with a flame of fire," and this was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Al-Farra' claimed that omitting the tanwin is like the expressions "wa-dar al-akhirah" (and the abode of the Hereafter) and "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque) and "salat al-ula" (the first prayer), where a thing is annexed to itself when its names differ. Al-Nahhas said: the annexation of a thing to itself is impossible according to the Basrans, because the meaning of idafa in language is the joining of one thing to another; it is impossible for a thing to be joined to itself. A thing is annexed to another only so that the meaning of possession or kind may be made clear, and it is impossible for it to be shown to be the possessor of itself or of its own kind. "Shihab qabas" is an idafa of kind and genus, as you say, "this is a garment of silk" and "a ring of iron" and the like. "Shihab" is any bearer of light, such as a star or a lit stick. "Qabas" is the name of what is taken (uqtubisa) from an ember and the like, so the meaning is "a shihab of qabas" (a brand from a flame). It is said: "aqbastu qabsan," and the noun is "qabas," as you say: "qabadtu qabdan," and the noun is "qabd." Whoever reads "bi-shihabin qabasin" makes it a substitute (badal) for it. Al-Mahdawi said: or it is an attribute (sifah) of it, because "qabas" may be a noun that is not an attribute, and it may be an attribute. As for it not being an attribute, it is because they say "qabastuhu aqbasuhu qabsan," and "qabas" means "that which is taken." When it is an attribute, the better is that it be a descriptive (na't). The idafa is better when it is not an attribute, and it is the idafa of kind to its genus, like "a ring of silver" and the like. If it were read with the accusative of "qabas," as a specification (bayan) or a state (hal), it would be better. In other than the Qur'an it is permitted to say "bi-shihabin qabasan," as a verbal noun (masdar), or a specification, or a state. ﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: the original of the "ta'" (t) is "ta'," and it was changed here to "ta'" (t-to-t form) ... [translation note: the original reads "أَصْلُ الطَّاءِ تَاءٌ فَأُبْدِلَ مِنْهَا هُنَا طَاءً" meaning the ta' in "tasṭalūna" is originally "ta'" (ت) that was changed to "ta'" (ط)], because the ta' is emphatic (mutbaqah) and the sad is emphatic, so their combination is good. Its meaning is "they seek warmth from the cold." It is said: "istalā yaṣṭalī" when one seeks warmth. The poet said:
"Fire is the fruit of winter, so whoever wants to eat the fruits in winter, let him seek warmth."
Al-Zajjaj: every white thing that has light is a shihab. Abu 'Ubaydah: the shihab is fire. Abu al-Najm said:
"As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light and then became extinguished."
Ahmad ibn Yahya: the origin of the shihab is a stick with an ember at one end and no fire at the other. The saying of al-Nahhas on it is good: the shihab is a far-reaching ray, and from it comes the star that extends its light in the sky. The poet said:
"In his hand is a straight spear, well-shaped, in which is a point like the flame of a brand."
[[al-sa'dah: a spear-shaft that grows straight.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when Musa came to the one he thought was fire while it was light. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. When Musa saw the fire he stood near it, and he saw it coming out of the branch of a green tree, very intensely green, called al-'Ulayq. The fire does not increase except in size and blaze, and the tree does not increase except in greenness and beauty. He was amazed by it and reached toward it with a bundle of sticks in his hand to take a brand from it, but it inclined toward him, so he feared it and drew back. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, until its matter became clear: that it was commanded and he did not know who had commanded it, until "he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it." This meaning has already passed in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11 p. 172 onward and p. 113]].

(﴿was called﴾) That is, God called him, as He said: "And We called him from the right side of the mount."

(﴿that blessed﴾) Al-Zajjaj said: "anna" is in the place of the accusative, meaning "that it was blessed." He said: it may also be in the place of the nominative, making it the subject of what has no named agent. Abu Hatim related that in the reading of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid it is "that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it." Al-Nahhas said: the like of this is not found with a sound chain, and even if it were sound it would be explanatory, so the blessing returns to the fire and to those around it, the angels and Musa. Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah" and "barak Allah fika." Al-Tha'labi: the Arabs say "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak Allah 'alayka," and "barak Allah laka," four dialects. The poet said:
"So you were blessed as a newborn, and blessed as a growing youth, and blessed in gray hair when you became white-haired."
Al-Tabari: He said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and did not say "blessed is in the fire" according to the dialect of one who says "barakaka Allah." It is said "barakahu Allah," "barak lahu," "barak 'alayhi," and "barak fihi," with the same meaning, that is, blessing was upon whoever was in the fire, namely Musa, or upon whoever was near the fire, not that he was in its middle. Al-Suddi said: there were angels in the fire, so the blessing returns to Musa and the angels, that is, "blessed are you, O Musa, and the angels who are around it." This is a greeting from God to Musa and an honouring of him, just as He greeted Abraham through the tongues of the angels when they entered upon him, saying: "The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house" [[See vol. 9 p. 70]]. A third view was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "sanctified is whoever is in the fire," and he is God, glorified and exalted, meaning Himself, may He be sanctified and exalted. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the fire is the light of God, the Mighty and Majestic; God called Musa while he was in the light, and the interpretation of this is that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a great light and thought it was fire, because God appeared to Musa through His signs and His speech from the fire, not that He is located in a direction, "He who is in the heaven is God, and in the earth is God" [[See vol. 16 p. 121]], not that He is contained in them, but He manifests Himself in every act, so that by it the existence of the Doer is known. It was also said in this regard: "blessed is whoever is in the fire," meaning His authority and power. And it was said: "blessed is what is in the fire of the command of God, which He made a sign."

I say: Among what indicates the soundness of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas is what Muslim in his Sahih and Ibn Majah in his Sunan related, and the wording is his, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn every creature that His sight reaches." [[Perhaps the feminine pronoun is by way of the lights as "anwar."
(Footnote of Ibn Majah).]] Then Abu 'Ubaydah recited: "that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to God, Lord of the worlds." Al-Bayhaqi also related it. The wording of Muslim from Abu Musa: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood among us and spoke five words, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light, in another narration of Abu Bakr, fire. If He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn whatever of His creation His sight reaches." Abu 'Ubayd said: it is said that the subuhat (glories) are the majesty of His Face, and from it is said: "Subhan Allah" is only glorification and exaltation of Him. His saying "if He were to uncover it" means: if He lifted the veil from their eyes and did not strengthen them to see Him, they would burn and would not be able to bear it. Ibn Jurayj said: the fire is one of the veils, and they are seven veils: the veil of might, the veil of kingdom, the veil of sovereignty, the veil of fire, the veil of light, the veil of cloud, and the veil of water. In truth the created thing is veiled, and God is not veiled by anything. So the fire was light, and He mentioned it by the word "fire" because Musa supposed it to be fire, and the Arabs place one of the two in the place of the other. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fire was indeed the fire itself, and He made him hear His speech from its direction, and manifested His lordship to him from its side. This is as it is related that it is written in the Torah: "God came from Sinai, and shone forth from Se'ir, and was exalted from the mountains of Paran." So His coming from Sinai is His sending Musa from it; His shining from Se'ir is His sending Jesus the Messiah from it; and His being exalted from Paran is His sending Muhammad ﷺ; and Paran is Mecca. In "al-Qasas" there will come, God willing, further explanation of His making him hear His speech from the tree.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: a declaration of God, Lord of the worlds, as far removed from imperfection and as sanctified. It has already been mentioned in more than one place. The meaning: those around it say "and glory be to God," and the verb is omitted. It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, said it when he finished hearing the call, seeking help from God and declaring Him free of imperfection; al-Suddi said this. It was also said: it is from the speech of God, the Exalted. Its meaning: "and blessed is whoever glorifies God, the Lord of the worlds," related by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, God, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾: the "hu" (he) is a support pronoun (imad) and not a pronoun referring back, according to the Kufans. The correct view is that it refers to the matter and the affair. ("I am God, the Almighty") the Dominant, having none like Him. "The All-Wise" in His command and His action. It was said: Musa said, "O Lord, who is it that called?" He said to him: "Indeed, it" (that is, I am the one calling you) "I am God."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Musa thought that God had commanded him to let it go, so he let it go. It was also said: He said this to him only so that Musa would know that the One speaking to him is God, and that Musa is His messenger, and every prophet needs a sign within himself by which he knows his prophethood. In the verse there is an ellipsis: that is, "and throw down your staff," so he threw it from his hand, and it became a snake moving quickly as if it were a jann, which is a small, light snake. Al-Kalbi said: neither small nor large. It was also said: it was first turned into a small snake for him, and when he became at ease with it, it was turned into a large snake. It was also said: it turned at one time into a small snake, and at another into a moving serpent, which is the female, and at another into a thu'ban, which is the large male of snakes. It was also said: the meaning is that it turned into a thu'ban moving like a jann, having the bulk of the thu'ban and the lightness and quickness of the jann, and it is a snake that moves. The plural of jann is jinnan, and from it comes the hadith: "He forbade killing the jinnan which are in houses."

(﴿He turned back fleeing﴾) in fear, according to the habit of humans. (﴿and did not look back﴾): that is, he did not return. Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: he did not turn his head.

(﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾): that is, of the snake and its harm.

(﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾). The sentence is complete, then He made an exception of a disconnected kind, saying: (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾). It was also said: it is an exception from an omitted element, and the meaning is: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have done wrong (﴿except one who has done wrong﴾), then substituted good after evil," for he does not fear, as al-Farra' said.
