So he was punished through the intention when he wanted to strike and did not do it. Then the Israelite was empowered over him until he revealed his secret, because when the Israelite saw him rolling up his sleeves to strike, he thought he meant him, so he informed on him, and said: "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" (28:19). The Pharaonic man fled and informed Pharaoh of what the Israelite had revealed about Musa. The killing of the previous day had been kept secret, and no one knew who had killed. When Pharaoh learned of this, he sent to seek Musa in order to kill him, and the search intensified and they seized the main roads. A man came running and said: "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you" (28:20), and the rest of the verse. So he left as Allah had informed. Thus Musa's fear was only because of this offense. Even though his Lord brought him near, honored him, chose him, and spoke to him, the lingering suspicion went away from him and did not return.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease" (27:12). The discussion of this has already been given in Ta-Ha. [[See vol. 11, p. 191, first or second edition.]]

"Among nine signs" (fi tis'i ayat): Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about it is that the meaning is: this verse is included among nine signs. Al-Mahdawi said: The meaning is "Throw down your staff" and "insert your hand into your bosom," so these are two of the nine signs. Al-Qushayri said its meaning is like your saying "I went out among ten men, and you were one of them," meaning "I went out as the tenth of ten." So fi (among) here means min (from), because of its closeness to it, as you say "Take for me ten of the camels, among them two stallions," meaning "from them." Al-Asma'i, regarding the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Will he who has spent thirty months, in three states, ever be content?" [[In another narration: "Will he ever be content (ya'mun)?"]]

He said fi means min. It has also been said that fi means ma'a (with), so the signs are ten, among them the hand, and the nine are: the splitting (of the sea), the staff, the locusts, the lice, the flood, the blood, the frogs, the years of famine, and the obliteration (tamas) [[Tamas: to remove a thing from its form. Allah turned their wealth and money into stones. See vol. 8, p. 374.]]. The explanation of all of them has already been given.

"To Pharaoh and his people": Al-Farra' said: There is an implied element in the speech, indicated by the context, meaning: you are sent (mab'uth) or dispatched (mursal) to Pharaoh and his people.

"Indeed, they were a people of defiant wickedness" (27:12): meaning they were outside obedience to Allah. This has already been mentioned.

His saying, may He be exalted: "So when Our signs came to them, clear" (27:13): meaning clear and evident. Al-Akhfash said: It may also be mubsara (with the meaning of a verbal noun), as one says "al-walad majbana" (a child is a source of cowardice).

"They said, 'This is obvious magic'" (27:13): They continued in their habit of denial. Therefore He said: "And they rejected them while their souls were convinced of them, in wrongdoing and arrogance" (27:14). That is, they were certain that they were from Allah and were not magic, but they disbelieved in them and were too proud to believe in Musa. This shows that they were obstinate. "Zulman" (in wrongdoing) and "uluwwan" (in arrogance) are in the accusative as qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: they rejected them with a rejection that was wrongful and arrogant. The ba' (with) is extra, meaning "they rejected them," as Abu 'Ubayda said.

"So look," O Muhammad, "how was the outcome of the corrupters" (27:14): meaning the final fate of the disbelieving tyrants. Look at that with the eye of your heart and reflect upon it. The address is to him, but the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 15–16:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾. That is, understanding (fahman), as Qatadah said. It was also said: knowledge of the religion (al-din), of judgment (al-hukm) and other things, as He said: "And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail (labus) for you." It was also said: the craft of alchemy (al-kimiya'), but this is an anomalous (shadh) view. What God gave them both was prophethood, vicegerency (khilafah) on earth, and the Psalms (al-Zabur).

"And they said: Praise be to God, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants." In the verse is evidence of the nobility of knowledge, the elevation of its status, the precedence of its bearers and its people, that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings and most abundant portions, and that whoever is given it has been given excellence over many of God's believing servants. ﴿God will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees﴾. This has been mentioned earlier in more than one place.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud. He said: O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of everything﴾. Al-Kalbi said: Dawud had nineteen sons, and Sulayman inherited from among them his prophethood and his kingship. Had it been an inheritance of wealth, all his children would have shared it equally. Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it had been an inheritance of wealth, it would have been divided according to the number of heirs. God therefore singled out Sulayman with what Dawud had of wisdom and prophethood, and increased him from His bounty with a kingship that is not fitting for anyone after him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Dawud was from the Children of Israel and was a king, and Sulayman inherited his kingship and his station of prophethood, meaning that this passed to him after his father's death, so it was called inheritance figuratively. This is like the saying: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." His, peace be upon him, saying "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance" may mean that this is the practice and custom of the prophets, even though some of them did leave their property to heirs, such as Zakariyya according to the most well-known views concerning him. This is like when you say: "We, the company of Muslims, are only occupied with worship," meaning that this is the practice of most of them. From this is what Sibawayh related: "We, the company of Arabs, are the most generous of people to a guest." I say: this meaning has been mentioned earlier in the commentary on Maryam [see vol. 11, p. 81 ff., first or second edition], and the correct view is the first one, because of his, peace be upon him, saying: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance." It is general, and nothing is excluded from it except by evidence.

Muqatil said: Sulayman had a greater kingdom than Dawud and was a better judge than him, while Dawud was more intensive in worship than Sulayman. Another said: No prophet reached what his kingdom reached, for God, glory be to Him, subjected to him humans, jinn, birds and beasts, and gave him what He had not given anyone in the worlds. He inherited his father's kingship and prophethood, and after him he upheld his law (shari'ah). Every prophet who came after Musa, whether sent or not, was following the law of Musa, until the Messiah, peace be upon him, came and abrogated it. Between Sulayman and the Hijrah there are about eighteen hundred years. The Jews say one thousand three hundred and sixty-two years. It was also said: between his death and the birth of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is about one thousand seven hundred years, and the Jews subtract three hundred years from this. He lived somewhat over fifty years.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And he said: O people﴾. That is, Sulayman said to the Children of Israel, out of gratitude for God's blessings: "We have been taught the speech of birds," meaning God favoured us, in addition to what we inherited from Dawud of knowledge, prophethood and vicegerency on earth, by making us understand from the voices of birds the meanings that are in their souls. Muqatil said concerning the verse: Sulayman was sitting one day when a bird flew past him. He said to his companions: Do you know what this bird is saying? It said to me: "Peace be upon you, O king who has been given authority and prophet to the Children of Israel! May God give you honour and make you prevail over your enemy. I am going to my chicks and will pass by you again." Then it returned, and he said: It says: "Peace be upon you, O king who has been given authority. If you would permit me, I will gather food for my chicks until they grow up, then I will come to you, and then do with me what you wish." Sulayman informed them of what it had said, and he gave it permission, and it departed.

Farqad al-Sabakhi said: Sulayman passed by a nightingale (bulbul) on a tree, moving its head and wagging its tail. He said to his companions: Do you know what this nightingale is saying? They said: No, O Prophet of God. He said: It is saying: "I have eaten half a fruit, so the world is worth nothing." He passed by a hoopoe (hudhud) on a tree, and a boy had set a snare for it. Sulayman said to it: Beware, O hoopoe! It said: O Prophet of God, this is a boy who has no sense, so I will mock him. Then Sulayman returned and found it had fallen into the boy's snare, and the boy was holding it. He said: Hoopoe, what is this? It said: I did not see it until I fell into it, O Prophet of God. He said: Woe to you! You can see water beneath the earth, but you cannot see the trap! It said: O Prophet of God, when destiny descends, sight goes blind.

Ka'b said: A turtle-dove (warshan) called near Sulayman son of Dawud, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Give birth for death, and build for ruin." A ringdove (fakhitah) called, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Would that these creatures had not been created, and that, having been created, they had known for what purpose they were created." A peacock (tawus) called near him, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "As you judge, so you will be judged." A hoopoe called near him, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy." A sawfly or owl (surad) called near him, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Seek forgiveness from God, O sinners." That is why the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade killing it. It was also said that the surad is the one who guided Adam to the site of the House (the Ka'bah), and that it was the first to fast, and for this reason the surad is called "the fasting one" (al-sawwam), as related from Abu Hurayrah. A tit-lark (tit-tawa) called near him, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Every living thing will die, and every new thing will wear out." A swallow (khuttafah) called near him, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Send forward good, and you will find it." That is why the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade killing it. It was also said: Adam went out of Paradise and complained to God of loneliness, so God made him at ease with the swallow and bound it to houses, so it does not leave the children of Adam, for their comfort. He said: With it are four verses of the Book of God, mighty and majestic: "Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it..." up to the end, and it prolongs its voice at the words "the Mighty, the Wise."

A dove (hadarat hamamah) cooed near Sulayman, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, in number equal to all that is in His heavens and His earth." A ring-dove (qumri) called near Sulayman, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Great, the Guardian." Ka'b said: Sulayman conversed with them, and the crow said: "O God, curse the tax collector." The kite said: "Everything is perishing except His Face." The sand-grouse (qata) said: Whoever keeps silent is safe. The parrot said: Woe to him whose concern is the world. The frog said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Holy." The falcon said: "Glory be to my Lord and praise be to Him." The crab said: "Glory be to the One who is mentioned in every tongue, in every place."

Makhul said: A partridge (durraj) called near Sulayman, and he said: Do you know what it says? They said: No. He said: It says: "The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne." Al-Hasan said: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "When the rooster crows, it says: Remember God, O heedless ones." Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "When the vulture (nasr) cries out, it says: O son of Adam, live as you wish, for your end is death. When the eagle ('uqab) cries out, it says: Far from people is rest. When the lark (qunbar) cries out, it says: My God, curse those who hate the family of Muhammad. When the swallow (khuttaf) cries out, it recites: 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds' to the end, and it says: 'nor of those who go astray,' and it prolongs its voice with it as the reciter prolongs his."

Qatadah and al-Sha'bi said: This matter applies to birds only, based on His saying: "We have been taught the speech of birds." The ant (namlah) is a flying creature since it may have wings. Al-Sha'bi said: Likewise, this particular ant had two wings. Another group said: It applies to all animals, and He mentioned birds only because they were among Sulayman's troops, which he needed for shading from the sun and for dispatching on errands, so they were singled out for mention because of their frequent involvement, and because the affairs of other animals are rare and do not recur as often as those of birds. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: Speech (mantiq) may apply to what is understood without words, and God, mighty and majestic, knows best what He intended. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Whoever says that he knew only the speech of birds has greatly diminished his status, for people agree that he understood the speech of one who does not speak, and that speech was created for him from plants. Every plant would say to him: I am the tree of such-and-such, more beneficial than such-and-such and more harmful than such-and-such. So what do you suppose about animals?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 17:

There are two issues here.

The first concerns His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [his] hosts were gathered together for Solomon﴾. "Ḥushira" means was gathered together, and al-ḥashr (gathering) means assembling. From it is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: "And We gathered them together, and left none of them behind" (Qur'an 18:47). People differed concerning the size of the army of Solomon, peace be upon him. It is said that his encampment was a hundred farsakh by a hundred: twenty-five (farsakh) for the jinn, twenty-five for mankind, twenty-five for the birds, and twenty-five for the wild beasts. He had a thousand tents of glass upon wooden supports, in which were three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The reports about his encampment and the size of his army differ greatly, but the sound view is that his kingdom was vast, filling the earth, and that the entire inhabited world submitted to him.

"Fa-hum yuza'un" means: their first is driven back to their last, and they are held in check. Qatada said: each category had its wardens (wazaʿa) in their ranks and positions, from the seat (kursi) and from the earth when they walked upon it. It is said: "waza'tuhu, awza'uhu, wazʿan," meaning I restrained him. The wazi' (warden) in war is the one appointed over the ranks, who holds back those among them who advance.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ halted at Dhi Tuwa, meaning on the Day of Conquest, Abu Quhafa, whose sight had failed him by that day, said to his daughter: "Raise me up to Abu Qubays." She said: So I raised him up to it, and he said: "What do you see?" She said: "I see a dense black mass." He said: "Those are the horses." She said: "And I see a man from the mass coming and going." He said: "That is the warden, preventing them from spreading out." And he mentioned the rest of the report.

From this meaning is his saying, peace be upon him: "The Shaytan was never seen on any day more humiliated, more expelled, more despised, or more enraged than on the Day of 'Arafa. This is only because of what he sees of the descent of mercy and Allah's pardon of the great sins; except what he saw on the Day of Badr." It was said: "And what did he see, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Indeed he saw Jibril restraining the angels (yazaʿu al-malaʾika)." Recorded by al-Muwatta'.

In this same sense is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"When I rebuked grey hair for youth, and said: 'Enough, let me be sober, though whiteness is a restrainer.'"

Another:

"When we met, tears flowed from our eyelids; we restrained their flow with our fingers."

Another:

"None restrains the stubborn self from desire among people except one of full intellect and perfect character."

It is also said that it is from tawzi' in the sense of dispersing, and "al-qawm awza'" means groups. In the story: the devils wove for him a carpet of silk, a farsakh by a farsakh, of gold in silk. A golden throne was placed for him, and around him were three thousand thrones of gold and silver; the prophets sat on the golden thrones, and the scholars on the silver thrones.

The second issue: The verse is evidence for the appointment by the imam and the rulers of wardens who restrain the people and prevent some of them from oppressing others, since rulers cannot do that by themselves. Ibn 'Awn said: I heard al-Hasan say, while he was in his judicial session and saw what people were doing: "By Allah, nothing reforms these people except wardens." Al-Hasan also said: "People must have a warden (wazi'), that is, an authority (sultan) that restrains them." Ibn al-Qasim mentioned, saying: Malik narrated to us that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan used to say: "The imam restrains more than the Qur'an restrains," meaning of people. Ibn al-Qasim said: I said to Malik: "What is yazi'?" He said: "It restrains." Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: Some people have misunderstood the intended meaning of this statement, and thought that it means the power of the ruler deters people more than the limits (hudud) of the Qur'an deter them. This is ignorance of Allah and His wisdom. He said: Allah only established the hudud as a general and comprehensive public good, standing for the sustenance of creation, with nothing to add to them and nothing lacking in them, and nothing else suffices. But the oppressors have abused them, fallen short of them, and carried them out without good intention, not seeking the face of Allah in judging by them. So creation was not deterred by them. Had they ruled with justice and made their intention sincere, affairs would have been set right and the public would have been well.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 18–19 (part 1 of 2)**

There are six issues (masa'il) in this passage.

**The first issue:** His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾. Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that it was a valley in the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria)." Ka'b said: "It was at al-Ta'if."

(﴿The ant said, "O ants﴾)... al-Sha'bi said: "The ant had two wings, so she became one of the birds, and for this reason he (Sulayman) knew her speech. Had it not been so, he would not have known it. This has passed and will come again." Sulayman al-Taymi recited in Makkah "namlatun" and "al-namlu" with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the mim. It is also reported from him that both were read with a damma. The ant (namlah) was named so because of her tanammul, which is the abundance of her movement and the scarcity of her rest.

Ka'b said: "Sulayman, peace be upon him, passed by the valley of al-Sadir, one of the valleys of al-Ta'if, and came upon the valley of the ants. An ant stood up walking, and she was lame, waddling like a wolf in size, and she called out, 'O ants,' (the verse)..."

al-Zamakhshari said: "Sulayman heard her speech from three miles away. She was walking lame, waddling." It was said: "Her name was Tahiyah."

al-Suhayli said: "They mentioned the name of the ant that spoke to Sulayman, peace be upon him, and they said her name was Harmiya. I do not know how an ant can have a proper name, since ants do not name one another, and human beings cannot give a proper name to any one of them, because they are not distinguished from one another for humans. Nor are they under human ownership like horses, dogs and the like, for proper naming is found among the Arabs in such cases."

If it is said: "Proper naming is found in generic names, such as Tha'alah, Usamah, Ja'ar and Qatham for the hyena, and many similar examples, so the name of the ant is not different from these," the reply is that they claim it is a proper name for one specific ant among all the ants, whereas Tha'alah and the like are not restricted to one individual of the species. Rather, every individual of that species that you see is a Tha'alah. Likewise Usamah, Ibn Awa, Ibn 'Irs and what resembles them.

If what they said is correct, it has a justification: that this speaking ant was named by this name in the Torah, or in the Psalms, or in some of the scriptures, which God, exalted is He, named by this name, and made it known to the prophets before Sulayman, or to some of them. She was singled out for naming because of her speech and her faith. This is one justification.

The meaning of our statement "by her faith" is that she said to the ants: (﴿Let not Sulayman and his hosts crush you, while they do not perceive﴾). Her saying "while they do not perceive" is a considerate, believing remark, meaning that from the justice and virtue of Sulayman and the virtue of his hosts, they would not crush an ant or anything larger except without perceiving it.

It has been said that Sulayman's smile was joy at this word from her. For this reason he emphasized the smiling with His saying "laughing" (ḍāḥikan), since a smile may occur without laughter and without approval. Do you not see that they say: "He smiled the smile of an angry man," and "He smiled the smile of those who mock"? The smile of laughter is only from joy, and a prophet is not made joyful by a worldly matter; he is only made joyful by matters of the Hereafter and the religion. Her saying "while they do not perceive" points to religion, justice and compassion.

The parallel to the ant's words about Sulayman's hosts, "while they do not perceive," is God's saying about the hosts of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Then harm would befall you from them without knowledge﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 28.]], in consideration that they do not intend to shed the blood of a believer. Except that the one who praised the hosts of Sulayman was the ant, by God's permission, whereas the one who praised the hosts of Muhammad (ﷺ) is God, Mighty and Majestic, Himself, because of the excellence of the hosts of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the hosts of the other prophets, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) has excellence over all the prophets, may God's blessings and peace be upon them all.

Shahr ibn Hawshab recited "maskanakum" with a sukun on the sin, in the singular. In the Mushaf of Ubayy it reads "masakinakunna la yahtiminnakum." Sulayman al-Taymi recited "masakinakum la yahtiminnakunna," as mentioned by al-Nahhas, meaning: "Let them not break you by their trampling upon you, while they do not know of you." al-Mahdawi said: "God made the ant understand this so that it would be a miracle (mu'jizah) for Sulayman."

Wahb said: "God commanded the wind that no one should speak a word except that it would throw it into the hearing of Sulayman, because the devils intended to plot against him."

It has been said that this valley was in the land of Yemen, and that the ant was a small ant like the common ants. This was said by al-Kalbi. Nawf al-Shami and Shaqiq ibn Salamah said: "The ants of that valley were in the form of wolves in size." Buraydah al-Aslami said: "They were in the form of sheep."

Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Tirmidhi said: "If they were in this shape, then they have a voice. The voice of ants is only unnoticed because of the smallness of their bodies. Otherwise, voices exist in birds and beasts, and that is their speech. In those speeches there are meanings of glorification (tasbih) and other things, as in His saying: ﴿There is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 266 onward.]]."

I say: Her saying "let them not crush you" indicates the soundness of al-Kalbi's statement, for if they were in the form of wolves and sheep, they would not be crushed by trampling. And God knows best.

And she said: "Enter your dwellings," so the address came in the form of addressing human beings, because the ants here were treated as human beings when they spoke, as human beings speak.

Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi said: "I saw in some books that Sulayman said to her: 'Why did you warn the ants? Did you fear my injustice? Do you not know that I am a just prophet? Why did you say: "Let Sulayman and his hosts crush you"?' The ant said: 'Did you not hear my saying "while they do not perceive"? I did not intend the crushing of souls, but only the crushing of hearts, for fear that they would wish for what you have been given, or be tempted by the world, and be occupied with looking at your kingdom instead of glorification and remembrance.'

Sulayman said to her: 'Advise me.' She said: 'Do you know why your father was named Dawud?' He said: 'No.' She said: 'Because he healed the wound of his heart. Do you know why you were named Sulayman?' He said: 'No.' She said: 'Because you are sound (salim) in your inner side, for what you have been given, through the soundness of your breast. You have the right to join your father.' [[The wording in al-Tha'labi's "Qisas al-Anbiya'" is: "She said: 'Because you are sound (salim), you inclined to what you were given by the soundness of your breast, and you have the right to join your father David.'"]]"

Then she said: "Do you know why God subjected the wind to you?" He said: "No." She said: "He informed you that the whole world is wind."

(﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾) — marvelling. Then she hurried away to her people and said: "Do you have anything we can present to the Prophet of God?" They said: "What is the worth of what we could give him! By God, we have only one jujube (nabqah)." She said: "Good, bring it to me." They brought it to her, and she carried it in her mouth and set off dragging it. Then God commanded the wind, and it carried her, and she came cutting across humankind, jinn, scholars and prophets on the carpet, until she fell before him. Then she placed that jujube from her mouth into his palm, and began to recite:

*Do you not see that we present to God what is His?*
*Though He is self-sufficient, He accepts it.*
*Had He been presented with gifts proportionate to His majesty,*
*The sea and its shore would have fallen short of it one day.*
*But we present to the One whom we love,*
*So that He is pleased with it from us, and its giver is thanked.*
*That is only from the noble nature of His deeds,*
*For otherwise there is nothing in our kingdom that resembles it.*

He said to her: "May God bless you. For by that gift, they are the most thankful of God's creatures and the most numerous of God's creatures."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing four creatures: the hoopoe (hudhud), the screech owl (surad), the ant (namlah) and the bee (nahlah)." Abu Dawud recorded it, and Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq authenticated it, and it has been narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. It has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 270, first or second edition.]].

So the ant praised Sulayman and informed him, in the best way she could, that they would not crush you unknowingly, and that they would not do so deliberately. Thus she negated injustice from them. For this reason the killing of ants is forbidden, and the killing of the hoopoe, because it was Sulayman's guide to water and his messenger to Bilqis.

'Ikrimah said: "God only turned the evil of Sulayman away from the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents."

The screech owl (surad) is called al-Sawwam (the fasting one). It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The first to fast was the surad. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, left al-Sham for the Haram to build the House, al-Sakinah [[al-Sakinah: a cloud, as in the story. In the hadith of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, al-Sakinah is a wind that passes quickly. This is not clear.]] was with him, and the surad. The surad was his guide to the place, and al-Sakinah was its measure. When he reached the spot, al-Sakinah settled on the site of the House and called out: 'Build, O Ibrahim, according to the measure of my shadow.'"

The reason for the prohibition on killing the frog has passed in "al-A'raf," and in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 134, first or second edition.]] the prohibition on killing the bee. And praise be to God.

**The second issue:** Al-Hasan recited "lā yaḥaṭṭimannakum" (let them not crush you). He is also reported to have recited "lā yiḥaṭṭimannakum," and, from Abu Raja', "lā yuḥaṭṭimannakum." Al-ḥaṭm means breaking. One says ḥaṭamtuhu ḥaṭman, meaning I broke it, and it becomes taḥaṭṭama (it was broken). Al-taḥṭīm means breaking into pieces. The phrase "wa-hum lā yash'urūn" ("while they are unaware") may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to Solomon and his troops, with the verb governing the circumstance being "yaḥṭimannakum." It may also be a circumstantial clause referring to the ant, with the governing verb being "qālat," meaning she said this while the troops were heedless, just as you would say, "I stood up while the people were heedless." It may also be a circumstantial clause referring to the ants, again with "qālat" as the governing verb, meaning that the ants do not perceive that Solomon understands her speech. This interpretation is distant, and it will be discussed later.

**The third issue:** Muslim narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "An ant bit a prophet of the prophets, so he ordered the ants' settlement to be burned. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, you destroyed a community of the communities that glorify God?'" In another version: "Why not one ant?"

Our scholars said: It is said that this prophet was Moses (peace be upon him), and that he said: "My Lord, will You punish the people of a town for their sins when among them are the obedient?" It seems that God wished to show him this from Himself. So He made the heat afflict him until he took refuge under a tree, seeking relief in its shade, and beside it was an ant settlement. Sleep overcame him, and when he found the pleasure of sleep, an ant bit him and disturbed him. So he crushed them with his foot and destroyed them, and he burned that tree beside which were their dwellings. God then showed him the lesson in that as a sign: "When one ant bit you, how did you afflict the rest with its punishment!" It intends to alert him that punishment from God, exalted is He, is general; it becomes mercy for the obedient, purity and blessing, and evil and retribution for the disobedient.

On this basis, there is nothing in the hadith indicating disapproval or prohibition of killing ants. Whoever harms you, it is lawful for you to repel him from yourself. No creature of God is greater in sanctity than the believer, and you are permitted to repel him from yourself by killing or striking in proportion. How much more so with insects and creeping creatures that have been subjected to you and placed under your power. If one harms you, it is lawful for you to kill it. Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) was reported to have said: "Whatever ant harms you, kill it."

His saying "Why not one ant?" is evidence that whoever harms is harmed and may be killed. Whenever killing is for a benefit or for repelling harm, there is no harm in it according to the scholars. He spoke of "an ant" in general and did not specify the ant that bit him from others, because the intent was not retaliation. For if retaliation were intended, he would have said, "Why not your ant that bit you?" Instead he said, "Why not an ant in place of an ant?" So it included the innocent and the guilty alike. This was to make him aware that he had asked his Lord to punish a people among whom were both the obedient and the disobedient.

It has also been said: For this prophet, punishing animals by burning was permissible in his law (shar', the revealed law). Therefore God only rebuked him for burning a large number of ants, not for the act of burning itself. Do you not see His saying, "Why not one ant?" That is, why did you not burn only one ant? This differs from our law (shari'ah), for the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited punishing with fire, and he said: "No one punishes with fire except God." Likewise, killing ants was permissible in the law of that prophet, for God did not rebuke him for the act of killing ants in principle. As for our law, the prohibition has come in the hadiths of Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah. Malik disliked killing ants, except when they cause harm and cannot be repelled except by killing.

It has also been said: God rebuked this prophet because he took revenge on his own behalf by destroying a multitude that had harmed him, one individual. The better course would have been patience and forgiveness. But it occurred to the prophet that this kind of creature harms the children of Adam, and the sanctity of the children of Adam is greater than the sanctity of other non-speaking animals. Had this consideration stood alone, without being combined with personal satisfaction of the self (tashaffī ṭab'ī), he would not have been rebuked. But when personal satisfaction was added to it, as the context of the hadith indicates, he was rebuked for it. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, "Are you destroying a community of the communities that glorify God because an ant bit you?" implies that this glorification is by speech and utterance, just as God informed us that the ants have a manner of speech, which Solomon (peace be upon him) understood, and that was a miracle for him, and he smiled at her words. This clearly indicates that ants have speech and utterance, but not everyone hears it. Rather, it is heard by whoever God wills among those to whom He breaks habit, be they prophets or saints. We do not deny this on the ground that we do not hear it, for failure to perceive does not necessitate the non-existence of what is perceived in itself. Furthermore, a person finds speech and discourse within himself, and it is not heard from him unless he speaks with his tongue. God broke the habit for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and let him hear the speech of the soul from people who spoke to themselves, and he informed them of what was in their souls. Many of our imams have transmitted this in books on the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ). Likewise, this happened to many whom God honored among the saints, in more than one instance. It was of this that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke when he said: "Among my community there are inspired ones (muḥaddathūn), and ʿUmar is among them." This meaning has already been discussed under the glorification of inanimate things in the commentary on Surah al-Isra' (Subḥān). It is glorification by tongue and speech, not glorification by indication of state. And praise be to God.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: "So he smiled, laughing at her speech." Ibn al-Sumayqa' recited "ḍaḥikan" without the alif, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) governed by a deleted verb that is indicated by "tabassama." It is as if he said, "He laughed a laugh." This is the position of Sibawayh. According to others than Sibawayh, it is in the accusative by the same word "fatabassama," because it carries the meaning of "ḍaḥika" (he laughed). The one who recited "ḍāḥikan" makes it an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "tabassama." The meaning is that he smiled to the extent of laughing, because laughing encompasses smiling, while smiling is less than laughing and is its beginning. It is said: basama (with a fatḥah) yabsimu basman, so he is bāsim, and ibtasama and tabassama. Al-mabsim means the mouth or teeth, like al-majlis from jalasa yajlisu. A man who smiles much is mibsām or bassām. Thus smiling is the beginning of laughing, and laughing refers to both the beginning and the end. However, laughing implies more than smiling. When it increases and a person cannot control himself, it is called qahqahah (loud laughter). Smiling is the laughter of the prophets (peace be upon them) in most of their affairs.

It is recorded in the Sahih, from Jabir ibn Samurah, when he was asked, "Did you sit with the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes, often. He would not rise from his prayer place where he prayed the dawn prayer, or the morning, until the sun rose. When it rose, he would stand up. They would talk and discuss matters of the Jahiliyyah, and they would laugh and smile." Also in it, from Sa'd, who said: "A man of the polytheists had inflicted much harm on the Muslims," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Shoot, may my father and mother be your ransom." Sa'd said: "I drew an arrow for him without an iron head and struck his side. He fell, and his private part was uncovered. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed until I saw his molars." [Note: "Inflicted much harm" means he had overwhelmed them and acted among them as fire does. From the margin of Muslim.]

He (peace be upon him) was smiling in most of his circumstances. He also laughed in other circumstances, a laugh higher than smiling and less than the complete laughter in which the uvula is visible. Rarely, when his astonishment was extreme, he might laugh until his molars showed. The scholars disliked excessive laughter from him, as Luqman said to his son: "My son, beware of excessive laughter, for it kills the heart." It has been transmitted as a saying traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) from the hadith of Abu Dharr and others. The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed when Sa'd shot the man and struck him. That was only joy at hitting the target, not at the uncovering of the man's private part, for he (ﷺ) is far above such things.

**The sixth issue:** There is no disagreement among the scholars that all animals have understanding and intellect. Al-Shafi'i said: "The pigeon is the most intelligent of birds." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The ant is a clever, strong, and very perceptive creature. It stores provisions, makes granaries, splits grain into two halves so that it will not sprout, and splits coriander into four pieces, because when it is split in two it would sprout. It eats half of what it gathered in its year and keeps the rest for future use." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "These are special kinds of knowledge with us, and the ant has attained them by God's creation of this for it." Al-Ustadh Abu al-Muzaffar Shahpur al-Isfara'ini said: "It is not unlikely that animals perceive the origination of the world, the origination of created things, and the oneness of God. But we do not understand them, and they do not understand us. As for our pursuit of them while they flee from us, that is due to the rule of kind."

**His, exalted is He, saying:** "And he said, 'My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and my parents.'" Here "an" is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah). "Awza'nī" means "inspire me with that." It derives from wazi'a, as if he said: "Restrain me from what displeases You." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "The People of the Book claim that Solomon's mother was the wife of Uriah, whom God tested David with, or that after her husband's death David married her, and she bore him Solomon (peace be upon him)." More explanation of this will come in Surah Sad, God willing, in the commentary on His saying: "And David thought that We had only tested him" (verse 24 of the mentioned surah).

"And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants." That is, along with Your servants, according to Ibn Zayd. It has also been said: the meaning is "within the category of Your righteous servants."

*Do you not see that we present to God what is His?*
*Though He is self-sufficient, He accepts it.*
*Had He been presented with gifts proportionate to His majesty,*
*The sea and its shore would have fallen short of it one day.*
*But we present to the One whom we love,*
*So that He is pleased with it from us, and its giver is thanked.*
*That is only from the noble nature of His deeds,*
*For otherwise there is nothing in our kingdom that resembles it.*

He said to her: "May God bless you. For by that gift, they are the most thankful of God's creatures and the most numerous of God's creatures."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing four creatures: the hoopoe (hudhud), the screech owl (surad), the ant (namlah) and the bee (nahlah)." Abu Dawud recorded it, and Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq authenticated it, and it has been narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. It has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 270, first or second edition.]].

So the ant praised Sulayman and informed him, in the best way she could, that they would not crush you unknowingly, and that they would not do so deliberately. Thus she negated injustice from them. For this reason the killing of ants is forbidden, and the killing of the hoopoe, because it was Sulayman's guide to water and his messenger to Bilqis.

'Ikrimah said: "God only turned the evil of Sulayman away from the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents."

The screech owl (surad) is called al-Sawwam (the fasting one). It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The first to fast was the surad. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, left al-Sham for the Haram to build the House, al-Sakinah [[al-Sakinah: a cloud, as in the story. In the hadith of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, al-Sakinah is a wind that passes quickly. This is not clear.]] was with him, and the surad. The surad was his guide to the place, and al-Sakinah was its measure. When he reached the spot, al-Sakinah settled on the site of the House and called out: 'Build, O Ibrahim, according to the measure of my shadow.'"

The reason for the prohibition on killing the frog has passed in "al-A'raf," and in "al-Nahl" [[See vol. 10, p. 134, first or second edition.]] the prohibition on killing the bee. And praise be to God.

**The second issue:** Al-Hasan recited "lā yaḥaṭṭimannakum" (let them not crush you). He is also reported to have recited "lā yiḥaṭṭimannakum," and, from Abu Raja', "lā yuḥaṭṭimannakum." Al-ḥaṭm means breaking. One says ḥaṭamtuhu ḥaṭman, meaning I broke it, and it becomes taḥaṭṭama (it was broken). Al-taḥṭīm means breaking into pieces. The phrase "wa-hum lā yash'urūn" ("while they are unaware") may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to Solomon and his troops, with the verb governing the circumstance being "yaḥṭimannakum." It may also be a circumstantial clause referring to the ant, with the governing verb being "qālat," meaning she said this while the troops were heedless, just as you would say, "I stood up while the people were heedless." It may also be a circumstantial clause referring to the ants, again with "qālat" as the governing verb, meaning that the ants do not perceive that Solomon understands her speech. This interpretation is distant, and it will be discussed later.

**The third issue:** Muslim narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "An ant bit a prophet of the prophets, so he ordered the ants' settlement to be burned. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, you destroyed a community of the communities that glorify God?'" In another version: "Why not one ant?"

Our scholars said: It is said that this prophet was Moses (peace be upon him), and that he said: "My Lord, will You punish the people of a town for their sins when among them are the obedient?" It seems that God wished to show him this from Himself. So He made the heat afflict him until he took refuge under a tree, seeking relief in its shade, and beside it was an ant settlement. Sleep overcame him, and when he found the pleasure of sleep, an ant bit him and disturbed him. So he crushed them with his foot and destroyed them, and he burned that tree beside which were their dwellings. God then showed him the lesson in that as a sign: "When one ant bit you, how did you afflict the rest with its punishment!" It intends to alert him that punishment from God, exalted is He, is general; it becomes mercy for the obedient, purity and blessing, and evil and retribution for the disobedient.

On this basis, there is nothing in the hadith indicating disapproval or prohibition of killing ants. Whoever harms you, it is lawful for you to repel him from yourself. No creature of God is greater in sanctity than the believer, and you are permitted to repel him from yourself by killing or striking in proportion. How much more so with insects and creeping creatures that have been subjected to you and placed under your power. If one harms you, it is lawful for you to kill it. Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) was reported to have said: "Whatever ant harms you, kill it."

His saying "Why not one ant?" is evidence that whoever harms is harmed and may be killed. Whenever killing is for a benefit or for repelling harm, there is no harm in it according to the scholars. He spoke of "an ant" in general and did not specify the ant that bit him from others, because the intent was not retaliation. For if retaliation were intended, he would have said, "Why not your ant that bit you?" Instead he said, "Why not an ant in place of an ant?" So it included the innocent and the guilty alike. This was to make him aware that he had asked his Lord to punish a people among whom were both the obedient and the disobedient.

It has also been said: For this prophet, punishing animals by burning was permissible in his law (shar', the revealed law). Therefore God only rebuked him for burning a large number of ants, not for the act of burning itself. Do you not see His saying, "Why not one ant?" That is, why did you not burn only one ant? This differs from our law (shari'ah), for the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited punishing with fire, and he said: "No one punishes with fire except God." Likewise, killing ants was permissible in the law of that prophet, for God did not rebuke him for the act of killing ants in principle. As for our law, the prohibition has come in the hadiths of Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayrah. Malik disliked killing ants, except when they cause harm and cannot be repelled except by killing.

It has also been said: God rebuked this prophet because he took revenge on his own behalf by destroying a multitude that had harmed him, one individual. The better course would have been patience and forgiveness. But it occurred to the prophet that this kind of creature harms the children of Adam, and the sanctity of the children of Adam is greater than the sanctity of other non-speaking animals. Had this consideration stood alone, without being combined with personal satisfaction of the self (tashaffī ṭab'ī), he would not have been rebuked. But when personal satisfaction was added to it, as the context of the hadith indicates, he was rebuked for it. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, "Are you destroying a community of the communities that glorify God because an ant bit you?" implies that this glorification is by speech and utterance, just as God informed us that the ants have a manner of speech, which Solomon (peace be upon him) understood, and that was a miracle for him, and he smiled at her words. This clearly indicates that ants have speech and utterance, but not everyone hears it. Rather, it is heard by whoever God wills among those to whom He breaks habit, be they prophets or saints. We do not deny this on the ground that we do not hear it, for failure to perceive does not necessitate the non-existence of what is perceived in itself. Furthermore, a person finds speech and discourse within himself, and it is not heard from him unless he speaks with his tongue. God broke the habit for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and let him hear the speech of the soul from people who spoke to themselves, and he informed them of what was in their souls. Many of our imams have transmitted this in books on the miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ). Likewise, this happened to many whom God honored among the saints, in more than one instance. It was of this that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke when he said: "Among my community there are inspired ones (muḥaddathūn), and ʿUmar is among them." This meaning has already been discussed under the glorification of inanimate things in the commentary on Surah al-Isra' (Subḥān). It is glorification by tongue and speech, not glorification by indication of state. And praise be to God.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: "So he smiled, laughing at her speech." Ibn al-Sumayqa' recited "ḍaḥikan" without the alif, and it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) governed by a deleted verb that is indicated by "tabassama." It is as if he said, "He laughed a laugh." This is the position of Sibawayh. According to others than Sibawayh, it is in the accusative by the same word "fatabassama," because it carries the meaning of "ḍaḥika" (he laughed). The one who recited "ḍāḥikan" makes it an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "tabassama." The meaning is that he smiled to the extent of laughing, because laughing encompasses smiling, while smiling is less than laughing and is its beginning. It is said: basama (with a fatḥah) yabsimu basman, so he is bāsim, and ibtasama and tabassama. Al-mabsim means the mouth or teeth, like al-majlis from jalasa yajlisu. A man who smiles much is mibsām or bassām. Thus smiling is the beginning of laughing, and laughing refers to both the beginning and the end. However, laughing implies more than smiling. When it increases and a person cannot control himself, it is called qahqahah (loud laughter). Smiling is the laughter of the prophets (peace be upon them) in most of their affairs.

It is recorded in the Sahih, from Jabir ibn Samurah, when he was asked, "Did you sit with the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes, often. He would not rise from his prayer place where he prayed the dawn prayer, or the morning, until the sun rose. When it rose, he would stand up. They would talk and discuss matters of the Jahiliyyah, and they would laugh and smile." Also in it, from Sa'd, who said: "A man of the polytheists had inflicted much harm on the Muslims," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Shoot, may my father and mother be your ransom." Sa'd said: "I drew an arrow for him without an iron head and struck his side. He fell, and his private part was uncovered. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed until I saw his molars." [Note: "Inflicted much harm" means he had overwhelmed them and acted among them as fire does. From the margin of Muslim.]

He (peace be upon him) was smiling in most of his circumstances. He also laughed in other circumstances, a laugh higher than smiling and less than the complete laughter in which the uvula is visible. Rarely, when his astonishment was extreme, he might laugh until his molars showed. The scholars disliked excessive laughter from him, as Luqman said to his son: "My son, beware of excessive laughter, for it kills the heart." It has been transmitted as a saying traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) from the hadith of Abu Dharr and others. The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed when Sa'd shot the man and struck him. That was only joy at hitting the target, not at the uncovering of the man's private part, for he (ﷺ) is far above such things.

**The sixth issue:** There is no disagreement among the scholars that all animals have understanding and intellect. Al-Shafi'i said: "The pigeon is the most intelligent of birds." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The ant is a clever, strong, and very perceptive creature. It stores provisions, makes granaries, splits grain into two halves so that it will not sprout, and splits coriander into four pieces, because when it is split in two it would sprout. It eats half of what it gathered in its year and keeps the rest for future use." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "These are special kinds of knowledge with us, and the ant has attained them by God's creation of this for it." Al-Ustadh Abu al-Muzaffar Shahpur al-Isfara'ini said: "It is not unlikely that animals perceive the origination of the world, the origination of created things, and the oneness of God. But we do not understand them, and they do not understand us. As for our pursuit of them while they flee from us, that is due to the rule of kind."

**His, exalted is He, saying:** "And he said, 'My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and my parents.'" Here "an" is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah). "Awza'nī" means "inspire me with that." It derives from wazi'a, as if he said: "Restrain me from what displeases You." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "The People of the Book claim that Solomon's mother was the wife of Uriah, whom God tested David with, or that after her husband's death David married her, and she bore him Solomon (peace be upon him)." More explanation of this will come in Surah Sad, God willing, in the commentary on His saying: "And David thought that We had only tested him" (verse 24 of the mentioned surah).

"And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants." That is, along with Your servants, according to Ibn Zayd. It has also been said: the meaning is "within the category of Your righteous servants."

**Issue One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. He mentions another matter that occurred to him on the journey in which the ants were mentioned earlier. *Tafaqqud* means seeking out what has gone missing from you. *Al-tayr* (the birds) is a collective noun whose singular is *tair*. Here *al-tayr* refers to the species of birds and to their flocks. They used to accompany him on his travels and shade him with their wings.

People differed about the meaning of his inspecting the birds. One group said: this was in accordance with what the care of royal affairs requires, and with his attention to every part of them. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Another group said: rather, he inspected the birds because the sun had come in from the place where the hoopoe was when it was absent, so this was the reason for inspecting the birds, in order to find out from where the sun had entered. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: he only sought the hoopoe because he needed to know how deep the water was beneath the surface of the earth, since he had halted in a barren wilderness where there was no water. The hoopoe could see the inside and the outside of the earth, so it would tell Solomon where the water was, and then the jinn would extract it in a short time, stripping the surface of the earth away from it as a sheep is skinned. This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas on the authority of Ibn Salam.

Abu Mijlaz said: Ibn 'Abbas said to 'Abdullah ibn Salam: "I want to ask you about three issues." He said: "You ask me while you recite the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes, three times." He said: "Why did Solomon inspect the hoopoe in particular, rather than the rest of the birds?" He said: "He needed water and did not know its depth, or he said its distance, and the hoopoe knew that, unlike the other birds, so he inspected it."

In the *Kitab al-Naqqash* it is stated: the hoopoe was an engineer. It was also reported that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq heard Ibn 'Abbas mention the matter of the hoopoe, and said to him: "Stop, O one who stops (much)! How can the hoopoe see beneath the earth when it does not see the snare when it falls into it?!" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind." Mujahid said: it was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "How did he inspect the hoopoe among the birds?" He said: "He alighted at a place and did not know how far the water was, while the hoopoe was guided to it, so he wanted to ask it." Mujahid said: I said: "How could it be guided when a boy sets a snare for it and catches it?" He said: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "No one can give this answer except a scholar of the Qur'an." I say: this answer was already given by the hoopoe to Solomon, as mentioned above.

They also recited:

*When Allah wills a matter for a man, who has intellect, insight and vision,*
*and a stratagem he devises to avert what the decrees bring upon him of harm,*
*He covers over his hearing and his intellect, and draws out his mind as a hair is drawn out.*
*Then, when He has executed His judgment upon him, He returns his intellect to him so that he may take heed.*

Al-Kalbi said: he had only one hoopoe on his journey. And Allah knows best.

**Issue Two:** In this verse there is evidence that the ruler (*imam*) should inspect the conditions of his subjects and protect them. Consider the hoopoe, despite its small size: how its condition was not hidden from Solomon. How much more so, then, should this be true of the great affairs of the kingdom. May Allah have mercy on 'Umar, for he followed this course. He said: "If a lamb on the bank of the Euphrates were seized by a wolf, 'Umar would be held accountable for it." So what do you think of a governor through whose hands cities are conquered, while the subjects are lost and the shepherds are lost too?

In the *Sahih* it is reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab set out for Syria, until when he reached Sargh [[Sargh (with the *ra* vowelled or unvowelled): a village in the Wadi Tabuk on the route to Syria.]], the commanders of the armies met him, Abu 'Ubaydah and his companions, and informed him that the plague had broken out in Syria. (The hadith continues.) Our scholars said: this departure by 'Umar took place after Bayt al-Maqdis had been conquered, in the year seventeen (AH), as recorded by Khalifah ibn Khayyat.

He would inspect the conditions of his subjects and of his commanders personally. The Qur'an and the Sunnah have indicated, and we have explained, what the ruler is obliged to do in inspecting the conditions of his subjects, personally carrying this out, and travelling for it, however long the journey. May Allah have mercy on Ibn al-Mubarak when he says:

*Has anything corrupted the religion except the kings*
*and the evil scholars and their monks?*

**Issue Three:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe﴾. That is: what is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see it? This is of the type of inversion (*qalb*) whose meaning is not understood from the wording alone. It is like your saying: "What is the matter with me that I see you downcast?", meaning: what is the matter with you? *Al-hudhud* is a well-known bird, and *hadhdhadah* is its call.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the intended meaning of the speech is "the hoopoe is absent", but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and so he asked in the form of a rebuke about this necessary consequence. This is a kind of conciseness. The interrogative in the phrase "What is the matter with me" takes the place of the *alif* that would be followed by *am*.

It has also been said: he said "What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe" because he considered his own state. He knew that he had been granted great dominion and that creation had been subjected to him. Thus the obligation of thankfulness fell upon him, through establishing obedience and maintaining justice. When he lost the blessing of the hoopoe, he feared that he might have fallen short in his duty of thankfulness, and for this reason it was taken from him. So he began to inspect himself, saying: "What is the matter with me?"

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the Sufi shaykhs do this when they lose what they hoped for; they inspect their deeds. This is in matters of etiquette. So how about us today, when we fall short in the obligatory duties!

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Hisham and Ayyub recited *mali* with a fatha on the *ya'*, and likewise in *Ya-Sin*: ﴿And what is the matter with me that I do not worship Him who originated me﴾. Hamzah and Ya'qub made it sukun. The rest, the Madinan readers and Abu 'Amr, recited the one in *Ya-Sin* with a fatha and this one with sukun. Abu 'Amr said: because this one in *al-Naml* is an interrogative, whereas the other is a negation. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the sukun in "fa-qala ma li".

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: some people claimed that they wished to distinguish between what is an initial subject (*mubtada'*) and what is conjoined to what precedes it. This is nothing. It is simply the *ya'* of the self (*ya' al-nafs*): among the Arabs some pronounce it with a fatha and some with a sukun, so they recited in both dialects. The eloquent usage for the *ya'* of the self is that it should be vowelled with a fatha, since it is a noun and consists of a single letter, and it was preferable not to make it sukun, which would diminish the noun.

﴿Or was he among the absent?﴾ Here *am* means "rather".

**Issue Four:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾. This is evidence that the punishment is proportionate to the offence, not to the size of the body. Nevertheless, the one being punished is shown leniency in terms of time and manner. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj that his punishment of the bird was by plucking its feathers. Ibn Jurayj said: all of its feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: its two wings. Solomon did this to the hoopoe as a severe measure against disobedient ones, and as a punishment for its neglect of its duty and its rank. It seems that Allah permitted him to do so, just as He permitted the slaughter of animals and birds for food and other benefits. And Allah knows best.

In *Nawadir al-Usul* it is stated: he said: Sulayman ibn Humayd Abu al-Rabi' al-Iyadi related to us, he said: 'Awn ibn 'Umarah related to us, from al-Husayn al-Ju'fi, from al-Zubayr ibn al-Khirrit, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Allah only turned Solomon's evil away from the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents. (This will come later.)

It has also been said: his punishment is that it be placed among its opposites. From some of them: the narrowest prison is the company of one's opponents. It was also said: "I will oblige it to serve its equals." It was said: "I will confine it in a cage." It was said: "I will make it a target for the sun after plucking it." It was said: "I will banish it from my service." Kings discipline by estrangement, by separating the body from what it is accustomed to.

The verb is emphasized with the heavy *nun*, and it is obligatory, whether heavy or light. Abu Hatim said: if it were recited as "la-u'adhdhibannahu 'adhaban shadidan aw la-adhbahannahu", it would be permissible.

﴿Or he shall bring me a clear authority﴾, that is, with a clear proof. The *lam* in "la-ya'tiyannani" is not the *lam* of oath, because Solomon would not swear by the act of the hoopoe. But since it came directly after "la-u'adhdhibannahu", which is something by which an oath may be sworn, he gave it the same treatment. Ibn Kathir alone recited "la-ya'tiyannanni" with two *nun*s.

**Issue Five:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So it tarried not long﴾, that is, the hoopoe. The majority of readers recited with a *damma* on the *kaf*, while 'Asim alone recited it with a *fatha*. The meaning in both recitations is "it remained." Sibawayh said: *makatha yamkutha mukuthan*, just as they say *qa'ada ya'qudu qu'udan*. He said: *makatha* is like *zarufa*. Others said: the *fatha* is better because of His saying "*makithina*" (remaining), since it derives from *makatha*. It is said: *makatha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun*, and *makutha yamkutha* like *'azuma ya'zumu*, so he is *makith* like *'azim*. And *makutha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun* like *hamudha yahmudu*, so he is *hamid*.

The pronoun in "makatha" may refer to Solomon, meaning: Solomon remained, after the inspection and the threat, not for a long time, that is, not for a long period. It may also refer to the hoopoe, which is the more common view.

Then it came: ﴿and said: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. This is the **sixth issue**: that is, I have learned what you have not learned of the matter. In this there is a refutation of those who say that prophets know the unseen. Al-Farra' reported *ahatu* with the *ta'* assimilated into the *ta'*. He also reported *ahattu* with the *ta'* changed into a *ta'* and assimilated.

**Issue Seven:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾. He informed Solomon of what he did not know, and he defended himself against what Solomon had threatened him with, namely punishment and slaughter.

The majority recited *Saba'in* with *tanwin* (*sarf*). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *Saba'a* with a *fatha* on the *hamzah* and without *tanwin* (*tark al-sarf*). The first reading is that it is the name of a man, after whom a people were named. On this is the line of the poet:

*"Those who come to water, and Taym are on the heights of Saba',*
*the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."*

Al-Zajjaj denied that it was the name of a man, and said: "Saba'" is the name of a city known as Ma'rib in Yemen, between it and San'a' a three days' journey. He recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

*"From Saba', those present at Ma'rib, when they built,*
*apart from its flood, the great dam."*

He said: "As for one who does not apply the diptotic declension (lam yasrif), he says it is the name of a city. As for one who applies it, which is the more common practice, it is because it is the name of a land (al-balad), and so it is a masculine noun named after a masculine noun." It was also said that it is the name of a woman after whom the city was named. The sound view is that it is the name of a man, as in the Tirmidhi collection, from the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi, from the Prophet (ﷺ). This will come, God willing, later.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This hadith was hidden from al-Zajjaj, so he struck out blindly." Al-Farra' claimed that al-Ru'asi asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about Saba', and he said: "I do not know what it is." Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Farra' interpreted Abu 'Amr's words to mean that he withheld declension because the word was unknown, and that when a thing is not known it is not declined." Al-Nahhas said: "Abu 'Amr is too exalted to say such a thing. The report of al-Ru'asi from him contains no evidence that he withheld declension because he did not know the word. He only said, 'I do not know it.' If a grammarian is asked about a noun and says, 'I do not know it,' this is no proof that he would withhold declension from it. Rather, the truth lies otherwise: when one does not know the word, the obligation is to decline it, because the original state of nouns is declension. A noun is withheld from declension only because of a cause that enters upon it. The original state is established with certainty, so it is not removed by something unknown." He then mentioned much speech from the grammarians and said at the end: "The ruling on 'Saba'' is what the authoritative report indicates: that it is originally the name of a man. If you apply declension to it, that is because it has become the name of a tribe. If you do not apply declension, you make it the name of a tribe, like Thamud. However, the preferred view according to Sibawayh is declension, and his argument on this is decisive, because since this name can take both masculine and feminine forms, the masculine is more appropriate, since it is the original and the lighter."

Eighth: The verse indicates that the junior may say to the senior, and the student to the scholar: "I have what you do not have," when he has verified and is certain of it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, despite his greatness and knowledge, may Allah be pleased with him, did not have knowledge of seeking permission. The knowledge of tayammum was with 'Ammar and others, and it was hidden from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, so that they said: "The one in major impurity should not perform tayammum." The ruling on the menstruating woman being permitted to leave (Mecca after tawaf) was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit did not know it. The washing of the head of the one in ihram was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but it was hidden from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama. Many such examples exist, so we will not lengthen them.

Ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. When the hoopoe said, "I have come to you from Saba' with certain news," Sulayman said, "And what is that news?" He said, "I found a woman ruling over them," meaning Bilqis daughter of Sharahil, who ruled the people of Saba'. It is said: How was her location hidden from Sulayman, when the distance between his station and her land was near, being a journey of three (days) between Sana'a and Ma'rib? The answer is that Allah, exalted is He, hid that from him for a wisdom, just as He hid Yusuf's place from Ya'qub. It is related that one of her parents was from the jinn. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a matter the atheists deny, and they say: 'The jinn do not eat or give birth.' They lie, may Allah curse them all. That is true, and their marriage is rationally permissible. If it is established by transmission, then so be it." I say: Abu Dawud related from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "A delegation of the jinn came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, forbid your community to clean themselves with a bone, dung, or a skull, for Allah has placed provision for us in them.'" In Sahih Muslim it says: He said: "For you is every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, which falls into your hands with more meat than it had, and every dung is fodder for your animals." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not clean yourselves with them, for they are the food of your jinn brothers." In Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: I asked, "What is the matter with the bone and the dung?" He said: "They are from the food of the jinn. A delegation of jinn of Nasibin came to me, excellent jinn, and they asked me for provisions. So I asked Allah, exalted is He, that they should not pass by a bone or dung without finding food on it." All of this is explicit that they eat. As for their marriage, the reference to it has already been made in "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra') [[See vol. 10, p. 289, first or second edition.]] at His saying: "And share with them in wealth and children." Wuhayb ibn Jarir ibn Hazim related from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, from 'Uthman ibn Hadir, who said: The mother of Bilqis was from the jinn, called Balʿama daughter of Shaysan. More explanation of this will come, God willing.

Tenth: Al-Bukhari related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Khosrow their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is an explicit text that a woman cannot be a caliph, and there is no disagreement about it." It is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not authentically established from him. Perhaps it was transmitted from him as it was transmitted from Abu Hanifa, that she may judge only in matters in which she is a witness, not that she be a judge absolutely, nor that a written document be issued stating that so-and-so is placed in authority over judgment. Rather, the proper way is arbitration and delegation in a single case. This is the most reasonable assumption about Abu Hanifa and Ibn Jarir. It is related from 'Umar that he appointed a woman over the market inspection (hisba). But this is not authentic, so do not pay attention to it, for it is one of the fabrications of the innovators in hadith. This question was debated by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, the Maliki Ash'ari, with Abu al-Faraj ibn Tarar, the shaykh of the Shafi'is. Abu al-Faraj said: "The evidence that a woman may judge is that the purpose of judgments is the enforcement of the judge's rulings, the hearing of evidence, and the settlement of disputes between litigants, and this is possible for a woman as it is for a man." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr objected to him and refuted his statement by appealing to the Great Imamate, since its purpose is guarding the frontiers, managing affairs, protecting the realm, collecting the land tax and returning it to its rightful recipients, and this cannot be done by a woman as it can be done by a man. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The words of both shaykhs on this question are worthless, for a woman cannot appear in a council, nor mix with men, nor converse with them as an equal with an equal, for if she is a young woman it is forbidden to look at her or speak with her, and if she is a barzah [[The barzah here means an older woman who does not veil as a young woman does, yet is chaste, sensible, and sits with people and talks with them.]] there is no single assembly in which she gathers with men, mingling with them and debating them. Whoever imagines this, or believes it, will never prosper."

Eleventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she has been given of everything﴾: this is hyperbole, meaning of what a kingdom needs. It was also said: the meaning is that she was given of everything in her time, a thing, and the object was omitted because the speech indicates it.

(And she has a great throne): that is, a seat, and it was described as great in its form and in the rank of sovereignty. It was said: it was of gold, and she sat upon it. It was also said: "throne" here means kingship, but the first is more correct, because of His saying: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask how the hoopoe equated the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah in the description of greatness? I say: there is a vast difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is glorifying it in comparison to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the throne of Allah as great is glorifying it in relation to what He created of the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Abbas said: Her throne was eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high in the sky, adorned with pearls, red rubies, and green emeralds. Qatada said: its legs were pearls and jewels, and it was covered with brocade and silk, and had seven locks upon it. Muqatil said: it was eighty cubits [by eighty cubits] [[From b and k.]] and its height from the ground was eighty cubits, and it was adorned with jewels. Ibn Ishaq said: Women served her, and there were six hundred women for her service. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that she was a woman who was made ruler over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from an unbelieving people.

Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It was said: this people were among those who worshipped the sun, because they were heretics, as is related. It was also said: they were Magians who worshipped lights. It is related from Nafi' that the pause is at "throne" ('arsh). Al-Mahdawi said: "Then 'great' (ʿazim) is connected to what follows it, and according to this it would have to be: 'great' that I found her, meaning my finding her an unbeliever." Ibn al-Anbari said: "'And she has a great throne' is a good pause, and it is not permissible to pause at 'throne' and begin with 'great, I found her' except for one who reads with a fatha, because 'great' is an adjective of 'throne.' If it were connected to 'I found her' you would say 'great (feminine) I found her,' and this is impossible in every respect." Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Shahriyar related to me, saying: Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn ibn al-Aswad al-'Ijli related to us, from some people of knowledge, that he said: The pause is at "throne" and the beginning is at "great," meaning: great is their worship of the sun and the moon. He said: I have heard someone support this view and argue that her throne is too insignificant and too minor a matter for Allah to describe it as great. Ibn al-Anbari said: "My preferred view is what I mentioned first, because there is no evidence for implying the worship of the sun and moon. It is not unreasonable for the hoopoe to describe her throne as great when he saw it extending in length and width, and its following the grammatical case of 'throne' is evidence that it is its adjective."

(And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them): that is, what they were engaged in of disbelief. (And turned them away from the way): that is, from the path of monotheism. By this he shows that what is not the path of monotheism is not a path by which one truly benefits.

**(So they are not guided)** to God and His oneness. **Thirteenth**: His saying, ﴿that they should not prostrate to God﴾. Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read "ألا يسجدوا لله" with the *shaddah* on "ألّا" (*alla*, "that not"). Ibn al-Anbari said: "*fa-hum la yahtadun*" is not a complete stop for those who read "ألّا" with the *shaddah*, because the meaning is: "Satan made their deeds seem good to them, so that they would not prostrate." Al-Nahhas said: it is "*an*" with "*la*" added to it, and "*an*" is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said: it depends on "zayyana" (made seem good), meaning "He made it seem good to them so that they would not prostrate to God." Al-Kisa'i said: it depends on "fa-sadda-hum" (so He barred them), meaning "He barred them from prostrating." In both views it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). Al-Yazidi and Ali ibn Sulayman said: "*an*" is a substitute (*badal*) for "a'malahum" (their deeds) and is in the accusative position. Abu 'Amr said: "*an*" is in the genitive position as a substitute for "al-sabil" (the way). It was also said: the governing word for it is "la yahtadun," meaning "they are not guided that they should prostrate to God," i.e., they do not know that this is obligatory upon them. In this view "la" is extra, as in His saying, "*ma mana'aka alla tasjuda*" ("what prevented you from prostrating?"), meaning "what prevented you from prostrating?" On this reading there is no place for a prostration, because it is a report about them abandoning prostration, either through adornment, through barring, or through preventing guidance.
