Al-Zuhri, al-Kisa'i and others read: "ألا يا اسجدوا لله" ("alla"), with a light pronunciation,[[Alusi: "ألا" with light pronunciation, meaning that it is for opening speech (*istiftah*), and "يا" is a vocative particle, with the addressee omitted, i.e., "Alā yā qawm usjudū" (Oh people, prostrate!). The alif of "يا" and the alif of connection (*hamzat al-wasl*) in "usjudū" were dropped, and the yā was written joined to the sīn, contrary to analogy.]] meaning "Alā yā hā'ulā'i usjudū" ("Oh, you people, prostrate!"), because "يا" is used to address nouns, not verbs. Sibawayh recited:

*Yā la'nata Allāhi wal-aqwāmi kullihim*
*wal-ṣāliḥīna 'alā Sam'ān min jār*

Sibawayh said: the "yā" is not for the curse, because if it were for the curse he would have put it in the accusative, since it would become a vocative with a following genitive; rather its underlying form is "Yā hā'ulā'i la'natu Allāhi wal-aqwāmi 'alā Sam'ān" ("O you people, the curse of God and the peoples be upon Sam'ān"). Some transmitted from the Arabs by hearing: "Alā yā irḥamū, alā yā uṣduqū" ("Oh, have mercy! Oh, be truthful!"). They intend: "Alā yā qawmu irḥamū, uṣduqū" ("Oh people, have mercy, be truthful!"). According to this reading, "usjudū" is in the jussive position as an imperative, and one pauses at "alā yā," then begins: "usjudū." Al-Kisa'i said: "I never heard the elders reciting it except with the light pronunciation, with the intention of the imperative." In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "*Alā hal tasjudūna lillāh*" with *ta'* and *nūn*. In the reading of Ubayy: "*Alā tasjudūna lillāh*." These two readings are a proof for the one who reads it lightly.

Al-Zajjaj said: the light reading requires the obligation of prostration, unlike the heavy reading. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the heavy reading. Abu Hatim said: the light reading is a good option, except that in it the report is cut off from the matter of Sheba and then returns to mentioning them, whereas the heavy reading is a report that follows one part after another without a break in its middle. Al-Nahhas said something similar. He said: the light reading is remote, because the speech would be an interjection (*mu'tarid*), whereas with the heavy reading the speech is coherent. Also, the written text (*sawad*) is not in agreement with this reading, because two alifs have been deleted from it, and such abbreviation is only done by deleting a single alif, as in "*Yā 'Īsā ibn Maryam*."

Ibn al-Anbari said: the alif of "usjudū" is dropped, as it is dropped with "hā'ulā'i" when it is shown. When the alif of "yā" was dropped and the alif of "usjudū" joined to it, it too was dropped. Its dropping is taken as an indication of abbreviation and as a preference for what is lighter and has fewer letters.

Al-Jawhari said at the end of his book: Some said: "yā" in this place is only for alerting (*tanbīh*), as if he had said: "Alā usjudū lillāh." When "yā" for alerting was introduced before it, the alif in "usjudū" was dropped because it is an alif of connection, and the alif in "yā" went away because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters, since it and the sīn are both unvoweled. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Alā yā-slamī yā dāra Mayya 'alā al-bilā*
*wa lā zāla munhalan bi-ja'rā'ika al-qaṭr*

Al-Jurjani said: it is an interjected speech from the hoopoe, or from Solomon, or from God, meaning "*alā li-yasjudū*" ("Let them prostrate!"), like His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the days of God﴾. It was said that it is an imperative, meaning "*li-yaghfirū*" ("let them forgive"). On this view, the writing of the Mushaf is also arranged, meaning there is no vocative here.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was said that it is from the speech of the hoopoe up to His saying, "the Mighty," and this is the view of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq. It is objected that he is not addressed, so how can he speak with the meaning of a legal ruling? It is possible that it is from the saying of Solomon when the hoopoe informed him about the people. It is also possible that it is from the saying of God, the Exalted, so it is an interjection between the two statements, and this is the established view upon reflection. The heavy reading of "ألّا" gives that the speech belongs to the hoopoe, whereas the light reading prevents that. The light reading requires the command to prostrate to God, the Mighty and Majestic, due to the imperative, as we have explained.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "Is the prostration of recitation obligatory in both readings, or in one of them?" I say: It is obligatory in both, because the places of prostration are either a command to do it, or praise for the one who did it, or blame for the one who abandoned it, and one of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is blame for the one who abandons it. I say: God has reported about the disbelievers that they prostrate, as in "al-Inshiqaq," and the Prophet ﷺ prostrated in it, as is established in al-Bukhari and others; so likewise in "al-Naml." And God knows best. Al-Zamakhshari: What al-Zajjaj mentioned about the obligation of prostration with the light reading and not the heavy reading is not to be relied upon.

﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾ (*al-khab'*): the hidden of the heavens is its rain, and the hidden of the earth is its treasures and its plants. Qatadah said: *al-khab'* is secret. Al-Nahhas said: this is better, i.e., whatever is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and it is shown by "what you conceal and what you disclose." [[In the manuscript of the original, with the *bā'*, and it is the reading of the common people, as will come.]] Ikrimah and Malik ibn Dinar read: "*al-khabu*" with a *fatha* on the *bā'* and without a *hamzah*. Al-Mahdawi said: this is the analogical lightening, and he mentioned those who drop the *hamzah* when stopping. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Hatim related that Ikrimah read "*al-khaba*" with a non-hamzated alif, and claimed that this is not permissible in Arabic, and argued that if he lightens the *hamzah* he moves its vowel onto the *bā'* and says "*al-khab fi al-samawat wal-ard*," and if he changes the *hamzah* he says "*al-khabyi*" with the *bā'* sukun and a *yā'* after it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach them, except that when he left his town he did not meet anyone more knowledgeable than him. Sibawayh related from the Arabs that they change the *hamzah* into an alif when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is open-vowelled; they change it into a *wāw* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is closed-vowelled; and they change it into a *yā'* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is vowelled with a kasra. So they say: "*hadha al-wathw*," "I was amazed at the *wathy*," "I saw the *wathā*," from "*wuthi'at yaduhu*" (his hand was sprained). Likewise: "*hadha al-khabw*," "I was amazed at the *khabyi*," and "I saw the *khaba*." This was done because the *hamzah* is light, so these letters were substituted for it. Sibawayh related from a group of the Banu Tamim and Banu Asad that they say: "*hadha al-khabu*," they put a *ḍamma* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, and they keep the *hamzah*, and they put a kasra on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a kasra, and they put a *fatha* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *fatha*. Sibawayh also related that they put a kasra even when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, but this is from the Banu Tamim, so they say "*al-radī'*" [[*al-radih* means the companion.]], and he claimed that they did not put a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* because they disliked a *ḍamma* preceded by a kasra, since there is no pattern *fi'ul* in the language. All these are dialects that differ from the dialect in which the community recited. In the reading of Abdullah: "*alladhī yukhriju al-khaba min al-samawat*," and "*min*" and "*fi*" alternate; the Arabs say: "*la-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fīkum*," meaning "*minkum*," as al-Farra' said.

﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾: The common reading is with *yā'* in both. This reading indicates that the verse is from the speech of the hoopoe, and that God singled him out with knowledge of His oneness and the obligation to prostrate to Him, and of the denial of their prostration to the sun, and of attributing it to Satan, and of his adorning it for them, with what He singled him out with from among the birds and all other animals, of subtle knowledge that sound minds hardly reach. Al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Hafs and al-Kisa'i read "*tukhfūna*" and "*tu'linūna*" with *tā'*, in address. This reading indicates that the verse is from the address of God, the Mighty and Majestic, to the nation of Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿God— there is no god but He, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾: Ibn Muhaysin read "*al-'azīmi*" with *raf'* as an adjective of God. The rest read with *khafḍ* as an adjective of "the Throne." It was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is within it and in its grasp.

**Fourteenth**: His saying, ﴿We shall see﴾ (*sanandhuru*), from "seeing," which is reflection and examination.

(أَصَدَقْتَ أَمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ) in your statement. Here "kunta" means "anta" (you are). He said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, and he did not say "we shall look into your affair," because when the hoopoe openly boasted of knowledge in his words, ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, Sulayman openly replied to him, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or lied.﴾ That was a rebuke (kifa'an) to what he had said. Fifteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, is evidence that the imam must accept the excuse of his subjects and ward off punishment from them based on the inner state of their excuses, despite the outward appearance of their conditions, because Sulayman did not punish the hoopoe when it offered its excuse to him. The hoopoe's truthfulness became an excuse only because it reported something that called for jihad, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, was fond of jihad. In the Sahih: "No one loves excuses more than Allah; for this reason He sent down the Book and sent the Messengers." Umar accepted the excuse of al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi and did not punish him. However, the imam may test such an excuse when a legal ruling of the Shari'a depends on it, as Sulayman did, for when the hoopoe said, ﴿I found a woman ruling over them, who has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne﴾, desire did not stir him, nor did love of increasing his kingdom move him to seek more, until it said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah.﴾ Then what he heard angered him, and he sought to verify what he had been told and to acquire knowledge of what was hidden from him in this matter, so he said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars.﴾ A similar report is found in the Sahih from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, when Umar consulted the people about the miscarriage of a woman (al-imlas, i.e., a woman whose belly is struck so that she casts out her fetus). Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba said: "I witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) judge in such a case that a ghurra (a slave or a female slave) must be given." He said: Umar said, "Bring me someone who will testify with you." So Muhammad ibn Maslama testified for him. In another narration, Umar said, "Do not leave until you bring the way out of this matter," so I left and found Muhammad ibn Maslama, brought him, and he testified. A similar report is the hadith of Abu Musa concerning seeking permission (to enter) and other matters. Sixteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: In it there are five readings. "Fa-alqihi ilayhim" with the yā' affirmed in pronunciation. With the yā' omitted and the kasra remaining to indicate it, "fa-alqihi ilayhim." With the hā' pronounced with a ḍamma and the wāw kept, according to the original form, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." With the wāw omitted and the ḍamma kept, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." The fifth dialect, which Hamza recited, is with the hā' sukun: "fa-alqih ilayhim." Al-Nahhas said: According to the grammarians this is not permissible except by a remote stratagem, namely by assuming a pause. I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: "Do not pay attention to this justification. If it were permissible to join (the word to what follows) while intending a pause, it would be permissible to drop the i'rab (grammatical inflection) from nouns." He said: "ilayhim" is in the plural form, and he did not say "ilayha," because he had said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun﴾. It is as if he said: "Cast it to those whose religion is this," out of concern for the matter of religion and his preoccupation with it over other things, and for this reason the address in the letter was framed in the plural. It is narrated in the stories of this verse that the hoopoe arrived and found walls and barriers between this queen and him, so it made for an opening (kuwwa) which Bilqis had made so that the sun might enter through it at its rising, because of her worship of it. It entered through it and dropped the letter upon Bilqis, who, it is said, was asleep. When she awoke she found it and was startled, thinking someone had entered upon her. Then she stood up and found her condition as she had known it, so she looked toward the opening, anxious about the matter of the sun, and saw the hoopoe, and then she understood. Wahb and Ibn Zayd said: There was an opening facing the sunrise, and when the sun rose she would prostrate. The hoopoe blocked it with its wing, so the sun rose while she did not know. When she was slow to notice the sun and stood to look, it threw the document to her. When she saw the seal she trembled and submitted, for the kingdom of Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in his ring. She read it, then gathered the chiefs of her people and addressed them with what comes after. Muqatil said: The hoopoe carried the letter in its beak and flew until it stood over the head of the woman, while around her were the troops and soldiers. It fluttered for a while while the people looked at it. The woman raised her head, and it dropped the letter into her lap. Seventeenth issue: This verse is evidence for sending letters to polytheists, conveying the call to them, and inviting them to Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Kisra, Qaysar, and to every tyrant, as has been mentioned in Al 'Imran. Eighteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Then turn away from them﴾. His command to turn away is a matter of good manners, so that he withdraws in the manner in which one behaves with kings. The meaning is: remain nearby until you see their response. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to turn away in the sense of returning to him, i.e., "cast it and return." He said: His saying, ﴿then watch what they return﴾, is in the sense of coming before his saying, ﴿then turn away,﴾ and the arrangement of the speech is clearer: i.e., cast it, then turn away, and in the meantime, "watch" means wait. It was also said: "watch" means "know," as in His saying, ﴿the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. That is: know what they return, i.e., what they answer and what words they return. It was also said: ﴿then watch what they return﴾ means they exchange words among themselves.

**Issue One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. He mentions another matter that occurred to him on the journey in which the ants were mentioned earlier. *Tafaqqud* means seeking out what has gone missing from you. *Al-tayr* (the birds) is a collective noun whose singular is *tair*. Here *al-tayr* refers to the species of birds and to their flocks. They used to accompany him on his travels and shade him with their wings.

People differed about the meaning of his inspecting the birds. One group said: this was in accordance with what the care of royal affairs requires, and with his attention to every part of them. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Another group said: rather, he inspected the birds because the sun had come in from the place where the hoopoe was when it was absent, so this was the reason for inspecting the birds, in order to find out from where the sun had entered. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: he only sought the hoopoe because he needed to know how deep the water was beneath the surface of the earth, since he had halted in a barren wilderness where there was no water. The hoopoe could see the inside and the outside of the earth, so it would tell Solomon where the water was, and then the jinn would extract it in a short time, stripping the surface of the earth away from it as a sheep is skinned. This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas on the authority of Ibn Salam.

Abu Mijlaz said: Ibn 'Abbas said to 'Abdullah ibn Salam: "I want to ask you about three issues." He said: "You ask me while you recite the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes, three times." He said: "Why did Solomon inspect the hoopoe in particular, rather than the rest of the birds?" He said: "He needed water and did not know its depth, or he said its distance, and the hoopoe knew that, unlike the other birds, so he inspected it."

In the *Kitab al-Naqqash* it is stated: the hoopoe was an engineer. It was also reported that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq heard Ibn 'Abbas mention the matter of the hoopoe, and said to him: "Stop, O one who stops (much)! How can the hoopoe see beneath the earth when it does not see the snare when it falls into it?!" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind." Mujahid said: it was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "How did he inspect the hoopoe among the birds?" He said: "He alighted at a place and did not know how far the water was, while the hoopoe was guided to it, so he wanted to ask it." Mujahid said: I said: "How could it be guided when a boy sets a snare for it and catches it?" He said: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "No one can give this answer except a scholar of the Qur'an." I say: this answer was already given by the hoopoe to Solomon, as mentioned above.

They also recited:

*When Allah wills a matter for a man, who has intellect, insight and vision,*
*and a stratagem he devises to avert what the decrees bring upon him of harm,*
*He covers over his hearing and his intellect, and draws out his mind as a hair is drawn out.*
*Then, when He has executed His judgment upon him, He returns his intellect to him so that he may take heed.*

Al-Kalbi said: he had only one hoopoe on his journey. And Allah knows best.

**Issue Two:** In this verse there is evidence that the ruler (*imam*) should inspect the conditions of his subjects and protect them. Consider the hoopoe, despite its small size: how its condition was not hidden from Solomon. How much more so, then, should this be true of the great affairs of the kingdom. May Allah have mercy on 'Umar, for he followed this course. He said: "If a lamb on the bank of the Euphrates were seized by a wolf, 'Umar would be held accountable for it." So what do you think of a governor through whose hands cities are conquered, while the subjects are lost and the shepherds are lost too?

In the *Sahih* it is reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab set out for Syria, until when he reached Sargh [[Sargh (with the *ra* vowelled or unvowelled): a village in the Wadi Tabuk on the route to Syria.]], the commanders of the armies met him, Abu 'Ubaydah and his companions, and informed him that the plague had broken out in Syria. (The hadith continues.) Our scholars said: this departure by 'Umar took place after Bayt al-Maqdis had been conquered, in the year seventeen (AH), as recorded by Khalifah ibn Khayyat.

He would inspect the conditions of his subjects and of his commanders personally. The Qur'an and the Sunnah have indicated, and we have explained, what the ruler is obliged to do in inspecting the conditions of his subjects, personally carrying this out, and travelling for it, however long the journey. May Allah have mercy on Ibn al-Mubarak when he says:

*Has anything corrupted the religion except the kings*
*and the evil scholars and their monks?*

**Issue Three:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe﴾. That is: what is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see it? This is of the type of inversion (*qalb*) whose meaning is not understood from the wording alone. It is like your saying: "What is the matter with me that I see you downcast?", meaning: what is the matter with you? *Al-hudhud* is a well-known bird, and *hadhdhadah* is its call.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the intended meaning of the speech is "the hoopoe is absent", but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and so he asked in the form of a rebuke about this necessary consequence. This is a kind of conciseness. The interrogative in the phrase "What is the matter with me" takes the place of the *alif* that would be followed by *am*.

It has also been said: he said "What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe" because he considered his own state. He knew that he had been granted great dominion and that creation had been subjected to him. Thus the obligation of thankfulness fell upon him, through establishing obedience and maintaining justice. When he lost the blessing of the hoopoe, he feared that he might have fallen short in his duty of thankfulness, and for this reason it was taken from him. So he began to inspect himself, saying: "What is the matter with me?"

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the Sufi shaykhs do this when they lose what they hoped for; they inspect their deeds. This is in matters of etiquette. So how about us today, when we fall short in the obligatory duties!

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Hisham and Ayyub recited *mali* with a fatha on the *ya'*, and likewise in *Ya-Sin*: ﴿And what is the matter with me that I do not worship Him who originated me﴾. Hamzah and Ya'qub made it sukun. The rest, the Madinan readers and Abu 'Amr, recited the one in *Ya-Sin* with a fatha and this one with sukun. Abu 'Amr said: because this one in *al-Naml* is an interrogative, whereas the other is a negation. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the sukun in "fa-qala ma li".

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: some people claimed that they wished to distinguish between what is an initial subject (*mubtada'*) and what is conjoined to what precedes it. This is nothing. It is simply the *ya'* of the self (*ya' al-nafs*): among the Arabs some pronounce it with a fatha and some with a sukun, so they recited in both dialects. The eloquent usage for the *ya'* of the self is that it should be vowelled with a fatha, since it is a noun and consists of a single letter, and it was preferable not to make it sukun, which would diminish the noun.

﴿Or was he among the absent?﴾ Here *am* means "rather".

**Issue Four:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾. This is evidence that the punishment is proportionate to the offence, not to the size of the body. Nevertheless, the one being punished is shown leniency in terms of time and manner. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj that his punishment of the bird was by plucking its feathers. Ibn Jurayj said: all of its feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: its two wings. Solomon did this to the hoopoe as a severe measure against disobedient ones, and as a punishment for its neglect of its duty and its rank. It seems that Allah permitted him to do so, just as He permitted the slaughter of animals and birds for food and other benefits. And Allah knows best.

In *Nawadir al-Usul* it is stated: he said: Sulayman ibn Humayd Abu al-Rabi' al-Iyadi related to us, he said: 'Awn ibn 'Umarah related to us, from al-Husayn al-Ju'fi, from al-Zubayr ibn al-Khirrit, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Allah only turned Solomon's evil away from the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents. (This will come later.)

It has also been said: his punishment is that it be placed among its opposites. From some of them: the narrowest prison is the company of one's opponents. It was also said: "I will oblige it to serve its equals." It was said: "I will confine it in a cage." It was said: "I will make it a target for the sun after plucking it." It was said: "I will banish it from my service." Kings discipline by estrangement, by separating the body from what it is accustomed to.

The verb is emphasized with the heavy *nun*, and it is obligatory, whether heavy or light. Abu Hatim said: if it were recited as "la-u'adhdhibannahu 'adhaban shadidan aw la-adhbahannahu", it would be permissible.

﴿Or he shall bring me a clear authority﴾, that is, with a clear proof. The *lam* in "la-ya'tiyannani" is not the *lam* of oath, because Solomon would not swear by the act of the hoopoe. But since it came directly after "la-u'adhdhibannahu", which is something by which an oath may be sworn, he gave it the same treatment. Ibn Kathir alone recited "la-ya'tiyannanni" with two *nun*s.

**Issue Five:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So it tarried not long﴾, that is, the hoopoe. The majority of readers recited with a *damma* on the *kaf*, while 'Asim alone recited it with a *fatha*. The meaning in both recitations is "it remained." Sibawayh said: *makatha yamkutha mukuthan*, just as they say *qa'ada ya'qudu qu'udan*. He said: *makatha* is like *zarufa*. Others said: the *fatha* is better because of His saying "*makithina*" (remaining), since it derives from *makatha*. It is said: *makatha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun*, and *makutha yamkutha* like *'azuma ya'zumu*, so he is *makith* like *'azim*. And *makutha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun* like *hamudha yahmudu*, so he is *hamid*.

The pronoun in "makatha" may refer to Solomon, meaning: Solomon remained, after the inspection and the threat, not for a long time, that is, not for a long period. It may also refer to the hoopoe, which is the more common view.

Then it came: ﴿and said: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. This is the **sixth issue**: that is, I have learned what you have not learned of the matter. In this there is a refutation of those who say that prophets know the unseen. Al-Farra' reported *ahatu* with the *ta'* assimilated into the *ta'*. He also reported *ahattu* with the *ta'* changed into a *ta'* and assimilated.

**Issue Seven:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾. He informed Solomon of what he did not know, and he defended himself against what Solomon had threatened him with, namely punishment and slaughter.

The majority recited *Saba'in* with *tanwin* (*sarf*). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *Saba'a* with a *fatha* on the *hamzah* and without *tanwin* (*tark al-sarf*). The first reading is that it is the name of a man, after whom a people were named. On this is the line of the poet:

*"Those who come to water, and Taym are on the heights of Saba',*
*the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."*

Al-Zajjaj denied that it was the name of a man, and said: "Saba'" is the name of a city known as Ma'rib in Yemen, between it and San'a' a three days' journey. He recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

*"From Saba', those present at Ma'rib, when they built,*
*apart from its flood, the great dam."*

He said: "As for one who does not apply the diptotic declension (lam yasrif), he says it is the name of a city. As for one who applies it, which is the more common practice, it is because it is the name of a land (al-balad), and so it is a masculine noun named after a masculine noun." It was also said that it is the name of a woman after whom the city was named. The sound view is that it is the name of a man, as in the Tirmidhi collection, from the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi, from the Prophet (ﷺ). This will come, God willing, later.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This hadith was hidden from al-Zajjaj, so he struck out blindly." Al-Farra' claimed that al-Ru'asi asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about Saba', and he said: "I do not know what it is." Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Farra' interpreted Abu 'Amr's words to mean that he withheld declension because the word was unknown, and that when a thing is not known it is not declined." Al-Nahhas said: "Abu 'Amr is too exalted to say such a thing. The report of al-Ru'asi from him contains no evidence that he withheld declension because he did not know the word. He only said, 'I do not know it.' If a grammarian is asked about a noun and says, 'I do not know it,' this is no proof that he would withhold declension from it. Rather, the truth lies otherwise: when one does not know the word, the obligation is to decline it, because the original state of nouns is declension. A noun is withheld from declension only because of a cause that enters upon it. The original state is established with certainty, so it is not removed by something unknown." He then mentioned much speech from the grammarians and said at the end: "The ruling on 'Saba'' is what the authoritative report indicates: that it is originally the name of a man. If you apply declension to it, that is because it has become the name of a tribe. If you do not apply declension, you make it the name of a tribe, like Thamud. However, the preferred view according to Sibawayh is declension, and his argument on this is decisive, because since this name can take both masculine and feminine forms, the masculine is more appropriate, since it is the original and the lighter."

Eighth: The verse indicates that the junior may say to the senior, and the student to the scholar: "I have what you do not have," when he has verified and is certain of it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, despite his greatness and knowledge, may Allah be pleased with him, did not have knowledge of seeking permission. The knowledge of tayammum was with 'Ammar and others, and it was hidden from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, so that they said: "The one in major impurity should not perform tayammum." The ruling on the menstruating woman being permitted to leave (Mecca after tawaf) was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit did not know it. The washing of the head of the one in ihram was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but it was hidden from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama. Many such examples exist, so we will not lengthen them.

Ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. When the hoopoe said, "I have come to you from Saba' with certain news," Sulayman said, "And what is that news?" He said, "I found a woman ruling over them," meaning Bilqis daughter of Sharahil, who ruled the people of Saba'. It is said: How was her location hidden from Sulayman, when the distance between his station and her land was near, being a journey of three (days) between Sana'a and Ma'rib? The answer is that Allah, exalted is He, hid that from him for a wisdom, just as He hid Yusuf's place from Ya'qub. It is related that one of her parents was from the jinn. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a matter the atheists deny, and they say: 'The jinn do not eat or give birth.' They lie, may Allah curse them all. That is true, and their marriage is rationally permissible. If it is established by transmission, then so be it." I say: Abu Dawud related from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "A delegation of the jinn came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, forbid your community to clean themselves with a bone, dung, or a skull, for Allah has placed provision for us in them.'" In Sahih Muslim it says: He said: "For you is every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, which falls into your hands with more meat than it had, and every dung is fodder for your animals." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not clean yourselves with them, for they are the food of your jinn brothers." In Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: I asked, "What is the matter with the bone and the dung?" He said: "They are from the food of the jinn. A delegation of jinn of Nasibin came to me, excellent jinn, and they asked me for provisions. So I asked Allah, exalted is He, that they should not pass by a bone or dung without finding food on it." All of this is explicit that they eat. As for their marriage, the reference to it has already been made in "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra') [[See vol. 10, p. 289, first or second edition.]] at His saying: "And share with them in wealth and children." Wuhayb ibn Jarir ibn Hazim related from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, from 'Uthman ibn Hadir, who said: The mother of Bilqis was from the jinn, called Balʿama daughter of Shaysan. More explanation of this will come, God willing.

Tenth: Al-Bukhari related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Khosrow their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is an explicit text that a woman cannot be a caliph, and there is no disagreement about it." It is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not authentically established from him. Perhaps it was transmitted from him as it was transmitted from Abu Hanifa, that she may judge only in matters in which she is a witness, not that she be a judge absolutely, nor that a written document be issued stating that so-and-so is placed in authority over judgment. Rather, the proper way is arbitration and delegation in a single case. This is the most reasonable assumption about Abu Hanifa and Ibn Jarir. It is related from 'Umar that he appointed a woman over the market inspection (hisba). But this is not authentic, so do not pay attention to it, for it is one of the fabrications of the innovators in hadith. This question was debated by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, the Maliki Ash'ari, with Abu al-Faraj ibn Tarar, the shaykh of the Shafi'is. Abu al-Faraj said: "The evidence that a woman may judge is that the purpose of judgments is the enforcement of the judge's rulings, the hearing of evidence, and the settlement of disputes between litigants, and this is possible for a woman as it is for a man." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr objected to him and refuted his statement by appealing to the Great Imamate, since its purpose is guarding the frontiers, managing affairs, protecting the realm, collecting the land tax and returning it to its rightful recipients, and this cannot be done by a woman as it can be done by a man. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The words of both shaykhs on this question are worthless, for a woman cannot appear in a council, nor mix with men, nor converse with them as an equal with an equal, for if she is a young woman it is forbidden to look at her or speak with her, and if she is a barzah [[The barzah here means an older woman who does not veil as a young woman does, yet is chaste, sensible, and sits with people and talks with them.]] there is no single assembly in which she gathers with men, mingling with them and debating them. Whoever imagines this, or believes it, will never prosper."

Eleventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she has been given of everything﴾: this is hyperbole, meaning of what a kingdom needs. It was also said: the meaning is that she was given of everything in her time, a thing, and the object was omitted because the speech indicates it.

(And she has a great throne): that is, a seat, and it was described as great in its form and in the rank of sovereignty. It was said: it was of gold, and she sat upon it. It was also said: "throne" here means kingship, but the first is more correct, because of His saying: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask how the hoopoe equated the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah in the description of greatness? I say: there is a vast difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is glorifying it in comparison to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the throne of Allah as great is glorifying it in relation to what He created of the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Abbas said: Her throne was eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high in the sky, adorned with pearls, red rubies, and green emeralds. Qatada said: its legs were pearls and jewels, and it was covered with brocade and silk, and had seven locks upon it. Muqatil said: it was eighty cubits [by eighty cubits] [[From b and k.]] and its height from the ground was eighty cubits, and it was adorned with jewels. Ibn Ishaq said: Women served her, and there were six hundred women for her service. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that she was a woman who was made ruler over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from an unbelieving people.

Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It was said: this people were among those who worshipped the sun, because they were heretics, as is related. It was also said: they were Magians who worshipped lights. It is related from Nafi' that the pause is at "throne" ('arsh). Al-Mahdawi said: "Then 'great' (ʿazim) is connected to what follows it, and according to this it would have to be: 'great' that I found her, meaning my finding her an unbeliever." Ibn al-Anbari said: "'And she has a great throne' is a good pause, and it is not permissible to pause at 'throne' and begin with 'great, I found her' except for one who reads with a fatha, because 'great' is an adjective of 'throne.' If it were connected to 'I found her' you would say 'great (feminine) I found her,' and this is impossible in every respect." Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Shahriyar related to me, saying: Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn ibn al-Aswad al-'Ijli related to us, from some people of knowledge, that he said: The pause is at "throne" and the beginning is at "great," meaning: great is their worship of the sun and the moon. He said: I have heard someone support this view and argue that her throne is too insignificant and too minor a matter for Allah to describe it as great. Ibn al-Anbari said: "My preferred view is what I mentioned first, because there is no evidence for implying the worship of the sun and moon. It is not unreasonable for the hoopoe to describe her throne as great when he saw it extending in length and width, and its following the grammatical case of 'throne' is evidence that it is its adjective."

(And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them): that is, what they were engaged in of disbelief. (And turned them away from the way): that is, from the path of monotheism. By this he shows that what is not the path of monotheism is not a path by which one truly benefits.

**(So they are not guided)** to God and His oneness. **Thirteenth**: His saying, ﴿that they should not prostrate to God﴾. Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read "ألا يسجدوا لله" with the *shaddah* on "ألّا" (*alla*, "that not"). Ibn al-Anbari said: "*fa-hum la yahtadun*" is not a complete stop for those who read "ألّا" with the *shaddah*, because the meaning is: "Satan made their deeds seem good to them, so that they would not prostrate." Al-Nahhas said: it is "*an*" with "*la*" added to it, and "*an*" is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said: it depends on "zayyana" (made seem good), meaning "He made it seem good to them so that they would not prostrate to God." Al-Kisa'i said: it depends on "fa-sadda-hum" (so He barred them), meaning "He barred them from prostrating." In both views it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). Al-Yazidi and Ali ibn Sulayman said: "*an*" is a substitute (*badal*) for "a'malahum" (their deeds) and is in the accusative position. Abu 'Amr said: "*an*" is in the genitive position as a substitute for "al-sabil" (the way). It was also said: the governing word for it is "la yahtadun," meaning "they are not guided that they should prostrate to God," i.e., they do not know that this is obligatory upon them. In this view "la" is extra, as in His saying, "*ma mana'aka alla tasjuda*" ("what prevented you from prostrating?"), meaning "what prevented you from prostrating?" On this reading there is no place for a prostration, because it is a report about them abandoning prostration, either through adornment, through barring, or through preventing guidance.

Al-Zuhri, al-Kisa'i and others read: "ألا يا اسجدوا لله" ("alla"), with a light pronunciation,[[Alusi: "ألا" with light pronunciation, meaning that it is for opening speech (*istiftah*), and "يا" is a vocative particle, with the addressee omitted, i.e., "Alā yā qawm usjudū" (Oh people, prostrate!). The alif of "يا" and the alif of connection (*hamzat al-wasl*) in "usjudū" were dropped, and the yā was written joined to the sīn, contrary to analogy.]] meaning "Alā yā hā'ulā'i usjudū" ("Oh, you people, prostrate!"), because "يا" is used to address nouns, not verbs. Sibawayh recited:

*Yā la'nata Allāhi wal-aqwāmi kullihim*
*wal-ṣāliḥīna 'alā Sam'ān min jār*

Sibawayh said: the "yā" is not for the curse, because if it were for the curse he would have put it in the accusative, since it would become a vocative with a following genitive; rather its underlying form is "Yā hā'ulā'i la'natu Allāhi wal-aqwāmi 'alā Sam'ān" ("O you people, the curse of God and the peoples be upon Sam'ān"). Some transmitted from the Arabs by hearing: "Alā yā irḥamū, alā yā uṣduqū" ("Oh, have mercy! Oh, be truthful!"). They intend: "Alā yā qawmu irḥamū, uṣduqū" ("Oh people, have mercy, be truthful!"). According to this reading, "usjudū" is in the jussive position as an imperative, and one pauses at "alā yā," then begins: "usjudū." Al-Kisa'i said: "I never heard the elders reciting it except with the light pronunciation, with the intention of the imperative." In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "*Alā hal tasjudūna lillāh*" with *ta'* and *nūn*. In the reading of Ubayy: "*Alā tasjudūna lillāh*." These two readings are a proof for the one who reads it lightly.

Al-Zajjaj said: the light reading requires the obligation of prostration, unlike the heavy reading. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the heavy reading. Abu Hatim said: the light reading is a good option, except that in it the report is cut off from the matter of Sheba and then returns to mentioning them, whereas the heavy reading is a report that follows one part after another without a break in its middle. Al-Nahhas said something similar. He said: the light reading is remote, because the speech would be an interjection (*mu'tarid*), whereas with the heavy reading the speech is coherent. Also, the written text (*sawad*) is not in agreement with this reading, because two alifs have been deleted from it, and such abbreviation is only done by deleting a single alif, as in "*Yā 'Īsā ibn Maryam*."

Ibn al-Anbari said: the alif of "usjudū" is dropped, as it is dropped with "hā'ulā'i" when it is shown. When the alif of "yā" was dropped and the alif of "usjudū" joined to it, it too was dropped. Its dropping is taken as an indication of abbreviation and as a preference for what is lighter and has fewer letters.

Al-Jawhari said at the end of his book: Some said: "yā" in this place is only for alerting (*tanbīh*), as if he had said: "Alā usjudū lillāh." When "yā" for alerting was introduced before it, the alif in "usjudū" was dropped because it is an alif of connection, and the alif in "yā" went away because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters, since it and the sīn are both unvoweled. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Alā yā-slamī yā dāra Mayya 'alā al-bilā*
*wa lā zāla munhalan bi-ja'rā'ika al-qaṭr*

Al-Jurjani said: it is an interjected speech from the hoopoe, or from Solomon, or from God, meaning "*alā li-yasjudū*" ("Let them prostrate!"), like His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the days of God﴾. It was said that it is an imperative, meaning "*li-yaghfirū*" ("let them forgive"). On this view, the writing of the Mushaf is also arranged, meaning there is no vocative here.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was said that it is from the speech of the hoopoe up to His saying, "the Mighty," and this is the view of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq. It is objected that he is not addressed, so how can he speak with the meaning of a legal ruling? It is possible that it is from the saying of Solomon when the hoopoe informed him about the people. It is also possible that it is from the saying of God, the Exalted, so it is an interjection between the two statements, and this is the established view upon reflection. The heavy reading of "ألّا" gives that the speech belongs to the hoopoe, whereas the light reading prevents that. The light reading requires the command to prostrate to God, the Mighty and Majestic, due to the imperative, as we have explained.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "Is the prostration of recitation obligatory in both readings, or in one of them?" I say: It is obligatory in both, because the places of prostration are either a command to do it, or praise for the one who did it, or blame for the one who abandoned it, and one of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is blame for the one who abandons it. I say: God has reported about the disbelievers that they prostrate, as in "al-Inshiqaq," and the Prophet ﷺ prostrated in it, as is established in al-Bukhari and others; so likewise in "al-Naml." And God knows best. Al-Zamakhshari: What al-Zajjaj mentioned about the obligation of prostration with the light reading and not the heavy reading is not to be relied upon.

﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾ (*al-khab'*): the hidden of the heavens is its rain, and the hidden of the earth is its treasures and its plants. Qatadah said: *al-khab'* is secret. Al-Nahhas said: this is better, i.e., whatever is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and it is shown by "what you conceal and what you disclose." [[In the manuscript of the original, with the *bā'*, and it is the reading of the common people, as will come.]] Ikrimah and Malik ibn Dinar read: "*al-khabu*" with a *fatha* on the *bā'* and without a *hamzah*. Al-Mahdawi said: this is the analogical lightening, and he mentioned those who drop the *hamzah* when stopping. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Hatim related that Ikrimah read "*al-khaba*" with a non-hamzated alif, and claimed that this is not permissible in Arabic, and argued that if he lightens the *hamzah* he moves its vowel onto the *bā'* and says "*al-khab fi al-samawat wal-ard*," and if he changes the *hamzah* he says "*al-khabyi*" with the *bā'* sukun and a *yā'* after it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach them, except that when he left his town he did not meet anyone more knowledgeable than him. Sibawayh related from the Arabs that they change the *hamzah* into an alif when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is open-vowelled; they change it into a *wāw* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is closed-vowelled; and they change it into a *yā'* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is vowelled with a kasra. So they say: "*hadha al-wathw*," "I was amazed at the *wathy*," "I saw the *wathā*," from "*wuthi'at yaduhu*" (his hand was sprained). Likewise: "*hadha al-khabw*," "I was amazed at the *khabyi*," and "I saw the *khaba*." This was done because the *hamzah* is light, so these letters were substituted for it. Sibawayh related from a group of the Banu Tamim and Banu Asad that they say: "*hadha al-khabu*," they put a *ḍamma* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, and they keep the *hamzah*, and they put a kasra on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a kasra, and they put a *fatha* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *fatha*. Sibawayh also related that they put a kasra even when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, but this is from the Banu Tamim, so they say "*al-radī'*" [[*al-radih* means the companion.]], and he claimed that they did not put a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* because they disliked a *ḍamma* preceded by a kasra, since there is no pattern *fi'ul* in the language. All these are dialects that differ from the dialect in which the community recited. In the reading of Abdullah: "*alladhī yukhriju al-khaba min al-samawat*," and "*min*" and "*fi*" alternate; the Arabs say: "*la-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fīkum*," meaning "*minkum*," as al-Farra' said.

﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾: The common reading is with *yā'* in both. This reading indicates that the verse is from the speech of the hoopoe, and that God singled him out with knowledge of His oneness and the obligation to prostrate to Him, and of the denial of their prostration to the sun, and of attributing it to Satan, and of his adorning it for them, with what He singled him out with from among the birds and all other animals, of subtle knowledge that sound minds hardly reach. Al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Hafs and al-Kisa'i read "*tukhfūna*" and "*tu'linūna*" with *tā'*, in address. This reading indicates that the verse is from the address of God, the Mighty and Majestic, to the nation of Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿God— there is no god but He, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾: Ibn Muhaysin read "*al-'azīmi*" with *raf'* as an adjective of God. The rest read with *khafḍ* as an adjective of "the Throne." It was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is within it and in its grasp.

**Fourteenth**: His saying, ﴿We shall see﴾ (*sanandhuru*), from "seeing," which is reflection and examination.

(أَصَدَقْتَ أَمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ) in your statement. Here "kunta" means "anta" (you are). He said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, and he did not say "we shall look into your affair," because when the hoopoe openly boasted of knowledge in his words, ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, Sulayman openly replied to him, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or lied.﴾ That was a rebuke (kifa'an) to what he had said. Fifteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, is evidence that the imam must accept the excuse of his subjects and ward off punishment from them based on the inner state of their excuses, despite the outward appearance of their conditions, because Sulayman did not punish the hoopoe when it offered its excuse to him. The hoopoe's truthfulness became an excuse only because it reported something that called for jihad, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, was fond of jihad. In the Sahih: "No one loves excuses more than Allah; for this reason He sent down the Book and sent the Messengers." Umar accepted the excuse of al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi and did not punish him. However, the imam may test such an excuse when a legal ruling of the Shari'a depends on it, as Sulayman did, for when the hoopoe said, ﴿I found a woman ruling over them, who has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne﴾, desire did not stir him, nor did love of increasing his kingdom move him to seek more, until it said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah.﴾ Then what he heard angered him, and he sought to verify what he had been told and to acquire knowledge of what was hidden from him in this matter, so he said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars.﴾ A similar report is found in the Sahih from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, when Umar consulted the people about the miscarriage of a woman (al-imlas, i.e., a woman whose belly is struck so that she casts out her fetus). Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba said: "I witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) judge in such a case that a ghurra (a slave or a female slave) must be given." He said: Umar said, "Bring me someone who will testify with you." So Muhammad ibn Maslama testified for him. In another narration, Umar said, "Do not leave until you bring the way out of this matter," so I left and found Muhammad ibn Maslama, brought him, and he testified. A similar report is the hadith of Abu Musa concerning seeking permission (to enter) and other matters. Sixteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: In it there are five readings. "Fa-alqihi ilayhim" with the yā' affirmed in pronunciation. With the yā' omitted and the kasra remaining to indicate it, "fa-alqihi ilayhim." With the hā' pronounced with a ḍamma and the wāw kept, according to the original form, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." With the wāw omitted and the ḍamma kept, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." The fifth dialect, which Hamza recited, is with the hā' sukun: "fa-alqih ilayhim." Al-Nahhas said: According to the grammarians this is not permissible except by a remote stratagem, namely by assuming a pause. I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: "Do not pay attention to this justification. If it were permissible to join (the word to what follows) while intending a pause, it would be permissible to drop the i'rab (grammatical inflection) from nouns." He said: "ilayhim" is in the plural form, and he did not say "ilayha," because he had said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun﴾. It is as if he said: "Cast it to those whose religion is this," out of concern for the matter of religion and his preoccupation with it over other things, and for this reason the address in the letter was framed in the plural. It is narrated in the stories of this verse that the hoopoe arrived and found walls and barriers between this queen and him, so it made for an opening (kuwwa) which Bilqis had made so that the sun might enter through it at its rising, because of her worship of it. It entered through it and dropped the letter upon Bilqis, who, it is said, was asleep. When she awoke she found it and was startled, thinking someone had entered upon her. Then she stood up and found her condition as she had known it, so she looked toward the opening, anxious about the matter of the sun, and saw the hoopoe, and then she understood. Wahb and Ibn Zayd said: There was an opening facing the sunrise, and when the sun rose she would prostrate. The hoopoe blocked it with its wing, so the sun rose while she did not know. When she was slow to notice the sun and stood to look, it threw the document to her. When she saw the seal she trembled and submitted, for the kingdom of Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in his ring. She read it, then gathered the chiefs of her people and addressed them with what comes after. Muqatil said: The hoopoe carried the letter in its beak and flew until it stood over the head of the woman, while around her were the troops and soldiers. It fluttered for a while while the people looked at it. The woman raised her head, and it dropped the letter into her lap. Seventeenth issue: This verse is evidence for sending letters to polytheists, conveying the call to them, and inviting them to Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Kisra, Qaysar, and to every tyrant, as has been mentioned in Al 'Imran. Eighteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Then turn away from them﴾. His command to turn away is a matter of good manners, so that he withdraws in the manner in which one behaves with kings. The meaning is: remain nearby until you see their response. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to turn away in the sense of returning to him, i.e., "cast it and return." He said: His saying, ﴿then watch what they return﴾, is in the sense of coming before his saying, ﴿then turn away,﴾ and the arrangement of the speech is clearer: i.e., cast it, then turn away, and in the meantime, "watch" means wait. It was also said: "watch" means "know," as in His saying, ﴿the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. That is: know what they return, i.e., what they answer and what words they return. It was also said: ﴿then watch what they return﴾ means they exchange words among themselves.

**Issue One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. He mentions another matter that occurred to him on the journey in which the ants were mentioned earlier. *Tafaqqud* means seeking out what has gone missing from you. *Al-tayr* (the birds) is a collective noun whose singular is *tair*. Here *al-tayr* refers to the species of birds and to their flocks. They used to accompany him on his travels and shade him with their wings.

People differed about the meaning of his inspecting the birds. One group said: this was in accordance with what the care of royal affairs requires, and with his attention to every part of them. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Another group said: rather, he inspected the birds because the sun had come in from the place where the hoopoe was when it was absent, so this was the reason for inspecting the birds, in order to find out from where the sun had entered. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: he only sought the hoopoe because he needed to know how deep the water was beneath the surface of the earth, since he had halted in a barren wilderness where there was no water. The hoopoe could see the inside and the outside of the earth, so it would tell Solomon where the water was, and then the jinn would extract it in a short time, stripping the surface of the earth away from it as a sheep is skinned. This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas on the authority of Ibn Salam.

Abu Mijlaz said: Ibn 'Abbas said to 'Abdullah ibn Salam: "I want to ask you about three issues." He said: "You ask me while you recite the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes, three times." He said: "Why did Solomon inspect the hoopoe in particular, rather than the rest of the birds?" He said: "He needed water and did not know its depth, or he said its distance, and the hoopoe knew that, unlike the other birds, so he inspected it."

In the *Kitab al-Naqqash* it is stated: the hoopoe was an engineer. It was also reported that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq heard Ibn 'Abbas mention the matter of the hoopoe, and said to him: "Stop, O one who stops (much)! How can the hoopoe see beneath the earth when it does not see the snare when it falls into it?!" Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind." Mujahid said: it was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "How did he inspect the hoopoe among the birds?" He said: "He alighted at a place and did not know how far the water was, while the hoopoe was guided to it, so he wanted to ask it." Mujahid said: I said: "How could it be guided when a boy sets a snare for it and catches it?" He said: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "No one can give this answer except a scholar of the Qur'an." I say: this answer was already given by the hoopoe to Solomon, as mentioned above.

They also recited:

*When Allah wills a matter for a man, who has intellect, insight and vision,*
*and a stratagem he devises to avert what the decrees bring upon him of harm,*
*He covers over his hearing and his intellect, and draws out his mind as a hair is drawn out.*
*Then, when He has executed His judgment upon him, He returns his intellect to him so that he may take heed.*

Al-Kalbi said: he had only one hoopoe on his journey. And Allah knows best.

**Issue Two:** In this verse there is evidence that the ruler (*imam*) should inspect the conditions of his subjects and protect them. Consider the hoopoe, despite its small size: how its condition was not hidden from Solomon. How much more so, then, should this be true of the great affairs of the kingdom. May Allah have mercy on 'Umar, for he followed this course. He said: "If a lamb on the bank of the Euphrates were seized by a wolf, 'Umar would be held accountable for it." So what do you think of a governor through whose hands cities are conquered, while the subjects are lost and the shepherds are lost too?

In the *Sahih* it is reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab set out for Syria, until when he reached Sargh [[Sargh (with the *ra* vowelled or unvowelled): a village in the Wadi Tabuk on the route to Syria.]], the commanders of the armies met him, Abu 'Ubaydah and his companions, and informed him that the plague had broken out in Syria. (The hadith continues.) Our scholars said: this departure by 'Umar took place after Bayt al-Maqdis had been conquered, in the year seventeen (AH), as recorded by Khalifah ibn Khayyat.

He would inspect the conditions of his subjects and of his commanders personally. The Qur'an and the Sunnah have indicated, and we have explained, what the ruler is obliged to do in inspecting the conditions of his subjects, personally carrying this out, and travelling for it, however long the journey. May Allah have mercy on Ibn al-Mubarak when he says:

*Has anything corrupted the religion except the kings*
*and the evil scholars and their monks?*

**Issue Three:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe﴾. That is: what is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see it? This is of the type of inversion (*qalb*) whose meaning is not understood from the wording alone. It is like your saying: "What is the matter with me that I see you downcast?", meaning: what is the matter with you? *Al-hudhud* is a well-known bird, and *hadhdhadah* is its call.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the intended meaning of the speech is "the hoopoe is absent", but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and so he asked in the form of a rebuke about this necessary consequence. This is a kind of conciseness. The interrogative in the phrase "What is the matter with me" takes the place of the *alif* that would be followed by *am*.

It has also been said: he said "What is the matter with me that I do not see the hoopoe" because he considered his own state. He knew that he had been granted great dominion and that creation had been subjected to him. Thus the obligation of thankfulness fell upon him, through establishing obedience and maintaining justice. When he lost the blessing of the hoopoe, he feared that he might have fallen short in his duty of thankfulness, and for this reason it was taken from him. So he began to inspect himself, saying: "What is the matter with me?"

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the Sufi shaykhs do this when they lose what they hoped for; they inspect their deeds. This is in matters of etiquette. So how about us today, when we fall short in the obligatory duties!

Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Hisham and Ayyub recited *mali* with a fatha on the *ya'*, and likewise in *Ya-Sin*: ﴿And what is the matter with me that I do not worship Him who originated me﴾. Hamzah and Ya'qub made it sukun. The rest, the Madinan readers and Abu 'Amr, recited the one in *Ya-Sin* with a fatha and this one with sukun. Abu 'Amr said: because this one in *al-Naml* is an interrogative, whereas the other is a negation. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd preferred the sukun in "fa-qala ma li".

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: some people claimed that they wished to distinguish between what is an initial subject (*mubtada'*) and what is conjoined to what precedes it. This is nothing. It is simply the *ya'* of the self (*ya' al-nafs*): among the Arabs some pronounce it with a fatha and some with a sukun, so they recited in both dialects. The eloquent usage for the *ya'* of the self is that it should be vowelled with a fatha, since it is a noun and consists of a single letter, and it was preferable not to make it sukun, which would diminish the noun.

﴿Or was he among the absent?﴾ Here *am* means "rather".

**Issue Four:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾. This is evidence that the punishment is proportionate to the offence, not to the size of the body. Nevertheless, the one being punished is shown leniency in terms of time and manner. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj that his punishment of the bird was by plucking its feathers. Ibn Jurayj said: all of its feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: its two wings. Solomon did this to the hoopoe as a severe measure against disobedient ones, and as a punishment for its neglect of its duty and its rank. It seems that Allah permitted him to do so, just as He permitted the slaughter of animals and birds for food and other benefits. And Allah knows best.

In *Nawadir al-Usul* it is stated: he said: Sulayman ibn Humayd Abu al-Rabi' al-Iyadi related to us, he said: 'Awn ibn 'Umarah related to us, from al-Husayn al-Ju'fi, from al-Zubayr ibn al-Khirrit, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Allah only turned Solomon's evil away from the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents. (This will come later.)

It has also been said: his punishment is that it be placed among its opposites. From some of them: the narrowest prison is the company of one's opponents. It was also said: "I will oblige it to serve its equals." It was said: "I will confine it in a cage." It was said: "I will make it a target for the sun after plucking it." It was said: "I will banish it from my service." Kings discipline by estrangement, by separating the body from what it is accustomed to.

The verb is emphasized with the heavy *nun*, and it is obligatory, whether heavy or light. Abu Hatim said: if it were recited as "la-u'adhdhibannahu 'adhaban shadidan aw la-adhbahannahu", it would be permissible.

﴿Or he shall bring me a clear authority﴾, that is, with a clear proof. The *lam* in "la-ya'tiyannani" is not the *lam* of oath, because Solomon would not swear by the act of the hoopoe. But since it came directly after "la-u'adhdhibannahu", which is something by which an oath may be sworn, he gave it the same treatment. Ibn Kathir alone recited "la-ya'tiyannanni" with two *nun*s.

**Issue Five:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So it tarried not long﴾, that is, the hoopoe. The majority of readers recited with a *damma* on the *kaf*, while 'Asim alone recited it with a *fatha*. The meaning in both recitations is "it remained." Sibawayh said: *makatha yamkutha mukuthan*, just as they say *qa'ada ya'qudu qu'udan*. He said: *makatha* is like *zarufa*. Others said: the *fatha* is better because of His saying "*makithina*" (remaining), since it derives from *makatha*. It is said: *makatha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun*, and *makutha yamkutha* like *'azuma ya'zumu*, so he is *makith* like *'azim*. And *makutha yamkutha fa-huwa makithun* like *hamudha yahmudu*, so he is *hamid*.

The pronoun in "makatha" may refer to Solomon, meaning: Solomon remained, after the inspection and the threat, not for a long time, that is, not for a long period. It may also refer to the hoopoe, which is the more common view.

Then it came: ﴿and said: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. This is the **sixth issue**: that is, I have learned what you have not learned of the matter. In this there is a refutation of those who say that prophets know the unseen. Al-Farra' reported *ahatu* with the *ta'* assimilated into the *ta'*. He also reported *ahattu* with the *ta'* changed into a *ta'* and assimilated.

**Issue Seven:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾. He informed Solomon of what he did not know, and he defended himself against what Solomon had threatened him with, namely punishment and slaughter.

The majority recited *Saba'in* with *tanwin* (*sarf*). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *Saba'a* with a *fatha* on the *hamzah* and without *tanwin* (*tark al-sarf*). The first reading is that it is the name of a man, after whom a people were named. On this is the line of the poet:

*"Those who come to water, and Taym are on the heights of Saba',*
*the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."*

Al-Zajjaj denied that it was the name of a man, and said: "Saba'" is the name of a city known as Ma'rib in Yemen, between it and San'a' a three days' journey. He recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

*"From Saba', those present at Ma'rib, when they built,*
*apart from its flood, the great dam."*

He said: "As for one who does not apply the diptotic declension (lam yasrif), he says it is the name of a city. As for one who applies it, which is the more common practice, it is because it is the name of a land (al-balad), and so it is a masculine noun named after a masculine noun." It was also said that it is the name of a woman after whom the city was named. The sound view is that it is the name of a man, as in the Tirmidhi collection, from the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi, from the Prophet (ﷺ). This will come, God willing, later.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This hadith was hidden from al-Zajjaj, so he struck out blindly." Al-Farra' claimed that al-Ru'asi asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about Saba', and he said: "I do not know what it is." Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Farra' interpreted Abu 'Amr's words to mean that he withheld declension because the word was unknown, and that when a thing is not known it is not declined." Al-Nahhas said: "Abu 'Amr is too exalted to say such a thing. The report of al-Ru'asi from him contains no evidence that he withheld declension because he did not know the word. He only said, 'I do not know it.' If a grammarian is asked about a noun and says, 'I do not know it,' this is no proof that he would withhold declension from it. Rather, the truth lies otherwise: when one does not know the word, the obligation is to decline it, because the original state of nouns is declension. A noun is withheld from declension only because of a cause that enters upon it. The original state is established with certainty, so it is not removed by something unknown." He then mentioned much speech from the grammarians and said at the end: "The ruling on 'Saba'' is what the authoritative report indicates: that it is originally the name of a man. If you apply declension to it, that is because it has become the name of a tribe. If you do not apply declension, you make it the name of a tribe, like Thamud. However, the preferred view according to Sibawayh is declension, and his argument on this is decisive, because since this name can take both masculine and feminine forms, the masculine is more appropriate, since it is the original and the lighter."

Eighth: The verse indicates that the junior may say to the senior, and the student to the scholar: "I have what you do not have," when he has verified and is certain of it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, despite his greatness and knowledge, may Allah be pleased with him, did not have knowledge of seeking permission. The knowledge of tayammum was with 'Ammar and others, and it was hidden from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, so that they said: "The one in major impurity should not perform tayammum." The ruling on the menstruating woman being permitted to leave (Mecca after tawaf) was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit did not know it. The washing of the head of the one in ihram was known to Ibn 'Abbas, but it was hidden from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama. Many such examples exist, so we will not lengthen them.

Ninth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. When the hoopoe said, "I have come to you from Saba' with certain news," Sulayman said, "And what is that news?" He said, "I found a woman ruling over them," meaning Bilqis daughter of Sharahil, who ruled the people of Saba'. It is said: How was her location hidden from Sulayman, when the distance between his station and her land was near, being a journey of three (days) between Sana'a and Ma'rib? The answer is that Allah, exalted is He, hid that from him for a wisdom, just as He hid Yusuf's place from Ya'qub. It is related that one of her parents was from the jinn. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a matter the atheists deny, and they say: 'The jinn do not eat or give birth.' They lie, may Allah curse them all. That is true, and their marriage is rationally permissible. If it is established by transmission, then so be it." I say: Abu Dawud related from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "A delegation of the jinn came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, forbid your community to clean themselves with a bone, dung, or a skull, for Allah has placed provision for us in them.'" In Sahih Muslim it says: He said: "For you is every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, which falls into your hands with more meat than it had, and every dung is fodder for your animals." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not clean yourselves with them, for they are the food of your jinn brothers." In Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: I asked, "What is the matter with the bone and the dung?" He said: "They are from the food of the jinn. A delegation of jinn of Nasibin came to me, excellent jinn, and they asked me for provisions. So I asked Allah, exalted is He, that they should not pass by a bone or dung without finding food on it." All of this is explicit that they eat. As for their marriage, the reference to it has already been made in "Subhan" (Surah al-Isra') [[See vol. 10, p. 289, first or second edition.]] at His saying: "And share with them in wealth and children." Wuhayb ibn Jarir ibn Hazim related from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, from 'Uthman ibn Hadir, who said: The mother of Bilqis was from the jinn, called Balʿama daughter of Shaysan. More explanation of this will come, God willing.

Tenth: Al-Bukhari related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Khosrow their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is an explicit text that a woman cannot be a caliph, and there is no disagreement about it." It is transmitted from Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not authentically established from him. Perhaps it was transmitted from him as it was transmitted from Abu Hanifa, that she may judge only in matters in which she is a witness, not that she be a judge absolutely, nor that a written document be issued stating that so-and-so is placed in authority over judgment. Rather, the proper way is arbitration and delegation in a single case. This is the most reasonable assumption about Abu Hanifa and Ibn Jarir. It is related from 'Umar that he appointed a woman over the market inspection (hisba). But this is not authentic, so do not pay attention to it, for it is one of the fabrications of the innovators in hadith. This question was debated by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, the Maliki Ash'ari, with Abu al-Faraj ibn Tarar, the shaykh of the Shafi'is. Abu al-Faraj said: "The evidence that a woman may judge is that the purpose of judgments is the enforcement of the judge's rulings, the hearing of evidence, and the settlement of disputes between litigants, and this is possible for a woman as it is for a man." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr objected to him and refuted his statement by appealing to the Great Imamate, since its purpose is guarding the frontiers, managing affairs, protecting the realm, collecting the land tax and returning it to its rightful recipients, and this cannot be done by a woman as it can be done by a man. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The words of both shaykhs on this question are worthless, for a woman cannot appear in a council, nor mix with men, nor converse with them as an equal with an equal, for if she is a young woman it is forbidden to look at her or speak with her, and if she is a barzah [[The barzah here means an older woman who does not veil as a young woman does, yet is chaste, sensible, and sits with people and talks with them.]] there is no single assembly in which she gathers with men, mingling with them and debating them. Whoever imagines this, or believes it, will never prosper."

Eleventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she has been given of everything﴾: this is hyperbole, meaning of what a kingdom needs. It was also said: the meaning is that she was given of everything in her time, a thing, and the object was omitted because the speech indicates it.

(And she has a great throne): that is, a seat, and it was described as great in its form and in the rank of sovereignty. It was said: it was of gold, and she sat upon it. It was also said: "throne" here means kingship, but the first is more correct, because of His saying: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask how the hoopoe equated the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah in the description of greatness? I say: there is a vast difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is glorifying it in comparison to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the throne of Allah as great is glorifying it in relation to what He created of the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Abbas said: Her throne was eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high in the sky, adorned with pearls, red rubies, and green emeralds. Qatada said: its legs were pearls and jewels, and it was covered with brocade and silk, and had seven locks upon it. Muqatil said: it was eighty cubits [by eighty cubits] [[From b and k.]] and its height from the ground was eighty cubits, and it was adorned with jewels. Ibn Ishaq said: Women served her, and there were six hundred women for her service. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that she was a woman who was made ruler over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from an unbelieving people.

Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It was said: this people were among those who worshipped the sun, because they were heretics, as is related. It was also said: they were Magians who worshipped lights. It is related from Nafi' that the pause is at "throne" ('arsh). Al-Mahdawi said: "Then 'great' (ʿazim) is connected to what follows it, and according to this it would have to be: 'great' that I found her, meaning my finding her an unbeliever." Ibn al-Anbari said: "'And she has a great throne' is a good pause, and it is not permissible to pause at 'throne' and begin with 'great, I found her' except for one who reads with a fatha, because 'great' is an adjective of 'throne.' If it were connected to 'I found her' you would say 'great (feminine) I found her,' and this is impossible in every respect." Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Shahriyar related to me, saying: Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn ibn al-Aswad al-'Ijli related to us, from some people of knowledge, that he said: The pause is at "throne" and the beginning is at "great," meaning: great is their worship of the sun and the moon. He said: I have heard someone support this view and argue that her throne is too insignificant and too minor a matter for Allah to describe it as great. Ibn al-Anbari said: "My preferred view is what I mentioned first, because there is no evidence for implying the worship of the sun and moon. It is not unreasonable for the hoopoe to describe her throne as great when he saw it extending in length and width, and its following the grammatical case of 'throne' is evidence that it is its adjective."

(And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them): that is, what they were engaged in of disbelief. (And turned them away from the way): that is, from the path of monotheism. By this he shows that what is not the path of monotheism is not a path by which one truly benefits.
