Abu al-Faraj said: "The evidence that a woman may judge is that the purpose of judgments is the enforcement of the judge's rulings, the hearing of evidence, and the settlement of disputes between litigants, and this is possible for a woman as it is for a man." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr objected to him and refuted his statement by appealing to the Great Imamate, since its purpose is guarding the frontiers, managing affairs, protecting the realm, collecting the land tax and returning it to its rightful recipients, and this cannot be done by a woman as it can be done by a man. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The words of both shaykhs on this question are worthless, for a woman cannot appear in a council, nor mix with men, nor converse with them as an equal with an equal, for if she is a young woman it is forbidden to look at her or speak with her, and if she is a barzah [[The barzah here means an older woman who does not veil as a young woman does, yet is chaste, sensible, and sits with people and talks with them.]] there is no single assembly in which she gathers with men, mingling with them and debating them. Whoever imagines this, or believes it, will never prosper."

Eleventh: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she has been given of everything﴾: this is hyperbole, meaning of what a kingdom needs. It was also said: the meaning is that she was given of everything in her time, a thing, and the object was omitted because the speech indicates it.

(And she has a great throne): that is, a seat, and it was described as great in its form and in the rank of sovereignty. It was said: it was of gold, and she sat upon it. It was also said: "throne" here means kingship, but the first is more correct, because of His saying: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask how the hoopoe equated the throne of Bilqis with the throne of Allah in the description of greatness? I say: there is a vast difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is glorifying it in comparison to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the throne of Allah as great is glorifying it in relation to what He created of the heavens and the earth." Ibn 'Abbas said: Her throne was eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high in the sky, adorned with pearls, red rubies, and green emeralds. Qatada said: its legs were pearls and jewels, and it was covered with brocade and silk, and had seven locks upon it. Muqatil said: it was eighty cubits [by eighty cubits] [[From b and k.]] and its height from the ground was eighty cubits, and it was adorned with jewels. Ibn Ishaq said: Women served her, and there were six hundred women for her service. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that she was a woman who was made ruler over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from an unbelieving people.

Twelfth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It was said: this people were among those who worshipped the sun, because they were heretics, as is related. It was also said: they were Magians who worshipped lights. It is related from Nafi' that the pause is at "throne" ('arsh). Al-Mahdawi said: "Then 'great' (ʿazim) is connected to what follows it, and according to this it would have to be: 'great' that I found her, meaning my finding her an unbeliever." Ibn al-Anbari said: "'And she has a great throne' is a good pause, and it is not permissible to pause at 'throne' and begin with 'great, I found her' except for one who reads with a fatha, because 'great' is an adjective of 'throne.' If it were connected to 'I found her' you would say 'great (feminine) I found her,' and this is impossible in every respect." Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Shahriyar related to me, saying: Abu 'Abdullah al-Husayn ibn al-Aswad al-'Ijli related to us, from some people of knowledge, that he said: The pause is at "throne" and the beginning is at "great," meaning: great is their worship of the sun and the moon. He said: I have heard someone support this view and argue that her throne is too insignificant and too minor a matter for Allah to describe it as great. Ibn al-Anbari said: "My preferred view is what I mentioned first, because there is no evidence for implying the worship of the sun and moon. It is not unreasonable for the hoopoe to describe her throne as great when he saw it extending in length and width, and its following the grammatical case of 'throne' is evidence that it is its adjective."

(And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them): that is, what they were engaged in of disbelief. (And turned them away from the way): that is, from the path of monotheism. By this he shows that what is not the path of monotheism is not a path by which one truly benefits.

**(So they are not guided)** to God and His oneness. **Thirteenth**: His saying, ﴿that they should not prostrate to God﴾. Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Hamzah read "ألا يسجدوا لله" with the *shaddah* on "ألّا" (*alla*, "that not"). Ibn al-Anbari said: "*fa-hum la yahtadun*" is not a complete stop for those who read "ألّا" with the *shaddah*, because the meaning is: "Satan made their deeds seem good to them, so that they would not prostrate." Al-Nahhas said: it is "*an*" with "*la*" added to it, and "*an*" is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said: it depends on "zayyana" (made seem good), meaning "He made it seem good to them so that they would not prostrate to God." Al-Kisa'i said: it depends on "fa-sadda-hum" (so He barred them), meaning "He barred them from prostrating." In both views it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). Al-Yazidi and Ali ibn Sulayman said: "*an*" is a substitute (*badal*) for "a'malahum" (their deeds) and is in the accusative position. Abu 'Amr said: "*an*" is in the genitive position as a substitute for "al-sabil" (the way). It was also said: the governing word for it is "la yahtadun," meaning "they are not guided that they should prostrate to God," i.e., they do not know that this is obligatory upon them. In this view "la" is extra, as in His saying, "*ma mana'aka alla tasjuda*" ("what prevented you from prostrating?"), meaning "what prevented you from prostrating?" On this reading there is no place for a prostration, because it is a report about them abandoning prostration, either through adornment, through barring, or through preventing guidance.

Al-Zuhri, al-Kisa'i and others read: "ألا يا اسجدوا لله" ("alla"), with a light pronunciation,[[Alusi: "ألا" with light pronunciation, meaning that it is for opening speech (*istiftah*), and "يا" is a vocative particle, with the addressee omitted, i.e., "Alā yā qawm usjudū" (Oh people, prostrate!). The alif of "يا" and the alif of connection (*hamzat al-wasl*) in "usjudū" were dropped, and the yā was written joined to the sīn, contrary to analogy.]] meaning "Alā yā hā'ulā'i usjudū" ("Oh, you people, prostrate!"), because "يا" is used to address nouns, not verbs. Sibawayh recited:

*Yā la'nata Allāhi wal-aqwāmi kullihim*
*wal-ṣāliḥīna 'alā Sam'ān min jār*

Sibawayh said: the "yā" is not for the curse, because if it were for the curse he would have put it in the accusative, since it would become a vocative with a following genitive; rather its underlying form is "Yā hā'ulā'i la'natu Allāhi wal-aqwāmi 'alā Sam'ān" ("O you people, the curse of God and the peoples be upon Sam'ān"). Some transmitted from the Arabs by hearing: "Alā yā irḥamū, alā yā uṣduqū" ("Oh, have mercy! Oh, be truthful!"). They intend: "Alā yā qawmu irḥamū, uṣduqū" ("Oh people, have mercy, be truthful!"). According to this reading, "usjudū" is in the jussive position as an imperative, and one pauses at "alā yā," then begins: "usjudū." Al-Kisa'i said: "I never heard the elders reciting it except with the light pronunciation, with the intention of the imperative." In the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "*Alā hal tasjudūna lillāh*" with *ta'* and *nūn*. In the reading of Ubayy: "*Alā tasjudūna lillāh*." These two readings are a proof for the one who reads it lightly.

Al-Zajjaj said: the light reading requires the obligation of prostration, unlike the heavy reading. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the heavy reading. Abu Hatim said: the light reading is a good option, except that in it the report is cut off from the matter of Sheba and then returns to mentioning them, whereas the heavy reading is a report that follows one part after another without a break in its middle. Al-Nahhas said something similar. He said: the light reading is remote, because the speech would be an interjection (*mu'tarid*), whereas with the heavy reading the speech is coherent. Also, the written text (*sawad*) is not in agreement with this reading, because two alifs have been deleted from it, and such abbreviation is only done by deleting a single alif, as in "*Yā 'Īsā ibn Maryam*."

Ibn al-Anbari said: the alif of "usjudū" is dropped, as it is dropped with "hā'ulā'i" when it is shown. When the alif of "yā" was dropped and the alif of "usjudū" joined to it, it too was dropped. Its dropping is taken as an indication of abbreviation and as a preference for what is lighter and has fewer letters.

Al-Jawhari said at the end of his book: Some said: "yā" in this place is only for alerting (*tanbīh*), as if he had said: "Alā usjudū lillāh." When "yā" for alerting was introduced before it, the alif in "usjudū" was dropped because it is an alif of connection, and the alif in "yā" went away because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters, since it and the sīn are both unvoweled. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Alā yā-slamī yā dāra Mayya 'alā al-bilā*
*wa lā zāla munhalan bi-ja'rā'ika al-qaṭr*

Al-Jurjani said: it is an interjected speech from the hoopoe, or from Solomon, or from God, meaning "*alā li-yasjudū*" ("Let them prostrate!"), like His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe that they should forgive those who do not expect the days of God﴾. It was said that it is an imperative, meaning "*li-yaghfirū*" ("let them forgive"). On this view, the writing of the Mushaf is also arranged, meaning there is no vocative here.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was said that it is from the speech of the hoopoe up to His saying, "the Mighty," and this is the view of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq. It is objected that he is not addressed, so how can he speak with the meaning of a legal ruling? It is possible that it is from the saying of Solomon when the hoopoe informed him about the people. It is also possible that it is from the saying of God, the Exalted, so it is an interjection between the two statements, and this is the established view upon reflection. The heavy reading of "ألّا" gives that the speech belongs to the hoopoe, whereas the light reading prevents that. The light reading requires the command to prostrate to God, the Mighty and Majestic, due to the imperative, as we have explained.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "Is the prostration of recitation obligatory in both readings, or in one of them?" I say: It is obligatory in both, because the places of prostration are either a command to do it, or praise for the one who did it, or blame for the one who abandoned it, and one of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is blame for the one who abandons it. I say: God has reported about the disbelievers that they prostrate, as in "al-Inshiqaq," and the Prophet ﷺ prostrated in it, as is established in al-Bukhari and others; so likewise in "al-Naml." And God knows best. Al-Zamakhshari: What al-Zajjaj mentioned about the obligation of prostration with the light reading and not the heavy reading is not to be relied upon.

﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾ (*al-khab'*): the hidden of the heavens is its rain, and the hidden of the earth is its treasures and its plants. Qatadah said: *al-khab'* is secret. Al-Nahhas said: this is better, i.e., whatever is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and it is shown by "what you conceal and what you disclose." [[In the manuscript of the original, with the *bā'*, and it is the reading of the common people, as will come.]] Ikrimah and Malik ibn Dinar read: "*al-khabu*" with a *fatha* on the *bā'* and without a *hamzah*. Al-Mahdawi said: this is the analogical lightening, and he mentioned those who drop the *hamzah* when stopping. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Hatim related that Ikrimah read "*al-khaba*" with a non-hamzated alif, and claimed that this is not permissible in Arabic, and argued that if he lightens the *hamzah* he moves its vowel onto the *bā'* and says "*al-khab fi al-samawat wal-ard*," and if he changes the *hamzah* he says "*al-khabyi*" with the *bā'* sukun and a *yā'* after it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: I heard Muhammad ibn Yazid say: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach them, except that when he left his town he did not meet anyone more knowledgeable than him. Sibawayh related from the Arabs that they change the *hamzah* into an alif when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is open-vowelled; they change it into a *wāw* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is closed-vowelled; and they change it into a *yā'* when the letter before it is unvoweled and it is vowelled with a kasra. So they say: "*hadha al-wathw*," "I was amazed at the *wathy*," "I saw the *wathā*," from "*wuthi'at yaduhu*" (his hand was sprained). Likewise: "*hadha al-khabw*," "I was amazed at the *khabyi*," and "I saw the *khaba*." This was done because the *hamzah* is light, so these letters were substituted for it. Sibawayh related from a group of the Banu Tamim and Banu Asad that they say: "*hadha al-khabu*," they put a *ḍamma* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, and they keep the *hamzah*, and they put a kasra on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a kasra, and they put a *fatha* on the unvoweled letter when the *hamzah* has a *fatha*. Sibawayh also related that they put a kasra even when the *hamzah* has a *ḍamma*, but this is from the Banu Tamim, so they say "*al-radī'*" [[*al-radih* means the companion.]], and he claimed that they did not put a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* because they disliked a *ḍamma* preceded by a kasra, since there is no pattern *fi'ul* in the language. All these are dialects that differ from the dialect in which the community recited. In the reading of Abdullah: "*alladhī yukhriju al-khaba min al-samawat*," and "*min*" and "*fi*" alternate; the Arabs say: "*la-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fīkum*," meaning "*minkum*," as al-Farra' said.

﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾: The common reading is with *yā'* in both. This reading indicates that the verse is from the speech of the hoopoe, and that God singled him out with knowledge of His oneness and the obligation to prostrate to Him, and of the denial of their prostration to the sun, and of attributing it to Satan, and of his adorning it for them, with what He singled him out with from among the birds and all other animals, of subtle knowledge that sound minds hardly reach. Al-Jahdari, Isa ibn Umar, Hafs and al-Kisa'i read "*tukhfūna*" and "*tu'linūna*" with *tā'*, in address. This reading indicates that the verse is from the address of God, the Mighty and Majestic, to the nation of Muhammad ﷺ.

﴿God— there is no god but He, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾: Ibn Muhaysin read "*al-'azīmi*" with *raf'* as an adjective of God. The rest read with *khafḍ* as an adjective of "the Throne." It was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is within it and in its grasp.

**Fourteenth**: His saying, ﴿We shall see﴾ (*sanandhuru*), from "seeing," which is reflection and examination.

(أَصَدَقْتَ أَمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ) in your statement. Here "kunta" means "anta" (you are). He said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, and he did not say "we shall look into your affair," because when the hoopoe openly boasted of knowledge in his words, ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, Sulayman openly replied to him, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or lied.﴾ That was a rebuke (kifa'an) to what he had said. Fifteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars﴾, is evidence that the imam must accept the excuse of his subjects and ward off punishment from them based on the inner state of their excuses, despite the outward appearance of their conditions, because Sulayman did not punish the hoopoe when it offered its excuse to him. The hoopoe's truthfulness became an excuse only because it reported something that called for jihad, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, was fond of jihad. In the Sahih: "No one loves excuses more than Allah; for this reason He sent down the Book and sent the Messengers." Umar accepted the excuse of al-Nu'man ibn 'Adi and did not punish him. However, the imam may test such an excuse when a legal ruling of the Shari'a depends on it, as Sulayman did, for when the hoopoe said, ﴿I found a woman ruling over them, who has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne﴾, desire did not stir him, nor did love of increasing his kingdom move him to seek more, until it said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah.﴾ Then what he heard angered him, and he sought to verify what he had been told and to acquire knowledge of what was hidden from him in this matter, so he said, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are one of the liars.﴾ A similar report is found in the Sahih from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, when Umar consulted the people about the miscarriage of a woman (al-imlas, i.e., a woman whose belly is struck so that she casts out her fetus). Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba said: "I witnessed the Prophet (ﷺ) judge in such a case that a ghurra (a slave or a female slave) must be given." He said: Umar said, "Bring me someone who will testify with you." So Muhammad ibn Maslama testified for him. In another narration, Umar said, "Do not leave until you bring the way out of this matter," so I left and found Muhammad ibn Maslama, brought him, and he testified. A similar report is the hadith of Abu Musa concerning seeking permission (to enter) and other matters. Sixteenth issue: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: In it there are five readings. "Fa-alqihi ilayhim" with the yā' affirmed in pronunciation. With the yā' omitted and the kasra remaining to indicate it, "fa-alqihi ilayhim." With the hā' pronounced with a ḍamma and the wāw kept, according to the original form, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." With the wāw omitted and the ḍamma kept, "fa-alqihu ilayhim." The fifth dialect, which Hamza recited, is with the hā' sukun: "fa-alqih ilayhim." Al-Nahhas said: According to the grammarians this is not permissible except by a remote stratagem, namely by assuming a pause. I heard Ali ibn Sulayman say: "Do not pay attention to this justification. If it were permissible to join (the word to what follows) while intending a pause, it would be permissible to drop the i'rab (grammatical inflection) from nouns." He said: "ilayhim" is in the plural form, and he did not say "ilayha," because he had said, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun﴾. It is as if he said: "Cast it to those whose religion is this," out of concern for the matter of religion and his preoccupation with it over other things, and for this reason the address in the letter was framed in the plural. It is narrated in the stories of this verse that the hoopoe arrived and found walls and barriers between this queen and him, so it made for an opening (kuwwa) which Bilqis had made so that the sun might enter through it at its rising, because of her worship of it. It entered through it and dropped the letter upon Bilqis, who, it is said, was asleep. When she awoke she found it and was startled, thinking someone had entered upon her. Then she stood up and found her condition as she had known it, so she looked toward the opening, anxious about the matter of the sun, and saw the hoopoe, and then she understood. Wahb and Ibn Zayd said: There was an opening facing the sunrise, and when the sun rose she would prostrate. The hoopoe blocked it with its wing, so the sun rose while she did not know. When she was slow to notice the sun and stood to look, it threw the document to her. When she saw the seal she trembled and submitted, for the kingdom of Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in his ring. She read it, then gathered the chiefs of her people and addressed them with what comes after. Muqatil said: The hoopoe carried the letter in its beak and flew until it stood over the head of the woman, while around her were the troops and soldiers. It fluttered for a while while the people looked at it. The woman raised her head, and it dropped the letter into her lap. Seventeenth issue: This verse is evidence for sending letters to polytheists, conveying the call to them, and inviting them to Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Kisra, Qaysar, and to every tyrant, as has been mentioned in Al 'Imran. Eighteenth issue: His saying, ﴿Then turn away from them﴾. His command to turn away is a matter of good manners, so that he withdraws in the manner in which one behaves with kings. The meaning is: remain nearby until you see their response. Wahb ibn Munabbih said this. Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to turn away in the sense of returning to him, i.e., "cast it and return." He said: His saying, ﴿then watch what they return﴾, is in the sense of coming before his saying, ﴿then turn away,﴾ and the arrangement of the speech is clearer: i.e., cast it, then turn away, and in the meantime, "watch" means wait. It was also said: "watch" means "know," as in His saying, ﴿the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. That is: know what they return, i.e., what they answer and what words they return. It was also said: ﴿then watch what they return﴾ means they exchange words among themselves.

**Sixth-century commentary** (note: translate the following as-is)

There are six issues in this passage.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿She said, "O chiefs..."﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and the meaning is: he went and threw it to them, and she heard them saying, "O chiefs." Then she described the letter as *noble* (karim), either because it came from someone great in her own estimation and in theirs, so she magnified it out of reverence for Sulayman, peace be upon him. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. Or she was indicating that it was sealed with a signet ring, so she called it noble because of its seal. It is reported that this is from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: because it began with "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every speech that does not begin with 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate' is *ajdham* (deficient)." It was also said: because he began it with himself, and only the great (*al-jullah*) do that. In the hadith of Ibn Umar, he wrote to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan giving him allegiance: "From Abd Allah to Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, Commander of the Believers: I acknowledge to you hearing and obedience as far as I am able, and my sons have also acknowledged this to you." It was also said: she imagined that it was a letter that had come from heaven, since the bearer was a bird. And it was said: *karim* means "good," as in His saying, "and a noble station" (maqam karim), meaning a good assembly. It was also said: she described it thus because of what it contained of gentle speech and admonition in calling to the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and good solicitation and courtesy, without containing abuse or curse, or anything that would disturb the soul, and without harsh or obscure speech, in keeping with the custom of the Messengers in calling to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Do you not see the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet (ﷺ): "Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition" (16:125), and His saying to Musa and Harun: "Speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear" (20:44)? All of these are fine opinions, and this is the best of them. It has been reported that no one wrote "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" before Sulayman. In the reading of [Abd Allah [[In the original: "and in the reading of Ubayy," which contradicts what the books of tafsir state. What is related from Ubayy is that he read "anna min Sulayman wa anna bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim" with an open hamza, a light nun, and without the ha.]]] it reads "wa innahu min Sulayman" with an added waw.

The second issue: describing the writing as *karim* (noble) is the highest of descriptions. Do you not see His saying, "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" (56:77)? The people of the age describe letters as *khatir* (weighty), *athir* (esteemed), and *mabrur* (righteous). If it is for a king, they say *al-Aziz* (the Mighty) and drop *al-Karim* out of heedlessness, though *al-Karim* is the most excellent of these qualities. As for describing it as *Aziz*, the Qur'an has been described with it in His saying: "And indeed it is a Mighty Book. Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it" (41:41–42). That is its might, and it belongs to no one except Him. So avoid it in your books, and substitute *al-Ali* (the Exalted), fulfilling the right of the office and safeguarding the religion. This was said by al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi.

The third issue: it was the custom of the earlier generations, when they wrote, to begin with themselves, "from so-and-so to so-and-so," and reports attest to this. Al-Rabi reported from Anas, who said: "No one was greater in sanctity than the Prophet (ﷺ), and his companions, when they wrote, began with themselves." Ibn Sirin said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people of Persia, when they wrote, began with their great ones, so a man should begin only with himself." Abu al-Layth said in his book *al-Bustan*: If one begins with the addressee, it is permissible, since the community has agreed upon it and did it for a benefit they perceived in it, or as an abrogation of what was before. So the better practice in our time is to begin with the addressee and then with oneself, because beginning with oneself is considered by him a belittling of the addressee and arrogance toward him, unless he is writing to one of his servants or a boy among his slaves.

The fourth issue: when a letter of greeting or the like arrives for a person, it is incumbent upon him to return a reply, because a letter from an absent person is like a greeting from a present one. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he regarded returning a letter as obligatory, just as he regarded returning a greeting as obligatory. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: they agreed on writing "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" at the beginning of books and letters, and on sealing them, because that is further from suspicion. On this the practice has proceeded, and the report from Umar ibn al-Khattab attests to it, that he said: "Any letter that is not sealed is *aghlaf* (unlocked/exposed)." And in the hadith: "The nobility of a letter is its seal." One of the men of letters, Ibn al-Muqaffa, said: "Whoever writes a letter to his brother and does not seal it has belittled him, because sealing is a seal." Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to write to the non-Arabs (*ajam*), it was said to him: "They will accept only a letter that has a seal on it." So he had a ring made, and engraved on its bezel: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." It is as if I see its gleam (*wabis*) and its whiteness in his hand. [[*Al-wabis*: the glitter and shine.]]

The sixth issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate."﴾ "Wa innahu" with a kasra in both places means: and indeed the speech [is], or: the opening of the speech is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Al-Farra permitted "anna-hu min Sulayman wa anna-hu" with a fatha on both, in the place of a nominative, as an apposition to "the letter," meaning: it was conveyed to me that it is from Sulayman. He also permitted that both be in the place of an accusative, by dropping the preposition, meaning: because it is from Sulayman, and because it [begins with] — as if she were giving as the reason for its nobility that it is from Sulayman and that it opens with "In the name of Allah." Al-Ashhab al-Uqayli and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read "allā taghlū" with a ghayn (*ghayn mu'jama*), and it was reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from *ghala yaghlu*, meaning to exceed the bounds and to be arrogant. It refers back to the meaning of the reading of the majority. "And come to me in submission" means: submitting, obedient, believing.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 32–34:**

There are three issues concerning this passage.

**The first issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿She said: "O chiefs, advise me in my affair."﴾ *Al-mala'* (the chiefs) are the nobles of the people. The discussion of this term has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah. [See vol. 3, p. 243 of the edition, first or second printing.] Ibn 'Abbas said: "There were with her a thousand *qayl*s (a *qayl* is a ruler below the supreme king)." It was also said: "Twelve thousand *qayl*s, with each *qayl* having a hundred thousand [men]." She began with good manners toward her people and consulted them about her affair, and she informed them that this was her consistent practice in every matter that arose, by her saying: "I would not decide a matter until you bear witness." How much more so in this great calamity. The chiefs answered her with what would gladden her eye, by informing her of their strength and might, and then they left the matter to her judgment. This was a fine exchange from all of them. Qatadah said: "It was mentioned to us that she had three hundred and thirteen men who were her counsellors, each one of them over ten thousand [men]."

**The second issue:** In this verse there is evidence for the validity of consultation (*mushawarah*). Allah Exalted said to His Prophet (ﷺ), in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾, either to seek help from opinions or to win over the allies. Allah Exalted also praised the virtuous with His saying: ﴿and whose affair is by consultation among themselves﴾. Consultation is one of the ancient customs, especially in war. Here is Bilqis, a pagan woman who used to worship the sun: "She said: 'O chiefs, advise me in my affair. I would not decide a matter until you bear witness,'" in order to test their resolve to resist their enemy, their determination in what sets their affair right, and their steadfastness in obeying her. She knew that if they did not give themselves, their wealth and their blood for her, she would have no capacity to resist her enemy. If their affair, their determination and their diligence were not united, that would be a help to their enemy against them. And if she did not test what they had and know the measure of their resolve, she would not be acting with insight into their affair. Perhaps her independent decision would lead to weakness in their obedience and to a flaw in the planning of their affair, whereas consulting them and taking their opinion would help toward what she wanted of strengthening their power and the severity of their defence. Do you not see their reply: ﴿They said: "We are people of strength and people of great might"﴾? Ibn 'Abbas said: "Among their strength was that one of them would gallop his horse until, when it became excited, he would squeeze its thighs and restrain it by his strength."

**The third issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the command is yours, so consider what you will command.﴾ They left the matter to her judgment despite what they had shown her of strength, might and severity. When they did this, she then informed them of what kings do with the towns they overpower. In this speech there is fear for her people, caution, and a magnification of the affair of Sulayman, peace be upon him. "And thus they do": it was said that this is from Bilqis's speech, as an emphasis of the meaning she intended. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is from the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informing Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community of this and telling them about it. Wahb said: when she read the letter to them, she did not recognise the name of Allah, so she said: "What is this?!" Some of the people said: "We do not think this is anything but a great *ifrit* (a powerful jinn) by which this king can accomplish whatever he wants," and so they silenced him. Another said: "I think they are three of the *afarit*," and so they silenced him. Then a young man who had knowledge said: "O mistress of kings! Sulayman is a king whom the King of heaven has given a great kingdom. He does not speak a word without beginning it with the naming of his God, and Allah is the name of the King of heaven, while the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate are His attributes." Thereupon she said: "Advise me in my affair." They said: ﴿We are people of strength﴾ in fighting, ﴿and people of great might﴾ in war and encounter. ﴿And the command is yours﴾: they returned their affair to her because of the blessing they had tested in her opinion, ﴿so consider what you will command.﴾ She ﴿said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it and make the most honoured of its people abased"﴾, they humiliate its nobles so that affairs may be set right for them. Thus Allah confirmed her saying. ﴿And thus they do.﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: ﴿and make the most honoured of its people abased﴾ is a complete pause, and then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, confirming her saying: ﴿And thus they do.﴾ A similar case is in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer. He wants to drive you out of your land"﴾, the speech is complete, and then Pharaoh said: ﴿"So what do you advise?"﴾. Ibn Shajarah said: it is the speech of Bilqis, so the pause is at ﴿And thus they do﴾, meaning: and thus will Sulayman do when he enters our lands.

Then he said: "Which animals have you seen that are most beautiful on land and sea?" They said: "O Prophet of Allah, we saw in such-and-such a sea animals spotted and varied in colour, having wings, manes and forelocks." So he commanded that they be brought, and they came and were tied on the right and left of the arena, and on the bricks of gold and silver, and they were given their fodder. Then he said: "Bring me the jinn's children," and he had them stand, in the finest bloom of youth, on the right and left of the arena. Then Sulayman, peace be upon him, sat on his throne in his assembly, and four thousand golden thrones were placed for him, with the same number on his left. He seated the prophets and scholars on them, and commanded the devils, the jinn and mankind to form ranks extending for farsakhs. He commanded the beasts of prey, the wild animals, the creeping things and the birds, and they lined up for farsakhs to his right and left. When the people drew near the arena and saw the kingdom of Sulayman, and saw the animals the like of which their eyes had never seen, more beautiful than them, dropping dung on the bricks of gold and silver, their own selves seemed small to them, and they threw away what they had with them of gifts. When they passed over it, they feared that they would be accused of this, so they threw what they had with them in that place. When they saw the devils, they saw a terrifying, awful sight, and they were frightened and afraid. The devils said to them: "Pass on, there is no harm upon you." So they passed by troop after troop of jinn, mankind, beasts, birds, beasts of prey and wild animals until they stood before Sulayman. Sulayman looked at them with a good look and a cheerful face. She had told her messenger: "If he looks at you with an angry look, know that he is a king, and let his appearance not frighten you, for I am mightier than him. But if you see the man to be cheerful and gentle, know that he is a sent prophet. Then understand his speech and return the answer." So the Hudhud informed Sulayman of that, as has been mentioned earlier. She had put a box of gold, in which she placed a single pearl, undrilled, and a bead with a crooked hole. She wrote a letter with her messenger, saying in it: "If you are a prophet, distinguish between the male servants and the female servants, inform me of what is in the box, make known to me the top of the staff from its bottom, drill the pearl with an even hole, insert a thread into the bead, and fill the cup with water of dew which is neither from the earth nor from the sky." When the messenger arrived and stood before Sulayman, he gave him the queen's letter. He looked into it and said: "Where is the box?" It was brought and he shook it, and Jibril informed him of what was in it. Then Sulayman informed them. The messenger said to him: "You have spoken the truth. Now drill the pearl and insert the thread into the bead." Sulayman asked the jinn and mankind about drilling it, and they were unable to do so. He said to the devils: "What is your opinion about it?" They said: "Send for the woodworm." The woodworm came and took a hair in its mouth until it came out through the other side. Sulayman said to it: "What is your need?" It said: "Make my sustenance be in the wood of the tree." He said to it: "That is yours." Then Sulayman said: "Who will thread this bead with the thread?" A white worm said: "I will, O Prophet of Allah." So the worm took the thread in its mouth, entered the hole, and came out the other side. Sulayman said to it: "What is your need?" It said: "Make my sustenance be in fruits." He said: "That is yours." Then he distinguished between the boys and the girls [the addition in brackets is from "Qisas al-Anbiya'" of al-Tha'labi]. Al-Suddi said: he commanded them to perform ablution. The boy poured water over the hand and foot quickly, and the girls poured from the left hand onto the right hand, and from the right onto the left, and he distinguished between them by this. It was also said: the girl would take water from the vessel with one of her hands, then carry it to the other hand, then strike the face with it, while the boy would take water from the vessel and strike the face with it, the girl pouring over the belly of her forearm, and the boy over the back of the forearm; the girl pours water copiously, and the boy pours it down over his hands; and he distinguished between them by this. Ya'la ibn Muslim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: Bilqis sent two hundred female and male servants, and she said: "If he is a prophet, he will know the males from the females." So he commanded them, and they performed ablution. Whoever among them began with his elbow before his palm, he said: "He is from the females." And whoever began with his palm before his elbow, he said: "He is from the males." Then he sent the staff into the air and said: "Whichever end reaches the ground first, that is its root." He commanded the horses to be run until they sweated, and he filled the cup with their sweat. Then Sulayman returned the gift. It is reported that when he returned the gift to her, and her messenger informed her of what he had witnessed, she said to her people: "This is a matter from heaven."

**Second issue:** The Prophet (ﷺ) would accept gifts and reciprocate them, and would not accept charity (ṣadaqah, obligatory or voluntary alms). Likewise Sulayman, peace be upon him, and all the other prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all. Bilqis made the acceptance or the rejection of the gift a sign of what was in his soul, based on what we have mentioned, namely whether Sulayman was a king or a prophet, because he had said to her in his letter: "Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." This is a matter in which no ransom is accepted and from which no gift is taken. This is not from the category of gift-giving that is established in the Sharia as permissible to accept; rather, it is a bribe (rishwah) and the exchange of truth for falsehood, and this is the bribe that is not lawful. As for a gift given purely out of affection and to maintain ties, it is permissible from anyone and in all circumstances, provided it does not come from a polytheist (mushrik).

**Third issue:** If it comes from a polytheist, there is the hadith: "I have been forbidden to accept the zabd of the polytheists," meaning their gifts and grants. It is also reported from him, peace be upon him, that he accepted it, as in the hadith of Malik from Thawr ibn Zayd al-Dayli and others. A group of scholars said that these two reports involve naskh (abrogation), while others said: there is no abrogating or abrogated element in them, and the meaning is that he would not accept the gift of one who hoped to gain the upper hand over him, to take his land and enter him into Islam, and Sulayman's situation was of this kind. He forbade accepting the gift of such a person out of caution against him. This is the best interpretation by the scholars regarding this, for it reconciles the hadiths. It has also been said other than this.

**Fourth issue:** Giving gifts is recommended, and gifts create affection and remove enmity. Malik narrated from 'Ata' ibn 'Abd Allah al-Khurasani who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shake hands, and rancour will depart; exchange gifts, and you will love one another, and hostility will depart." Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam narrated: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Exchange gifts, for it strengthens love and removes the troubles of the breast." Al-Daraqutni said: Ibn Bujayr alone narrated it from his father from Malik, and he was not reliable, and it is not authentically reported from Malik or from al-Zuhri. From Ibn Shihab who said: it reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Exchange gifts among yourselves, for gifts remove sakhimah (ill feeling)." Ibn Wahb said: I asked Yunus about sakhimah, what is it? He said: it is ghill (rancour). This hadith was connected by Uthman al-Waqqasi from al-Zuhri, and it is weak. In sum: it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) would accept gifts, and in this there is a good example. Among the excellence of gifts, together with following the Sunnah, is that they remove the sorenesses of souls and give both the giver and the receiver a warmth in meeting and sitting together. Indeed, he who said well:

"The gifts of people, one to another,
create in their hearts the bonds of union,
and sow in the inner heart affection and love,
and make them, when present, beautiful."

Another:

"Gifts have a share, when they arrive,
more favoured than a son in the sight of a compassionate father."

**Fifth issue:** It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Your companions are your partners in the gift." Its meaning has been disputed. It was said: it is to be taken literally. It was said: he shares with them out of generosity and manliness, and if he does not do so, he is not compelled to. Abu Yusuf said: this applies to fruits and the like. Some said: they are his partners in joy, not in the gift itself. The report is understood to apply to people like the Companions of the Suffah (Ashab al-Suffah, the poor companions who lived in the Prophet's mosque), and to khawaniq (hospices) and ribats (hostels). As for when the recipient is a jurist (faqih) of the jurists, singled out for it, then his companions have no share in it, but if he shares it with them, that is generosity and bounty from him.

**Sixth issue:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿so she will be waiting﴾, meaning: waiting ﴿to see what the messengers return with﴾. Qatadah said: may Allah have mercy on her, if she was intelligent in her Islam and her polytheism, she knew that a gift has an effect upon people. The alif was dropped in بِمَ (bima, "with what?") to distinguish it from the declarative مَا (ma). It is also permissible to retain it, as in the verse of Hassan ibn al-Mundhir satirising the Banu 'A'idh ibn 'Amr ibn Makhzum, and before it:

"And if you reform, you are my 'A'idh,
but the reform of the 'A'idh is towards corruption."

He says:

"Over what he rose, reviling me, a base man,
like a pig that has rolled in ashes."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 36–40 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he (the messenger) came to Sulayman, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth?"﴾ That is, when the messenger came to Sulayman with the gift, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth?"

Hamzah, Ya'qub and al-A'mash read it with a single doubled nūn and a following yā' that is retained. The rest read it with two nūns, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because it is written with two nūns in all the codices (al-masahif). Ishaq narrated from Nafi' that he used to read *"atumiddūnī"* with a single light nūn followed by a yā' in pronunciation. Ibn al-Anbari said: In this reading, the yā' must be retained when stopping, so that it agrees with the orthography of the codex. The original form of the nūn is doubling (tashdid), so the doubling was lightened in this position, just as it was lightened in: *ashhadu anaka 'alim* (I bear witness that you are a knower), whose original form is *annaka 'alim*. On this principle is built the reading of the one who read *"yushāqqūna fīhim"* and *"ataḥājjūnna fi'llāh"*. The Arabs have also said: *al-rijālu yaḍribūnī wa yaqṣidūnī* (the men strike me and intend me), and its origin is *yaḍribūnnī* and *yaqṣidūnnī*, since it is the assimilation (idgham) of *yaḍribūnanī* and *yaqṣidūnanī*. The poet said:

*tarhabīnī wa'l-jīdu minki li-Layla ... wa'l-ḥashā wa'l-bughāmu wa'l-'aynāni*

The original is *tarhabīnī*, and it was lightened. The meaning of *"atumiddūnan"* is: Do you add to me wealth beyond what you see of my possessions?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. That is, what He has given me of Islam, sovereignty and prophethood is better than what He has given you, so I do not rejoice in wealth. The word *"ātānī"* is written in all the codices without a yā'. Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Hafs read *"ātāniyal-lāh"* with an open yā'; when they stop, they drop it. As for Ya'qub, he retains it in pausal position and drops it in continuous recitation because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The rest read it without a yā' in both states.

(*Bal antum bi-hadiyyatikum tafraḥūn*) — because you are people of boasting and rivalry in worldly matters.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Return to them﴾. That is, Sulayman said to al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, the leader of the delegation: Return to them with their gift.

(*Fa-la-na'tiyannahum bi-junūdin lā qibala lahum bihā*) — the *lām* is the lām of oath, and the nūn is obligatory with it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu'l-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lām of emphasis (lām al-tawkīd). He also held that the particles (lām) are all three only: the lām of emphasis, the lām of command, and the lām of genitive (khafḍ). This is the view of the skilled grammarians, because they return each thing to its origin; but this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of *"lā qibala lahum bihā"* is: they have no power to withstand it.

(*Wa-lanukhrijannahum minhā*) — that is, from their land (*adhillatan wa hum ṣāghirūn*). It is said: *"minhā"* means from the town of Saba'. The town was already mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it."

*"Adhillatan"*: they have been stripped of their kingship and might. *"Wa hum ṣāghirūn"*: humiliated, abased, from *ṣighar* (smallness), which is abasement, if they do not submit. Then their messenger returned to her and informed her. She said: "I have known that he is not a king, and we have no power to fight a prophet of the prophets of Allah." Then she ordered her throne to be brought, and it was placed in seven chambers, one inside another, in the innermost of seven palaces. She locked the doors, set guards over it, and set out towards him with twelve thousand *qayl*s (chieftains) of the kings of Yemen, under each *qayl* one hundred thousand men. Ibn 'Abbas said: Sulayman was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him until he asked them about what they had come for. One day he saw dust (*rahaj*) near him and said: "What is this?" They said: "Bilqis, O Prophet of Allah." Sulayman said to his soldiers—Wahb and others said to the jinn—(*Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?*)

'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: Bilqis was one farsakh away from Sulayman when he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" She had left her throne in Saba' and appointed guards to watch over it. It is also said: when she sent the gift, she sent her envoys with her army to surprise (*litughāfiṣa*) Sulayman, peace be upon him, by killing him before he could prepare for her, if he was seeking kingship. When he learned of this, he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn 'Abbas said: His command to bring the throne was before he wrote the letter to her, and he did not write to her until the throne came to him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the verses is that this statement came from Sulayman, peace be upon him, after the arrival of her gift and his returning it to her, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter. The majority of the interpreters hold this view.

They differed concerning the purpose of summoning her throne. Qatadah said: It was described to him as great and excellent, so he wished to seize it before it would protect her and her people through Islam; and Islam is upon this religion. This is also the view of Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that comes from Allah, and to make it a proof of his prophethood, by taking it from her houses without an army or war. On this interpretation, *"muslimīn"* means *mustaslimīn* (submitting), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Zayd also said: He wished to test her intellect, and for this reason he said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided." It is also said: the jinn feared that Sulayman would marry her and a son would be born to him from her, and then they would not cease to be in servitude and service to the progeny of Sulayman. So they told Sulayman that there was a defect in her intellect, and he wished to test her with her throne. It is also said: he wished to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his saying: "And she has a great throne." This was said by al-Tabari. Qatadah said: He loved to see it when the hoopoe described it. The first view is held by most scholars, because of His saying: "before they come to me in submission"; and because, if she had embraced Islam, her property would have been forbidden to him, and it could not be brought except with her permission. It is reported that it was of silver and gold, inlaid with red rubies and jewels, and that it was within seven chambers, upon which were seven locks.

His saying, Exalted is He: (*Qāla 'ifrītun mina'l-jinn*). Thus the majority recited it. Abu Raja' and 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited *"'ifriyatun"*, and it is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah dislikes the *'ifriyah* (arrogant, cunning) and the *nifriyah*." This is an echo (ittibā') of *'ifriyah*. Qatadah said: It means the cunning one. Al-Nahhas said: For a strong one who has with him cunning and craftiness, it is said *'ifr*, *'ifriyah*, *'ifrit* and *'ufariyah*. It is also said: *'ifrit* means chief. A group recited *"qāla 'ifr"* with a kasra on the 'ayn, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Nahhas said: Whoever says *'ifriyah* makes its plural *'ifār*; and whoever says *'ifrit* has three options in the plural: if he wishes he says *'afārīt*, and if he wishes he says *'afār*, because the tā' is extra, as one says *ṭawāgh* as the plural of *ṭāghūt*; and if he wishes, he compensates for the tā' with a yā' and says *'afāriyy*. The *'ifrīt* is the strong, rebellious one among the devils, and the tā' is extra. They have also said: *tu'affarta al-rajul* when he takes on the character of harming. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The name of this *'ifrit* is Kawdan, recorded by al-Nahhas. It is also said: Dhakwan, recorded by al-Suhayli. Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i said: His name is Da'wan. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was Sakhr the jinni. From this name is the saying of Dhu'l-Rummah:

*ka-annahu kawkabun fī ithri 'ifriyatin musawwabun ... fī sawādi'l-layli munqaḍibu*

It is as if he were a star in the trail of an *'ifriyah*, descending through the blackness of the night.

Al-Kisa'i recited:

*idh qāla shaiṭānuhumu'l-'ifrītu ... laysa lakum mulkun wa lā tathbītu*

When their devil, the *'ifrīt*, said: "You have neither sovereignty nor steadfastness."

In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an *'ifrīt* from the jinn began to attack me last night, to cut off my prayer, but Allah enabled me against him, so I pushed him forcefully..." and he mentioned the hadith. In al-Bukhari, it reads: "...it *tafallata* upon me last night," instead of "began to attack (*yaftik*)." In the Muwatta', from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey (*usriya*), and he saw an *'ifrīt* from the jinn pursuing him with a flame of fire; whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned, he saw it. Jibril said: "Shall I not teach you words which, when you say them, its flame will be extinguished and it will fall on its face?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes." He said: "I seek refuge in the Generous Allah [in another version: I seek refuge in the Face of the Mighty Allah] and in the perfect words of Allah which neither the righteous nor the wicked can exceed, from the evil of what descends from the sky, and the evil of what ascends into it, [and the evil of what He has scattered in the earth, and the evil of what comes out of it,] and from the trials of night and day, and from the visitors of night and day, except a visitor who visits with good, O Most Merciful."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾. That is, from his council in which he judges.

(*Wa innī 'alayhi la-qawiyyun amīn*) — that is, strong to carry it, *"amīn"* trustworthy regarding what is in it. Ibn 'Abbas said: *amīn* over the private part of the woman; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Sulayman said: "I want faster than that." So (*Qāla alladhī 'indahu 'ilmun mina'l-kitābi anā ātīka bihi qabla an yartadda ilayka ṭarfuk*) — most of the commentators hold that the one who had knowledge of the Book was Asaf ibn Barkhiya, and he was from the Children of Israel. He was a *ṣiddīq* who memorised the Greatest Name of Allah, which when asked by it, He gives, and when called upon by it, He answers. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Greatest Name of Allah by which Asaf ibn Barkhiya supplicated is: *yā Ḥayyu yā Qayyūm*." It is said: in their language it is *ahayā sharāhayā*. Al-Zuhri said: The supplication of the one who had the Greatest Name of Allah was: "O our God and God of everything, one God; there is no god but You; bring me her throne." Then it was placed before him. Mujahid said: He supplicated and said: "O our God and God of everything, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." Al-Suhayli said: The one who had knowledge of the Book is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, the maternal cousin of Sulayman, and he had with him the Greatest Name of Allah from among the names of Allah, Exalted is He.

It is said: he is Sulayman himself, but this interpretation is not valid in the context of the discourse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A group said that he was Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the address in this interpretation is to the 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) when he said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place." It is as if Sulayman found this slow, so he said to him, in a belittling manner, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." The proponents of this view cited Sulayman's words, "This is of the bounty of my Lord." I say: What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned was said by al-Nahhas in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*, and it is a good opinion, God willing. Bahr said: He is an angel who holds the Book of Decrees, whom God sent at the 'ifrit's words. Al-Suhayli said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri' mentioned that he was Dabbah ibn Udd, but this is absolutely not valid, because Dabbah is the son of Udd ibn Tabikhah, whose name is 'Amr ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd. Ma'd lived in the time of Bakht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), and that was a long time after the era of Sulayman. If Ma'd was not in the era of Sulayman, how could Dabbah ibn Udd be, when he is five generations after him?! This is clear to anyone who reflects on it. Ibn Lahi'ah said: He is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. Ibn Zayd said: The one who had knowledge of the Book was a righteous man who was on an island among the islands of the sea. He went out that day to look at who inhabits the earth and whether God is worshipped or not. He found Sulayman, so he invoked one of God's names and the throne was brought. A seventh view: he was a man from the Children of Israel named Yamlikha, who knew the Greatest Name of God; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri. Ibn Abi Bazzah said: The man who had knowledge of the Book was named Asṭūm, and he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: It is only Sulayman, peace be upon him. Indeed, people think that he had a Name with him, but that is not so. Rather, he was a man of the Children of Israel, a scholar whom God had given knowledge and understanding. He said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." [Sulayman] said, "Bring it." He said, "You are the Prophet of God, son of the Prophet of God; if you invoke God, He will bring it to you." So Sulayman invoked God, and God brought him the throne. An eighth view: he is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. This was said by al-Nakha'i and narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the knowledge of the Book is his knowledge of the revealed books of God, or of what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It was also said: it is the knowledge of Sulayman's letter to Bilqis. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What the majority of people hold is that he was a righteous man from the Children of Israel named Asaf ibn Barkhiya. It is narrated that he prayed two units of prayer, then said to Sulayman, "O Prophet of God, extend your gaze." So [Sulayman] extended his gaze toward Yemen, and behold, the throne was there. Sulayman had not returned his gaze before it was with him. Mujahid said: "Their glance returning to them" means continuing to look until the glance returns to them, "dazed and exhausted" (Qur'an 67:4). It was also said that he meant the amount of time it takes to open one's eye and then blink, and this is like when you say: "Do such-and-such in the blink of an eye." This is more fitting, because if the act was from Sulayman, it is a miracle (mu'jizah), and if it was from Asaf or from another of God's friends (awliya'), it is a marvel (karamah), and the marvel of a friend of God is a miracle of the Prophet. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever said that the one with knowledge of the Book was Sulayman, who said to the 'ifrit, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," has denied the marvels of the friends of God. According to these people, what the 'ifrit did is neither a miracle nor a marvel, because the jinn are capable of such things. A substance cannot be in two places at once in one state. Rather, it can be conceived as follows: God annihilates the substance in the far east and then recreates it in a second state, which is the state after annihilation, in the far west; or He annihilates the intervening places and then recreates them. Al-Qushayri said: Wahb narrated it from Malik. It has also been said: rather, it was brought through the air, as Mujahid said. The distance between Sulayman and the throne was like the distance between Kufa and al-Hira. Malik said: It was in Yemen while Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in Syria. In the exegetical works it is related that the throne of Bilqis split at its place where it was, then sprang forth before Sulayman. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: The throne appeared from a tunnel beneath the earth. God knows best which of these was the case.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he saw it settled beside him﴾, that is, firmly established beside him.

(He said, "This is of the bounty of my Lord") that is, this victory and empowerment are from the bounty of my Lord.

(To test me) Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "to see" (li-yanzur). Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is figurative. The basic meaning of *ibtila'* (testing) is examination, that is, to examine me: whether I will be thankful for His blessing or ungrateful for it. (And whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self) that is, the benefit of that does not return except to himself, since by his gratitude he merits the perfection of the blessing, its continuance, and its increase. Gratitude is the tether of existing blessings, and by it lost blessings are obtained.

(And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous) that is, free of need for gratitude, and generous in bestowing favor.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 36–40 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he (the messenger) came to Sulayman, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth?"﴾ That is, when the messenger came to Sulayman with the gift, he said: "Do you provide me with wealth?"

Hamzah, Ya'qub and al-A'mash read it with a single doubled nūn and a following yā' that is retained. The rest read it with two nūns, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because it is written with two nūns in all the codices (al-masahif). Ishaq narrated from Nafi' that he used to read *"atumiddūnī"* with a single light nūn followed by a yā' in pronunciation. Ibn al-Anbari said: In this reading, the yā' must be retained when stopping, so that it agrees with the orthography of the codex. The original form of the nūn is doubling (tashdid), so the doubling was lightened in this position, just as it was lightened in: *ashhadu anaka 'alim* (I bear witness that you are a knower), whose original form is *annaka 'alim*. On this principle is built the reading of the one who read *"yushāqqūna fīhim"* and *"ataḥājjūnna fi'llāh"*. The Arabs have also said: *al-rijālu yaḍribūnī wa yaqṣidūnī* (the men strike me and intend me), and its origin is *yaḍribūnnī* and *yaqṣidūnnī*, since it is the assimilation (idgham) of *yaḍribūnanī* and *yaqṣidūnanī*. The poet said:

*tarhabīnī wa'l-jīdu minki li-Layla ... wa'l-ḥashā wa'l-bughāmu wa'l-'aynāni*

The original is *tarhabīnī*, and it was lightened. The meaning of *"atumiddūnan"* is: Do you add to me wealth beyond what you see of my possessions?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. That is, what He has given me of Islam, sovereignty and prophethood is better than what He has given you, so I do not rejoice in wealth. As for Ya'qub, he retains it in pausal position and drops it in continuous recitation because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The rest read it without a yā' in both states.

(*Bal antum bi-hadiyyatikum tafraḥūn*) — because you are people of boasting and rivalry in worldly matters.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Return to them﴾. That is, Sulayman said to al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, the leader of the delegation: Return to them with their gift.

(*Fa-la-na'tiyannahum bi-junūdin lā qibala lahum bihā*) — the *lām* is the lām of oath, and the nūn is obligatory with it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu'l-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lām of emphasis (lām al-tawkīd). He also held that the particles (lām) are all three only: the lām of emphasis, the lām of command, and the lām of genitive (khafḍ). This is the view of the skilled grammarians, because they return each thing to its origin; but this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of *"lā qibala lahum bihā"* is: they have no power to withstand it.

(*Wa-lanukhrijannahum minhā*) — that is, from their land (*adhillatan wa hum ṣāghirūn*). It is said: *"minhā"* means from the town of Saba'. The town was already mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it."

*"Adhillatan"*: they have been stripped of their kingship and might. *"Wa hum ṣāghirūn"*: humiliated, abased, from *ṣighar* (smallness), which is abasement, if they do not submit. Then their messenger returned to her and informed her. She said: "I have known that he is not a king, and we have no power to fight a prophet of the prophets of Allah." Then she ordered her throne to be brought, and it was placed in seven chambers, one inside another, in the innermost of seven palaces. She locked the doors, set guards over it, and set out towards him with twelve thousand *qayl*s (chieftains) of the kings of Yemen, under each *qayl* one hundred thousand men. Ibn 'Abbas said: Sulayman was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him until he asked them about what they had come for. One day he saw dust (*rahaj*) near him and said: "What is this?" They said: "Bilqis, O Prophet of Allah." Sulayman said to his soldiers—Wahb and others said to the jinn—(*Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?*)

'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: Bilqis was one farsakh away from Sulayman when he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" She had left her throne in Saba' and appointed guards to watch over it. It is also said: when she sent the gift, she sent her envoys with her army to surprise (*litughāfiṣa*) Sulayman, peace be upon him, by killing him before he could prepare for her, if he was seeking kingship. When he learned of this, he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn 'Abbas said: His command to bring the throne was before he wrote the letter to her, and he did not write to her until the throne came to him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the verses is that this statement came from Sulayman, peace be upon him, after the arrival of her gift and his returning it to her, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter. The majority of the interpreters hold this view.

They differed concerning the purpose of summoning her throne. Qatadah said: It was described to him as great and excellent, so he wished to seize it before it would protect her and her people through Islam; and Islam is upon this religion. This is also the view of Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that comes from Allah, and to make it a proof of his prophethood, by taking it from her houses without an army or war. On this interpretation, *"muslimīn"* means *mustaslimīn* (submitting), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Zayd also said: He wished to test her intellect, and for this reason he said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided." It is also said: the jinn feared that Sulayman would marry her and a son would be born to him from her, and then they would not cease to be in servitude and service to the progeny of Sulayman. So they told Sulayman that there was a defect in her intellect, and he wished to test her with her throne. It is also said: he wished to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his saying: "And she has a great throne." This was said by al-Tabari. Qatadah said: He loved to see it when the hoopoe described it. It is reported that it was of silver and gold, inlaid with red rubies and jewels, and that it was within seven chambers, upon which were seven locks.

His saying, Exalted is He: (*Qāla 'ifrītun mina'l-jinn*). Thus the majority recited it. Abu Raja' and 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited *"'ifriyatun"*, and it is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah dislikes the *'ifriyah* (arrogant, cunning) and the *nifriyah*." This is an echo (ittibā') of *'ifriyah*. Qatadah said: It means the cunning one. Al-Nahhas said: For a strong one who has with him cunning and craftiness, it is said *'ifr*, *'ifriyah*, *'ifrit* and *'ufariyah*. It is also said: *'ifrit* means chief. A group recited *"qāla 'ifr"* with a kasra on the 'ayn, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Nahhas said: Whoever says *'ifriyah* makes its plural *'ifār*; and whoever says *'ifrit* has three options in the plural: if he wishes he says *'afārīt*, and if he wishes he says *'afār*, because the tā' is extra, as one says *ṭawāgh* as the plural of *ṭāghūt*; and if he wishes, he compensates for the tā' with a yā' and says *'afāriyy*. The *'ifrīt* is the strong, rebellious one among the devils, and the tā' is extra. They have also said: *tu'affarta al-rajul* when he takes on the character of harming. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The name of this *'ifrit* is Kawdan, recorded by al-Nahhas. It is also said: Dhakwan, recorded by al-Suhayli. Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i said: His name is Da'wan. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was Sakhr the jinni. From this name is the saying of Dhu'l-Rummah:

*ka-annahu kawkabun fī ithri 'ifriyatin musawwabun ... fī sawādi'l-layli munqaḍibu*

It is as if he were a star in the trail of an *'ifriyah*, descending through the blackness of the night.

Al-Kisa'i recited:

*idh qāla shaiṭānuhumu'l-'ifrītu ... laysa lakum mulkun wa lā tathbītu*

When their devil, the *'ifrīt*, said: "You have neither sovereignty nor steadfastness."

In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an *'ifrīt* from the jinn began to attack me last night, to cut off my prayer, but Allah enabled me against him, so I pushed him forcefully..." and he mentioned the hadith. In al-Bukhari, it reads: "...it *tafallata* upon me last night," instead of "began to attack (*yaftik*)." In the Muwatta', from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey (*usriya*), and he saw an *'ifrīt* from the jinn pursuing him with a flame of fire; whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned, he saw it. Jibril said: "Shall I not teach you words which, when you say them, its flame will be extinguished and it will fall on its face?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes." He said: "I seek refuge in the Generous Allah [in another version: I seek refuge in the Face of the Mighty Allah] and in the perfect words of Allah which neither the righteous nor the wicked can exceed, from the evil of what descends from the sky, and the evil of what ascends into it, [and the evil of what He has scattered in the earth, and the evil of what comes out of it,] and from the trials of night and day, and from the visitors of night and day, except a visitor who visits with good, O Most Merciful."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾. That is, from his council in which he judges.

(*Wa innī 'alayhi la-qawiyyun amīn*) — that is, strong to carry it, *"amīn"* trustworthy regarding what is in it. He was a *ṣiddīq* who memorised the Greatest Name of Allah, which when asked by it, He gives, and when called upon by it, He answers. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Greatest Name of Allah by which Asaf ibn Barkhiya supplicated is: *yā Ḥayyu yā Qayyūm*." It is said: in their language it is *ahayā sharāhayā*. Al-Zuhri said: The supplication of the one who had the Greatest Name of Allah was: "O our God and God of everything, one God; there is no god but You; bring me her throne." Then it was placed before him. Mujahid said: He supplicated and said: "O our God and God of everything, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." Al-Suhayli said: The one who had knowledge of the Book is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, the maternal cousin of Sulayman, and he had with him the Greatest Name of Allah from among the names of Allah, Exalted is He.

It is said: he is Sulayman himself, but this interpretation is not valid in the context of the discourse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A group said that he was Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the address in this interpretation is to the 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) when he said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place." It is as if Sulayman found this slow, so he said to him, in a belittling manner, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." The proponents of this view cited Sulayman's words, "This is of the bounty of my Lord." I say: What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned was said by al-Nahhas in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*, and it is a good opinion, God willing. Bahr said: He is an angel who holds the Book of Decrees, whom God sent at the 'ifrit's words. Al-Suhayli said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri' mentioned that he was Dabbah ibn Udd, but this is absolutely not valid, because Dabbah is the son of Udd ibn Tabikhah, whose name is 'Amr ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd. Ma'd lived in the time of Bakht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), and that was a long time after the era of Sulayman. If Ma'd was not in the era of Sulayman, how could Dabbah ibn Udd be, when he is five generations after him?! This is clear to anyone who reflects on it. Ibn Lahi'ah said: He is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. Ibn Zayd said: The one who had knowledge of the Book was a righteous man who was on an island among the islands of the sea. He went out that day to look at who inhabits the earth and whether God is worshipped or not. He found Sulayman, so he invoked one of God's names and the throne was brought. A seventh view: he was a man from the Children of Israel named Yamlikha, who knew the Greatest Name of God; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri. Ibn Abi Bazzah said: The man who had knowledge of the Book was named Asṭūm, and he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: It is only Sulayman, peace be upon him. Indeed, people think that he had a Name with him, but that is not so. Rather, he was a man of the Children of Israel, a scholar whom God had given knowledge and understanding. He said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." [Sulayman] said, "Bring it." He said, "You are the Prophet of God, son of the Prophet of God; if you invoke God, He will bring it to you." So Sulayman invoked God, and God brought him the throne. An eighth view: he is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. This was said by al-Nakha'i and narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the knowledge of the Book is his knowledge of the revealed books of God, or of what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It was also said: it is the knowledge of Sulayman's letter to Bilqis. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What the majority of people hold is that he was a righteous man from the Children of Israel named Asaf ibn Barkhiya. It is narrated that he prayed two units of prayer, then said to Sulayman, "O Prophet of God, extend your gaze." So [Sulayman] extended his gaze toward Yemen, and behold, the throne was there. Sulayman had not returned his gaze before it was with him. Mujahid said: "Their glance returning to them" means continuing to look until the glance returns to them, "dazed and exhausted" (Qur'an 67:4). It was also said that he meant the amount of time it takes to open one's eye and then blink, and this is like when you say: "Do such-and-such in the blink of an eye." This is more fitting, because if the act was from Sulayman, it is a miracle (mu'jizah), and if it was from Asaf or from another of God's friends (awliya'), it is a marvel (karamah), and the marvel of a friend of God is a miracle of the Prophet. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever said that the one with knowledge of the Book was Sulayman, who said to the 'ifrit, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," has denied the marvels of the friends of God. According to these people, what the 'ifrit did is neither a miracle nor a marvel, because the jinn are capable of such things. A substance cannot be in two places at once in one state. Rather, it can be conceived as follows: God annihilates the substance in the far east and then recreates it in a second state, which is the state after annihilation, in the far west; or He annihilates the intervening places and then recreates them. Al-Qushayri said: Wahb narrated it from Malik. It has also been said: rather, it was brought through the air, as Mujahid said. The distance between Sulayman and the throne was like the distance between Kufa and al-Hira. Malik said: It was in Yemen while Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in Syria. In the exegetical works it is related that the throne of Bilqis split at its place where it was, then sprang forth before Sulayman. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: The throne appeared from a tunnel beneath the earth. God knows best which of these was the case.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he saw it settled beside him﴾, that is, firmly established beside him.

(He said, "This is of the bounty of my Lord") that is, this victory and empowerment are from the bounty of my Lord.

(To test me) Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "to see" (li-yanzur). Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is figurative. The basic meaning of *ibtila'* (testing) is examination, that is, to examine me: whether I will be thankful for His blessing or ungrateful for it. (And whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self) that is, the benefit of that does not return except to himself, since by his gratitude he merits the perfection of the blessing, its continuance, and its increase. Gratitude is the tether of existing blessings, and by it lost blessings are obtained.

(And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous) that is, free of need for gratitude, and generous in bestowing favor.

Hamzah, Ya'qub and al-A'mash read it with a single doubled nūn and a following yā' that is retained. The rest read it with two nūns, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because it is written with two nūns in all the codices (al-masahif). Ishaq narrated from Nafi' that he used to read *"atumiddūnī"* with a single light nūn followed by a yā' in pronunciation. Ibn al-Anbari said: In this reading, the yā' must be retained when stopping, so that it agrees with the orthography of the codex. The original form of the nūn is doubling (tashdid), so the doubling was lightened in this position, just as it was lightened in: *ashhadu anaka 'alim* (I bear witness that you are a knower), whose original form is *annaka 'alim*. On this principle is built the reading of the one who read *"yushāqqūna fīhim"* and *"ataḥājjūnna fi'llāh"*. The Arabs have also said: *al-rijālu yaḍribūnī wa yaqṣidūnī* (the men strike me and intend me), and its origin is *yaḍribūnnī* and *yaqṣidūnnī*, since it is the assimilation (idgham) of *yaḍribūnanī* and *yaqṣidūnanī*. *tarhabīnī wa'l-jīdu minki li-Layla ... wa'l-ḥashā wa'l-bughāmu wa'l-'aynāni*

The original is *tarhabīnī*, and it was lightened. The meaning of *"atumiddūnan"* is: Do you add to me wealth beyond what you see of my possessions?
