It is said: in their language it is *ahayā sharāhayā*. Al-Zuhri said: The supplication of the one who had the Greatest Name of Allah was: "O our God and God of everything, one God; there is no god but You; bring me her throne." Then it was placed before him. Mujahid said: He supplicated and said: "O our God and God of everything, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." Al-Suhayli said: The one who had knowledge of the Book is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, the maternal cousin of Sulayman, and he had with him the Greatest Name of Allah from among the names of Allah, Exalted is He.

It is said: he is Sulayman himself, but this interpretation is not valid in the context of the discourse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A group said that he was Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the address in this interpretation is to the 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) when he said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place." It is as if Sulayman found this slow, so he said to him, in a belittling manner, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." The proponents of this view cited Sulayman's words, "This is of the bounty of my Lord." I say: What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned was said by al-Nahhas in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*, and it is a good opinion, God willing. Bahr said: He is an angel who holds the Book of Decrees, whom God sent at the 'ifrit's words. Ma'd lived in the time of Bakht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), and that was a long time after the era of Sulayman. If Ma'd was not in the era of Sulayman, how could Dabbah ibn Udd be, when he is five generations after him?! This is clear to anyone who reflects on it. Ibn Lahi'ah said: He is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. Ibn Zayd said: The one who had knowledge of the Book was a righteous man who was on an island among the islands of the sea. He went out that day to look at who inhabits the earth and whether God is worshipped or not. He found Sulayman, so he invoked one of God's names and the throne was brought. A seventh view: he was a man from the Children of Israel named Yamlikha, who knew the Greatest Name of God; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri. Ibn Abi Bazzah said: The man who had knowledge of the Book was named Asṭūm, and he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: It is only Sulayman, peace be upon him. Indeed, people think that he had a Name with him, but that is not so. Rather, he was a man of the Children of Israel, a scholar whom God had given knowledge and understanding. He said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." [Sulayman] said, "Bring it." He said, "You are the Prophet of God, son of the Prophet of God; if you invoke God, He will bring it to you." So Sulayman invoked God, and God brought him the throne. An eighth view: he is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. This was said by al-Nakha'i and narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the knowledge of the Book is his knowledge of the revealed books of God, or of what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It was also said: it is the knowledge of Sulayman's letter to Bilqis. Sulayman had not returned his gaze before it was with him. The basic meaning of *ibtila'* (testing) is examination, that is, to examine me: whether I will be thankful for His blessing or ungrateful for it. Gratitude is the tether of existing blessings, and by it lost blessings are obtained.

(And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous) that is, free of need for gratitude, and generous in bestowing favor.

The original form of the nūn is doubling (tashdid), so the doubling was lightened in this position, just as it was lightened in: *ashhadu anaka 'alim* (I bear witness that you are a knower), whose original form is *annaka 'alim*. On this principle is built the reading of the one who read *"yushāqqūna fīhim"* and *"ataḥājjūnna fi'llāh"*. The Arabs have also said: *al-rijālu yaḍribūnī wa yaqṣidūnī* (the men strike me and intend me), and its origin is *yaḍribūnnī* and *yaqṣidūnnī*, since it is the assimilation (idgham) of *yaḍribūnanī* and *yaqṣidūnanī*. The poet said:

*tarhabīnī wa'l-jīdu minki li-Layla ... wa'l-ḥashā wa'l-bughāmu wa'l-'aynāni*

The original is *tarhabīnī*, and it was lightened. The meaning of *"atumiddūnan"* is: Do you add to me wealth beyond what you see of my possessions?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. That is, what He has given me of Islam, sovereignty and prophethood is better than what He has given you, so I do not rejoice in wealth. The word *"ātānī"* is written in all the codices without a yā'. Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Hafs read *"ātāniyal-lāh"* with an open yā'; when they stop, they drop it. As for Ya'qub, he retains it in pausal position and drops it in continuous recitation because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). The rest read it without a yā' in both states.

(*Bal antum bi-hadiyyatikum tafraḥūn*) — because you are people of boasting and rivalry in worldly matters.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Return to them﴾. That is, Sulayman said to al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, the leader of the delegation: Return to them with their gift.

(*Fa-la-na'tiyannahum bi-junūdin lā qibala lahum bihā*) — the *lām* is the lām of oath, and the nūn is obligatory with it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu'l-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lām of emphasis (lām al-tawkīd). He also held that the particles (lām) are all three only: the lām of emphasis, the lām of command, and the lām of genitive (khafḍ). This is the view of the skilled grammarians, because they return each thing to its origin; but this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of *"lā qibala lahum bihā"* is: they have no power to withstand it.

(*Wa-lanukhrijannahum minhā*) — that is, from their land (*adhillatan wa hum ṣāghirūn*). It is said: *"minhā"* means from the town of Saba'. The town was already mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it."

Then she ordered her throne to be brought, and it was placed in seven chambers, one inside another, in the innermost of seven palaces. Ibn Zayd also said: He wished to test her intellect, and for this reason he said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided." It is also said: the jinn feared that Sulayman would marry her and a son would be born to him from her, and then they would not cease to be in servitude and service to the progeny of Sulayman. So they told Sulayman that there was a defect in her intellect, and he wished to test her with her throne. Al-Nahhas said: For a strong one who has with him cunning and craftiness, it is said *'ifr*, *'ifriyah*, *'ifrit* and *'ufariyah*. It is also said: *'ifrit* means chief. A group recited *"qāla 'ifr"* with a kasra on the 'ayn, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Nahhas said: Whoever says *'ifriyah* makes its plural *'ifār*; and whoever says *'ifrit* has three options in the plural: if he wishes he says *'afārīt*, and if he wishes he says *'afār*, because the tā' is extra, as one says *ṭawāgh* as the plural of *ṭāghūt*; and if he wishes, he compensates for the tā' with a yā' and says *'afāriyy*. It is as if he were a star in the trail of an *'ifriyah*, descending through the blackness of the night.

When their devil, the *'ifrīt*, said: "You have neither sovereignty nor steadfastness."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Return to them﴾. That is, Sulayman said to al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, the leader of the delegation: Return to them with their gift.

(*Fa-la-na'tiyannahum bi-junūdin lā qibala lahum bihā*) — the *lām* is the lām of oath, and the nūn is obligatory with it. Al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu'l-Hasan ibn Kaysan say: It is the lām of emphasis (lām al-tawkīd). He also held that the particles (lām) are all three only: the lām of emphasis, the lām of command, and the lām of genitive (khafḍ). This is the view of the skilled grammarians, because they return each thing to its origin; but this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of *"lā qibala lahum bihā"* is: they have no power to withstand it.

(*Wa-lanukhrijannahum minhā*) — that is, from their land (*adhillatan wa hum ṣāghirūn*). It is said: *"minhā"* means from the town of Saba'. The town was already mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it."

*"Adhillatan"*: they have been stripped of their kingship and might. *"Wa hum ṣāghirūn"*: humiliated, abased, from *ṣighar* (smallness), which is abasement, if they do not submit. Then their messenger returned to her and informed her. She said: "I have known that he is not a king, and we have no power to fight a prophet of the prophets of Allah." Then she ordered her throne to be brought, and it was placed in seven chambers, one inside another, in the innermost of seven palaces. She locked the doors, set guards over it, and set out towards him with twelve thousand *qayl*s (chieftains) of the kings of Yemen, under each *qayl* one hundred thousand men. Ibn 'Abbas said: Sulayman was awe-inspiring, and no one would begin speaking to him until he asked them about what they had come for. One day he saw dust (*rahaj*) near him and said: "What is this?" They said: "Bilqis, O Prophet of Allah." Sulayman said to his soldiers—Wahb and others said to the jinn—(*Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?*)

'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad said: Bilqis was one farsakh away from Sulayman when he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" She had left her throne in Saba' and appointed guards to watch over it. It is also said: when she sent the gift, she sent her envoys with her army to surprise (*litughāfiṣa*) Sulayman, peace be upon him, by killing him before he could prepare for her, if he was seeking kingship. When he learned of this, he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn 'Abbas said: His command to bring the throne was before he wrote the letter to her, and he did not write to her until the throne came to him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent sense of the verses is that this statement came from Sulayman, peace be upon him, after the arrival of her gift and his returning it to her, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter. The majority of the interpreters hold this view.

They differed concerning the purpose of summoning her throne. Qatadah said: It was described to him as great and excellent, so he wished to seize it before it would protect her and her people through Islam; and Islam is upon this religion. This is also the view of Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that comes from Allah, and to make it a proof of his prophethood, by taking it from her houses without an army or war. On this interpretation, *"muslimīn"* means *mustaslimīn* (submitting), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Zayd also said: He wished to test her intellect, and for this reason he said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided." It is also said: the jinn feared that Sulayman would marry her and a son would be born to him from her, and then they would not cease to be in servitude and service to the progeny of Sulayman. So they told Sulayman that there was a defect in her intellect, and he wished to test her with her throne. It is also said: he wished to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his saying: "And she has a great throne." This was said by al-Tabari. Qatadah said: He loved to see it when the hoopoe described it. The first view is held by most scholars, because of His saying: "before they come to me in submission"; and because, if she had embraced Islam, her property would have been forbidden to him, and it could not be brought except with her permission. It is reported that it was of silver and gold, inlaid with red rubies and jewels, and that it was within seven chambers, upon which were seven locks.

His saying, Exalted is He: (*Qāla 'ifrītun mina'l-jinn*). Thus the majority recited it. Abu Raja' and 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited *"'ifriyatun"*, and it is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In a hadith: "Indeed Allah dislikes the *'ifriyah* (arrogant, cunning) and the *nifriyah*." This is an echo (ittibā') of *'ifriyah*. Qatadah said: It means the cunning one. Al-Nahhas said: For a strong one who has with him cunning and craftiness, it is said *'ifr*, *'ifriyah*, *'ifrit* and *'ufariyah*. It is also said: *'ifrit* means chief. A group recited *"qāla 'ifr"* with a kasra on the 'ayn, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Nahhas said: Whoever says *'ifriyah* makes its plural *'ifār*; and whoever says *'ifrit* has three options in the plural: if he wishes he says *'afārīt*, and if he wishes he says *'afār*, because the tā' is extra, as one says *ṭawāgh* as the plural of *ṭāghūt*; and if he wishes, he compensates for the tā' with a yā' and says *'afāriyy*. The *'ifrīt* is the strong, rebellious one among the devils, and the tā' is extra. They have also said: *tu'affarta al-rajul* when he takes on the character of harming. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The name of this *'ifrit* is Kawdan, recorded by al-Nahhas. It is also said: Dhakwan, recorded by al-Suhayli. Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i said: His name is Da'wan. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was Sakhr the jinni. From this name is the saying of Dhu'l-Rummah:

*ka-annahu kawkabun fī ithri 'ifriyatin musawwabun ... fī sawādi'l-layli munqaḍibu*

It is as if he were a star in the trail of an *'ifriyah*, descending through the blackness of the night.

Al-Kisa'i recited:

*idh qāla shaiṭānuhumu'l-'ifrītu ... laysa lakum mulkun wa lā tathbītu*

When their devil, the *'ifrīt*, said: "You have neither sovereignty nor steadfastness."

In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an *'ifrīt* from the jinn began to attack me last night, to cut off my prayer, but Allah enabled me against him, so I pushed him forcefully..." and he mentioned the hadith. In al-Bukhari, it reads: "...it *tafallata* upon me last night," instead of "began to attack (*yaftik*)." In the Muwatta', from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey (*usriya*), and he saw an *'ifrīt* from the jinn pursuing him with a flame of fire; whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned, he saw it. Jibril said: "Shall I not teach you words which, when you say them, its flame will be extinguished and it will fall on its face?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes." He said: "I seek refuge in the Generous Allah [in another version: I seek refuge in the Face of the Mighty Allah] and in the perfect words of Allah which neither the righteous nor the wicked can exceed, from the evil of what descends from the sky, and the evil of what ascends into it, [and the evil of what He has scattered in the earth, and the evil of what comes out of it,] and from the trials of night and day, and from the visitors of night and day, except a visitor who visits with good, O Most Merciful."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾. That is, from his council in which he judges.

(*Wa innī 'alayhi la-qawiyyun amīn*) — that is, strong to carry it, *"amīn"* trustworthy regarding what is in it. Ibn 'Abbas said: *amīn* over the private part of the woman; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Sulayman said: "I want faster than that." So (*Qāla alladhī 'indahu 'ilmun mina'l-kitābi anā ātīka bihi qabla an yartadda ilayka ṭarfuk*) — most of the commentators hold that the one who had knowledge of the Book was Asaf ibn Barkhiya, and he was from the Children of Israel. He was a *ṣiddīq* who memorised the Greatest Name of Allah, which when asked by it, He gives, and when called upon by it, He answers. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Greatest Name of Allah by which Asaf ibn Barkhiya supplicated is: *yā Ḥayyu yā Qayyūm*." It is said: in their language it is *ahayā sharāhayā*. Al-Zuhri said: The supplication of the one who had the Greatest Name of Allah was: "O our God and God of everything, one God; there is no god but You; bring me her throne." Then it was placed before him. Mujahid said: He supplicated and said: "O our God and God of everything, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." Al-Suhayli said: The one who had knowledge of the Book is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, the maternal cousin of Sulayman, and he had with him the Greatest Name of Allah from among the names of Allah, Exalted is He.

It is said: he is Sulayman himself, but this interpretation is not valid in the context of the discourse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A group said that he was Sulayman, peace be upon him, and the address in this interpretation is to the 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) when he said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place." It is as if Sulayman found this slow, so he said to him, in a belittling manner, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." The proponents of this view cited Sulayman's words, "This is of the bounty of my Lord." I say: What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned was said by al-Nahhas in his *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*, and it is a good opinion, God willing. Bahr said: He is an angel who holds the Book of Decrees, whom God sent at the 'ifrit's words. Al-Suhayli said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri' mentioned that he was Dabbah ibn Udd, but this is absolutely not valid, because Dabbah is the son of Udd ibn Tabikhah, whose name is 'Amr ibn Ilyas ibn Mudar ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd. Ma'd lived in the time of Bakht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), and that was a long time after the era of Sulayman. If Ma'd was not in the era of Sulayman, how could Dabbah ibn Udd be, when he is five generations after him?! This is clear to anyone who reflects on it. Ibn Lahi'ah said: He is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. Ibn Zayd said: The one who had knowledge of the Book was a righteous man who was on an island among the islands of the sea. He went out that day to look at who inhabits the earth and whether God is worshipped or not. He found Sulayman, so he invoked one of God's names and the throne was brought. A seventh view: he was a man from the Children of Israel named Yamlikha, who knew the Greatest Name of God; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri. Ibn Abi Bazzah said: The man who had knowledge of the Book was named Asṭūm, and he was a worshipper among the Children of Israel; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: It is only Sulayman, peace be upon him. Indeed, people think that he had a Name with him, but that is not so. Rather, he was a man of the Children of Israel, a scholar whom God had given knowledge and understanding. He said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." [Sulayman] said, "Bring it." He said, "You are the Prophet of God, son of the Prophet of God; if you invoke God, He will bring it to you." So Sulayman invoked God, and God brought him the throne. An eighth view: he is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. This was said by al-Nakha'i and narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the knowledge of the Book is his knowledge of the revealed books of God, or of what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It was also said: it is the knowledge of Sulayman's letter to Bilqis. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What the majority of people hold is that he was a righteous man from the Children of Israel named Asaf ibn Barkhiya. It is narrated that he prayed two units of prayer, then said to Sulayman, "O Prophet of God, extend your gaze." So [Sulayman] extended his gaze toward Yemen, and behold, the throne was there. Sulayman had not returned his gaze before it was with him. Mujahid said: "Their glance returning to them" means continuing to look until the glance returns to them, "dazed and exhausted" (Qur'an 67:4). It was also said that he meant the amount of time it takes to open one's eye and then blink, and this is like when you say: "Do such-and-such in the blink of an eye." This is more fitting, because if the act was from Sulayman, it is a miracle (mu'jizah), and if it was from Asaf or from another of God's friends (awliya'), it is a marvel (karamah), and the marvel of a friend of God is a miracle of the Prophet. Al-Qushayri said: Whoever said that the one with knowledge of the Book was Sulayman, who said to the 'ifrit, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," has denied the marvels of the friends of God. According to these people, what the 'ifrit did is neither a miracle nor a marvel, because the jinn are capable of such things. A substance cannot be in two places at once in one state. Rather, it can be conceived as follows: God annihilates the substance in the far east and then recreates it in a second state, which is the state after annihilation, in the far west; or He annihilates the intervening places and then recreates them. Al-Qushayri said: Wahb narrated it from Malik. It has also been said: rather, it was brought through the air, as Mujahid said. The distance between Sulayman and the throne was like the distance between Kufa and al-Hira. Malik said: It was in Yemen while Sulayman, peace be upon him, was in Syria. In the exegetical works it is related that the throne of Bilqis split at its place where it was, then sprang forth before Sulayman. 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad said: The throne appeared from a tunnel beneath the earth. God knows best which of these was the case.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he saw it settled beside him﴾, that is, firmly established beside him.

(He said, "This is of the bounty of my Lord") that is, this victory and empowerment are from the bounty of my Lord.

(To test me) Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is "to see" (li-yanzur). Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is figurative. The basic meaning of *ibtila'* (testing) is examination, that is, to examine me: whether I will be thankful for His blessing or ungrateful for it. (And whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own self) that is, the benefit of that does not return except to himself, since by his gratitude he merits the perfection of the blessing, its continuance, and its increase. Gratitude is the tether of existing blessings, and by it lost blessings are obtained.

(And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous) that is, free of need for gratitude, and generous in bestowing favor.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 27, verses 41–43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her"﴾, meaning: alter it. It was said: he made its top its bottom and its bottom its top. It was also said: it was altered by addition or subtraction. Al-Farra' and others said: he only ordered its disguising because the devils had told him that there was something wrong with her intellect, so he wanted to test her. It was also said: the jinn feared that Sulayman would marry her and that she would bear him a child, and then they would remain subjugated to the family of Sulayman forever. So they told Sulayman: "She is weak of mind, and her leg is like the leg of a donkey." So he said: "Disguise her throne for her," in order that we may know her intellect. Sulayman had a counselor among the jinn, who said: "How can I see her two shins without asking her to uncover them?" He replied: "I will make water in this palace and place glass over the water. She will think it is water, so she will lift her garment and you will see her two shins." This is the *sarh* (palace of glass) of which Allah, may He be exalted, informed. His saying, may He be exalted: (So when she came), meaning Bilqis, (it was said to her), "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it." She likened it to it because she had left it behind locked doors, so she neither affirmed nor denied, and Sulayman knew her perfect intellect. 'Ikrimah said: she was wise, so she said, "It is as if it were it." Muqatil said: she recognized it, but she made it ambiguous to them just as they had made it ambiguous to her; and if she had been asked, "Is this your throne?" she would have said, "Yes, it is." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl also said this. It was also said: Sulayman wanted to show her that the jinn and the devils were subjugated to him, so that she would know that this was prophethood and believe in him. It has been said that this was in response to her confusing the matter for him concerning the boys and the girls.

(And we were given knowledge before her) — it was said: this is from the saying of Bilqis, meaning: we were given knowledge of the truth of Sulayman's prophethood before this sign concerning the throne (and we were Muslims), submissive to his command. It was also said: it is from the saying of Sulayman, meaning: we were given knowledge of Allah's power over whatever He wills before this occasion. It was also said: "and we were given knowledge" refers to her Islam and her coming in obedience before her arrival. It was also said: it is from the speech of Sulayman's people. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had barred her﴾. Stopping at "besides Allah" is acceptable, and the meaning is: what she used to worship of the sun and the moon prevented her from worshipping Allah. "Ma" is in the nominative position. Al-Nahhas said: the meaning is, that her worship besides Allah and her worship of it barred her from knowing what we know [from becoming Muslim]. It is also permissible for "ma" to be in the accusative position, and the sense would be: Sulayman barred her from what she used to worship besides Allah, meaning he came between her and it. It is also permissible for the meaning to be: Allah barred her, that is, Allah prevented her from worshipping other than Him, so "'an" was dropped and the verb became transitive. Its parallel is: "And Musa chose his people" meaning from among his people. Sibawayh recited [the line of al-Farazdaq, meaning by "Abd Allah" the tribe, namely 'Abd Allah ibn Darim]:

"I was informed of 'Abd Allah in the plain, its noble clients have become honorable and its lineage base"

He held that the meaning in his view was: "I was informed about 'Abd Allah."

(Indeed she was of a disbelieving people.) Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "annaha" with a fatha on the hamza, and it is in the accusative position, meaning "because she." It is also permissible for it to be a substitute for "ma," in which case it is in the nominative position if "ma" is the subject of the barring. The kasra is for a fresh sentence.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi on surah 27, verse 44 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words, ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾

According to Sibawayh, the implied meaning is: "Enter into the palace," so the preposition *ilā* ("to") was omitted and the verb became transitive. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) considers this an error on Sibawayh's part, saying: "Because *dakhala* (to enter) already denotes the place entered." The palace (*al-ṣarḥ*) was a pool of glass with water beneath it and fish in it. Solomon built it to show her a kingdom greater than her own. This is related from Mujahid.

Qatada said: It was made of glass, with water behind it, *sabathathu lujjatan* ("she supposed it was a pool"), meaning water.

It was also said that *al-ṣarḥ* means a palace, related from Abu Ubayda, as in the line of verse [[The line is by Abu Dhu'ayb, in full: "On roads like the necks of gazelles, their landmarks are taken for palaces (ṣurūḥ)." He means these roads are like the necks of gazelles in their clarity.]]:

*taḥsibu aʿlāmahunna al-ṣurūḥā*
("they take their landmarks for palaces")

It was also said that *al-ṣarḥ* means a courtyard, as one says: "This is the courtyard (*ṣarḥat*) of the house and its open space," with the same meaning.

Abu Ubayda, in *Gharib al-Musannaf*, relates that *al-ṣarḥ* is any tall building raised high above the ground, and that *al-mumarrad* means long. Al-Nahhas said: The root of this is that every building made as a single, unmixed construction is called *ṣarḥ*, from their saying *labanun ṣarīḥ* ("pure milk"), meaning milk not mixed with water, and from their saying *ṣarraḥa bil-amr* ("he declared the matter plainly"), and from it *ʿarabiyyun ṣarīḥ* ("pure Arab").

It was also said that he built it to test the jinn's claim about her, that her mother was of the jinn and her leg was a donkey's leg. This is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

When she saw the water she was frightened and thought that he intended her to drown. She was also astonished that his throne was upon the water, and she saw what alarmed her. There was no alternative to obeying the command, so ﴿she uncovered her shins﴾.

Then she was found to have the most beautiful shins of people, free of what the jinn had claimed, except that they were thickly covered with hair. When she reached this point, Sulayman, after turning his gaze away from her, said to her: ﴿It is a palace paved smooth with glass.﴾

*Al-mumarrad* means the scraped and smoothed. From it comes *al-amrad* (the beardless). A man is said to *tamarrada* when the growth of his beard is delayed after reaching maturity. This is stated by al-Farra'. From it comes *al-shajara al-marda'* (a tree with no leaves on it) and *ramla marda'* (a sand dune that grows nothing). *Al-mumarrad* also means elongated, and from this the fortress is called *marid*. Abu Salih said: tall, in the shape of a palm tree. Ibn Shajara said: wide in its length and breadth. He said:

*ghadawtu ṣabāḥan bākiran fawajadtahum*
*qabīla al-ḍuḥā fī al-sābiriyyi al-mumarrad*

("I set out in the early morning and found them / before forenoon, in wide sābiriyy coats of mail")

That is, the wide coats of mail.

At that point Bilqis submitted, yielded, and became a Muslim, and she acknowledged that she had wronged herself, as will be explained.

When Sulayman, peace be upon him, saw her legs, he said to his counselor from among the devils: "How can I remove this hair without harming the body?" So the devil showed him how to make *al-nawra* (a depilatory paste), and from that day on the *nawra* and the bathhouses came into use. It is related that Sulayman then married her and settled her in al-Sham, as stated by al-Dahhak.

Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz said in the book of al-Naqqash: He married her and returned her to her kingdom in Yemen, and he would visit her by the wind once a month. She bore him a boy whom she named Dawud, who died in his lifetime.

In some reports the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Bilqis was one of the most beautiful women of the worlds, with fine shins, and she is among the wives of Sulayman, peace be upon him, in Paradise." Then ʿĀʾisha said: "Are her shins more beautiful than mine?" He said, peace be upon him: "You have more beautiful shins than hers in Paradise." This is mentioned by al-Qushayri.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to make bathhouses was Sulayman ibn Dawud. When he pressed his back against the wall and its heat touched him, he said: *Awwah* (an expression of pain) from the punishment of Allah."

Then he loved her with intense love and confirmed her in her kingdom in Yemen. He commanded the jinn, and they built for her three fortresses the like of which people had never seen for height: Salhun, Baynun, and ʿUmdan. Then Sulayman used to visit her once a month and stay with her for three days.

Al-Sha'bi related that some people from Himyar dug up the cemetery of the kings and found there a vaulted tomb containing a woman, with garments woven with gold, and at her head was a marble slab on which was written:

*yā ayyuhā al-aqwāmu ʿūjū maʿan*
*wa arbiʿū fī maqbarī al-ʿīsā*
*li-taʿlamū annī tilka allatī*
*qad kuntu udʿā al-dahra Bilqīsā*
*shayyadtu qaṣra al-mulki fī Ḥimyara*
*qawmī wa qidman kāna maʾnūsā*
*wa kuntu fī mulkī wa tadbīrihi*
*urghimu fī Allāhi al-maʿāṭīsā*
*baʿlī Sulaymānu al-Nabiyyu alladhī*
*qad kāna lil-tawrāti dirrīsā*
*wa sukhkhira al-rīḥu lahu markaban*
*tahubbu aḥyānan rawāmīsā*
*maʿa ibni Dāwuda al-Nabiyyi alladhī*
*qaddasahu al-Raḥmānu taqdīsā*

("O peoples, come together and halt at my tomb, the camels too, / so that you may know that I am the one who was called Bilqis for ages. / I built the palace of the kingdom in Himyar, my people, and of old it was familiar. / I was in my kingdom and its management, humbling the proud in the cause of Allah. / My husband is Sulayman the Prophet, who was a teacher of the Torah, / and the wind was made subject to him as a vehicle, blowing at times gently, / along with the son of Dawud the Prophet, whom the Merciful sanctified in holiness.")

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Sulayman did not marry her. He only said to her, "Choose a husband." She said, "One like me is not married off, and I once had a kingdom like the one I have." He said, "There is no escape from this in Islam." So she chose Dhu Tubba', king of Hamdan. He married her to him, returned her to Yemen, and ordered Zawba'ah, the amir of the jinn of Yemen, to obey him. Dhu Tubba' built the reservoirs (al-masani') for him, and he remained a ruler until Sulayman died.

Some said: No sound report has come concerning whether he married her or whether he gave her in marriage.

She is Bilqis bint al-Sarh ibn al-Hudahid ibn Shurahil ibn Adad ibn Hadar ibn al-Sarh ibn al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Sayfi ibn Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn Abir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

Her grandfather al-Hudahid was a king of great standing. He had forty sons, all of them kings, and he ruled the whole land of Yemen. Her father al-Sarh used to say to the kings of the outlying regions: "None of you is my equal." He refused to marry any of them, so they married him to a woman of the jinn called Rayhanah bint al-Sakan. She bore him Lukmah, who was Bilqis, and he had no other child besides her.

Abu Hurayrah said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "One of Bilqis's two parents was a jinn." Then her father died, and her people split into two factions against her. They made a man their ruler, and his conduct was bad until he committed adultery with the women of his subjects. Bilqis was seized by jealousy. She offered herself to him, and he married her. Then she gave him wine until she cut off his head, and she hung it on the gate of her house. So they made her their ruler.

Abu Bakrah said: Bilqis was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "A people will not prosper if they entrust their affairs to a woman."[[The hadith is narrated in al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi through Abu Bakrah concerning the daughter of Kisra. When news reached the Prophet (ﷺ) that the Persians had made the daughter of Kisra their ruler after his death, he (ﷺ) said: "And a people will not prosper if they entrust their affairs to a woman."]]

It is said that the reason for her father's marriage to a jinn woman was that he was a minister to a tyrannical king who seized the wives of his subjects. The minister was jealous, so he did not marry. Once, on a journey, he kept company with a man he did not know. The man asked him, "Do you have a wife?" He replied, "I will never marry, for the king of our land seizes women from their husbands." The man said, "If you marry my daughter, he will never seize her." The minister said, "But he will seize her." The man said, "We are a people of the jinn; he has no power over us." So he married his daughter, and she bore him Bilqis. Then the mother died, and Bilqis built a palace in the desert. Her father spoke carelessly about her story, and news of her reached the king. He said to him, "O so-and-so, this beautiful girl is with you, and you do not bring her to me, though you know my love for women." Then he ordered that the father be imprisoned. Bilqis sent to the king: "I am before you." So he prepared to set out for her palace. When he was about to enter, with those who were with him, she brought out to him maidens from the daughters of the jinn, in the likeness of the sun. They said to him, "Are you not ashamed? Our mistress says: Do you enter upon your wife with these men along with you?" So he dismissed them and entered alone. She closed the door on him, killed him with sandals, cut off his head and threw it to his army. They made her their commander, and she continued in that state until the hoopoe reported her news to Sulayman, peace be upon him.

This was because when Sulayman stopped at one of his stations, he sent the hoopoe. He rose toward the sky and saw the length and breadth of the world, and he saw the world to his right and left. He saw a garden of Bilqis in which there was a hoopoe, whose name was Ufayr. The hoopoe of Yemen said to the hoopoe of Sulayman, "Where have you come from, and where are you going?" He said, "I have come from al-Sham with my companion Sulayman ibn Dawud." He said, "And who is Sulayman?" He said, "The king of the jinn, the humans, the devils, the birds, the beasts, the wind, and everything between heaven and earth. And where are you from?" He said, "From this land. Its ruler is a woman called Bilqis. Under her hand are twelve thousand chieftains (qayl), and under each chieftain are a hundred thousand fighting men, apart from the women and children." So the hoopoe went with him and looked at Bilqis and her kingdom. Then he returned to Sulayman at the time of the afternoon prayer. Sulayman had missed him at the time of prayer and did not find him, and they were without water.

Ibn Abbas said in one narration: a breath of the sun had fallen upon him. Sulayman said to the chief of the birds, "Where is the place of so-and-so?" He said, "O Prophet of Allah, this is the place of the hoopoe." He said, "Where has he gone?" He said, "I do not know, may Allah set the king aright." So Sulayman became angry and said: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾, the verse.

Then he summoned the eagle, the lord of the birds, the strongest and the most powerful of them. He said, "What do you want, O Prophet of Allah?" He said, "Bring me the hoopoe at once." The eagle raised itself beneath the sky until it pressed against the air. It looked at the world, which was like a bowl before one of you. Suddenly it saw the hoopoe coming from the direction of Yemen. It swooped toward him and sank its talon into him. The hoopoe said to him, "I ask you by Allah, who empowered you and strengthened you, to have mercy on me." He said to him, "Woe to you, may your mother be bereaved! The Prophet of Allah, Sulayman, has sworn that he will punish you or slaughter you." Then he brought him, and the vultures and the rest of the armies of the birds met him. They said, "Woe to you! The Prophet of Allah has threatened you." He said, "What is my worth and what am I? Did he not make an exception?" They said, "Yes, he said: ﴿Or he shall bring me a clear authority﴾." Then he entered upon Sulayman and raised his head, and he lowered his tail and wings in humility before Sulayman, peace be upon him.

Sulayman said to him, "Where have you been, neglecting your service and your place? I will surely punish you with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter you." The hoopoe said to him, "O Prophet of Allah, remember your standing before Allah, which is like my standing before you." Sulayman's skin shivered and trembled, and he pardoned him.

Ikrimah said: Allah turned Sulayman away from slaughtering the hoopoe because it was dutiful to its parents, carrying food to them and feeding them.

Then Sulayman said to him, "What has delayed you?" The hoopoe said what Allah has told about Bilqis, her throne, and her people, as its explanation has already passed.

Al-Mawardi said: The view that the mother of Bilqis was a jinn woman is rejected by reason, because the two kinds differ, their natures are different, and their substances are separate. The human is corporeal, while the jinn is spiritual. Allah created the human from clay like pottery, and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire. Intermingling is prevented given this difference, and procreation is impossible given this divergence.

I say: This matter has already been discussed. Reason does not rule it out, given the reports that have come concerning it. If one considers the origin of creation, its origin is water, as has been explained earlier, and there is no remoteness in this. And Allah knows best. In the revelation: ﴿and share with them in wealth and children﴾, and this has already passed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾, as will come in Surat al-Rahman.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾. That is, by the polytheism she had been upon. This was said by Ibn Shajarah. Sufyan said: That is, by the assumption she had imagined about Sulayman, because when she was commanded to enter the palace (al-sarh), she thought it was deep water (lujjah), and that Sulayman intended to drown her in it. When it became clear to her that it was a palace smoothed with glass, she knew that she had wronged herself by that assumption.

"Inna" was given a kasra because it begins a statement after a verb of saying. Some Arabs read it with a fatha, so that the verb of saying governs it.

﴿"I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

If you pronounce "ma'a" with a sukun, it is a particle used for a meaning, with no disagreement among the grammarians. If you read it with a fatha, there are two views. One is that it is a noun meaning a place (zarf). The other is that it is a prepositional particle (harf khafd) built on the fatha, as stated by al-Nahhas.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verse 45–47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah"﴾. Its meaning has already been given.

(Then they became two factions contending) Mujahid said: that is, a believer and a disbeliever. He said: The contention is what Allah related in His saying: "Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" up to His saying: "disbelievers." It was also said: Their contention was that each faction said, "We are upon the truth, not you."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good?"﴾ Mujahid said: [i.e., seeking] the punishment before mercy. The meaning is: Why do you delay faith, which brings you reward, and hasten disbelief, which necessitates punishment? So the disbelievers, out of extreme denial, would say: "Bring us the punishment." It was also said: that is, why do you do what makes you deserving of punishment, not that they were asking for the punishment to be hastened.

(Why do you not seek forgiveness from Allah) That is, why do you not repent to Allah from polytheism?

(That perhaps you may receive mercy) That is, so that you may be shown mercy, and this has already been discussed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you and from those with you."﴾ That is, we consider you a bad omen. Ill omen (shu'm) is misfortune. There is nothing more harmful to sound judgment, nor more corrupting to planning, than belief in omens (tiyarah). Whoever thinks that the lowing of a cow or the croaking of a crow can turn back a decree or repel what has been decreed has indeed erred. The poet said:

The omens of time do not turn back a decree,
So excuse time and do not blame it.

Whatever day it singles out for good fortune,
And the deaths descend upon every day.

There is no day but in it is good fortune
And misfortune that flows to one people and then another.

The Arabs were among the people most given to omens. When they intended a journey, they would startle a bird; if it flew to the right, they proceeded and took it as auspicious, and if it flew to the left, they returned and took it as ill-omened. The Prophet ﷺ forbade this and said: "Leave birds in their nests [[al-Wakanat (with the kaf vowelled, or with fatha, or with sukun) are the plural of wakanah (with sukun), meaning the bird's nest and its lair. It is also narrated as: "ala makanatiha" (in their places).]]" as has already been explained in Surah al-Ma'idah [[See vol. 6, p. 60, first or second edition.]].

(He said, "Your omen is with Allah") That is, your calamities.

(Rather, you are a people being tested) That is, you are being tried. It was also said: you are being punished for your sins.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And there were in the city﴾, that is, in the city of Salih, which is al-Hijr, **(nine men of a group)**, that is, nine men from among the sons of their nobles. Al-Dahhak said: These nine were the great men of the city, and they used to cause corruption on the earth and command corruption. They sat near a huge rock, and Allah overturned it upon them. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: It has reached me that they used to clip dinars and dirhams, and that was among the corruption on the earth. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said the same. It was also said: their corruption was that they pursued people's faults and did not conceal them. It was also said: other than this. What is necessarily implied by the verse is what al-Dahhak and others said: that they were among the most prominent, the most handsome, and the wealthiest of the people, and that they were people of disbelief and many sins. The summary of their affair is that they caused corruption and did not set things right. The **rahṭ** (group) is a name for a company of people, as though they were leaders, each one of whom was followed by a rahṭ. Its plurals are arhuṭ and arahit. A poet said:

"Woe to the war that has placed the groups (arahit), so that they have found rest."

These mentioned men were the companions of Qudar, the slayer of the she-camel, as Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned. I say: their names have been disputed. Al-Ghaznawi said: Their names are Qudar ibn Salif, Mis'a', Aslam, Dasama, Dhuhaym, Dhi'ma, Dhi'yam, Qital, and Sadaq. Ibn Ishaq said: Their head was Qudar ibn Salif and Mis'a' ibn Mihra'; seven followed them, namely Bala' ibn Mayla', Du'ayr ibn Ghanm, Dhu'ab ibn Muhraj, and four whose names are not known. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned their names on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: al-Hudhayl ibn 'Abd Rabb, Ghanm ibn Ghanm, Ri'ab ibn Muhraj, Mus'ad ibn Muhraj, 'Umayr ibn Kardaba, 'Asim ibn Makhrama, Subayt ibn Sadaqa, Sam'an ibn Safi, and Qudar ibn Salif; they are the ones who strove in the slaying of the she-camel, and they were the most rebellious of the people of Salih, and they were from among the sons of their nobles. Al-Suhayli said: al-Naqqash mentioned the nine who used to cause corruption on the earth and did not set things right, and named them by their names; but that cannot be established by a narration. Nevertheless I mention it as personal effort and conjecture, but we mention it according to what we found in the book of Muhammad ibn Habib, and they are: Mus'ada ibn Dahr, also said Dahm; Qudar ibn Salif; Huraym, and Sawab, and Ri'ab, and Dabb, and Da'mа, and Harma, and Du'ayn ibn 'Umayr. I say: al-Mawardi has mentioned their names on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, saying: They are Da'ma, Du'ayam, Harma, Huraym, Dabb, Sawab, Ri'ab, Misṭah, and Qudar; and they were in the land of al-Hijr, which is the land of Sham.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾. It is permissible that "taqasamu" (swear to one another) be an imperative verb in the future form, meaning that some of them said to others: "Swear." It is also permissible that it be a past verb with the meaning of the present, as though he said: they said, swearing mutually by Allah. The evidence for this interpretation is the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "They cause corruption on the earth and do not set things right. Swear to one another by Allah," and there is no "qalu" in it. "We will surely attack him and his family, then we will surely say to his heir" is the reading of the majority with nun in both places, and Abu Hatim preferred it. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with ta' in both places, with the ta' and the lam pronounced with a damma, in the second person, meaning that they addressed one another with this; Abu 'Ubayd preferred it. Mujahid and Humayd read with ya' in both places, with the ya' and the lam pronounced with a damma, in the third person. **Al-bayat** (night attack) is the surprise attack upon the enemy at night. The meaning of "to his heir" is to the group of Salih who holds the right of blood-vengeance.

﴿We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾, that is, we were not present, and we do not know who killed him and his family.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ in our denial of killing him. The **mahlak** (destruction) means the destruction itself, and it is permissible that it be a place. [Note in the source: "mahlak" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam is the reading of the majority.] 'Asim and al-Sulami read (with a fatha on the mim and the lam), that is, the destruction; it is said: "daraba yadribu madraban," meaning darban (a striking). Al-Mufaddal and Abu Bakr read (with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam), so the noun of place is like "al-majlis" for the place of sitting, and it is permissible that it be a verbal noun, as in the Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿To Him is your return (marji'ukum)﴾, that is, your return (ruju'ukum).

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And there were in the city﴾, that is, in the city of Salih, which is al-Hijr, **(nine men of a group)**, that is, nine men from among the sons of their nobles. Al-Dahhak said: These nine were the great men of the city, and they used to cause corruption on the earth and command corruption. They sat near a huge rock, and Allah overturned it upon them. Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: It has reached me that they used to clip dinars and dirhams, and that was among the corruption on the earth. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said the same. It was also said: their corruption was that they pursued people's faults and did not conceal them. It was also said: other than this. What is necessarily implied by the verse is what al-Dahhak and others said: that they were among the most prominent, the most handsome, and the wealthiest of the people, and that they were people of disbelief and many sins. The summary of their affair is that they caused corruption and did not set things right. The **rahṭ** (group) is a name for a company of people, as though they were leaders, each one of whom was followed by a rahṭ. Its plurals are arhuṭ and arahit. A poet said:

"Woe to the war that has placed the groups (arahit), so that they have found rest."

These mentioned men were the companions of Qudar, the slayer of the she-camel, as Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned. I say: their names have been disputed. Al-Ghaznawi said: Their names are Qudar ibn Salif, Mis'a', Aslam, Dasama, Dhuhaym, Dhi'ma, Dhi'yam, Qital, and Sadaq. Ibn Ishaq said: Their head was Qudar ibn Salif and Mis'a' ibn Mihra'; seven followed them, namely Bala' ibn Mayla', Du'ayr ibn Ghanm, Dhu'ab ibn Muhraj, and four whose names are not known. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned their names on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: al-Hudhayl ibn 'Abd Rabb, Ghanm ibn Ghanm, Ri'ab ibn Muhraj, Mus'ad ibn Muhraj, 'Umayr ibn Kardaba, 'Asim ibn Makhrama, Subayt ibn Sadaqa, Sam'an ibn Safi, and Qudar ibn Salif; they are the ones who strove in the slaying of the she-camel, and they were the most rebellious of the people of Salih, and they were from among the sons of their nobles. Al-Suhayli said: al-Naqqash mentioned the nine who used to cause corruption on the earth and did not set things right, and named them by their names; but that cannot be established by a narration. Nevertheless I mention it as personal effort and conjecture, but we mention it according to what we found in the book of Muhammad ibn Habib, and they are: Mus'ada ibn Dahr, also said Dahm; Qudar ibn Salif; Huraym, and Sawab, and Ri'ab, and Dabb, and Da'mа, and Harma, and Du'ayn ibn 'Umayr. I say: al-Mawardi has mentioned their names on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, saying: They are Da'ma, Du'ayam, Harma, Huraym, Dabb, Sawab, Ri'ab, Misṭah, and Qudar; and they were in the land of al-Hijr, which is the land of Sham.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾. It is permissible that "taqasamu" (swear to one another) be an imperative verb in the future form, meaning that some of them said to others: "Swear." It is also permissible that it be a past verb with the meaning of the present, as though he said: they said, swearing mutually by Allah. The evidence for this interpretation is the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "They cause corruption on the earth and do not set things right. Swear to one another by Allah," and there is no "qalu" in it. "We will surely attack him and his family, then we will surely say to his heir" is the reading of the majority with nun in both places, and Abu Hatim preferred it. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with ta' in both places, with the ta' and the lam pronounced with a damma, in the second person, meaning that they addressed one another with this; Abu 'Ubayd preferred it. Mujahid and Humayd read with ya' in both places, with the ya' and the lam pronounced with a damma, in the third person. **Al-bayat** (night attack) is the surprise attack upon the enemy at night. The meaning of "to his heir" is to the group of Salih who holds the right of blood-vengeance.

﴿We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾, that is, we were not present, and we do not know who killed him and his family.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ in our denial of killing him. The **mahlak** (destruction) means the destruction itself, and it is permissible that it be a place. [Note in the source: "mahlak" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam is the reading of the majority.] 'Asim and al-Sulami read (with a fatha on the mim and the lam), that is, the destruction; it is said: "daraba yadribu madraban," meaning darban (a striking). (وَمَكَرُوا مَكْراً وَمَكَرْنا مَكْراً وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ) ﴿They plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they did not perceive.﴾ Their plot: it is narrated that these nine, when the three days after the slaughter of the she-camel were underway, and Salih had informed them of the coming of the punishment, agreed and swore together that they would come to Salih's house by night and kill him and his close family. They said: "If he is lying in his threat, we will inflict upon him what he deserves; and if he is truthful, we will have hastened it before him and cooled our souls." This was said by Mujahid and others. Ibn Abbas said: God Most High sent the angels that night, and Salih's house was filled with them. The nine came to Salih's house with their swords drawn, and the angels killed them by stoning (radkh bil-hijarah). They saw the stones but did not see who was throwing them. Qatadah said: They went out hastening toward Salih, and an angel was set upon them holding a rock in his hand, and he killed them. Al-Suddi said: They descended upon a cliff (jurf) of the earth, and it collapsed under them, and God destroyed them beneath it. It was also said: They hid in a cave near Salih's house, and a rock came down upon them and crushed them all. This is what their plot was. God's plot is His requiting them for that.

(فَانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ أَنَّا دَمَّرْناهُمْ وَقَوْمَهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ) ﴿So look at what the outcome of their plot was: We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ That is, by the Cry (al-sayhah) which destroyed them. It has been said that the destruction of all of them was by the cry of Jibril. The more apparent view is that the nine perished by a separate punishment, then the rest perished by the Cry and the Damdamah (the crushing). Al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i used to recite "أَنَّا" with a fatha. Ibn al-Anbari said: "According to this reading, it is not good to stop at ʿāqibatu makrihim, because anna dammarnāhum is the predicate of kāna." It is permissible to make it in the position of the nominative, as a substitute (ittiba') for ʿāqibah. It is permissible to make it in the position of the accusative according to al-Farra', and in the genitive according to al-Kisa'i, with the meaning: "because We destroyed them" and "for that We destroyed them." It is permissible to make it in the accusative position as a substitute for the position of kayfa. Accordingly, under these views it is not good to stop at makrihim.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu Amr recited "إِنَّا دَمَّرْناهُمْ" with a kasra on the alif, as a resumption (istinaf). According to this view, it is good to stop at makrihim. Al-Nahhas said: It is permissible that ʿāqibah be put in the accusative as the predicate of kāna, and that "innā" be in the nominative position as the subject of kāna. It is also permissible that it be in the nominative position by assuming an omitted subject (mubtada') as an explanation of the outcome, the estimate being: "it is that We destroyed them." Abu Hatim said: In the reading of Ubayy, "أَنْ دَمَّرْناهُمْ" confirms its being with a fatha.

قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خاوِيَةً بِما ظَلَمُوا﴾ ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged.﴾ The reading of the common people is with the accusative, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) according to al-Farra' and al-Nahhas, meaning: empty of their people, in ruin, with no dweller in them. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubaydah said: "khawiyah" is in the accusative as a cut-off (qat'), its underlying form being: "so those are their empty houses." When the alif and lam were removed from it, it was put in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative, like His saying: "and His is the religion, perpetual" (wa-lahu al-din wasiban). Isa ibn Umar, Nasr ibn Asim and al-Jahdari recited it with the nominative, as a predicate of "tilka," and "buyutuhum" as a substitute (badal) of "tilka." It is permissible that "buyutuhum" be an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) and "khawiyah" the predicate of "tilka." It is permissible that "khawiyah" be in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is empty," or as a substitute for "buyutuhum," because an indefinite noun may be a substitute for a definite noun.

It is also permissible that it be in the nominative position by assuming an omitted subject (mubtada') as an explanation of the outcome, the estimate being: "it is that We destroyed them." Abu Hatim said: In the reading of Ubayy, "أَنْ دَمَّرْناهُمْ" confirms its being with a fatha.

قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خاوِيَةً بِما ظَلَمُوا﴾ ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged.﴾ The reading of the common people is with the accusative, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) according to al-Farra' and al-Nahhas, meaning: empty of their people, in ruin, with no dweller in them. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubaydah said: "khawiyah" is in the accusative as a cut-off (qat'), its underlying form being: "so those are their empty houses." When the alif and lam were removed from it, it was put in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative, like His saying: "and His is the religion, perpetual" (wa-lahu al-din wasiban). Isa ibn Umar, Nasr ibn Asim and al-Jahdari recited it with the nominative, as a predicate of "tilka," and "buyutuhum" as a substitute (badal) of "tilka." It is permissible that "buyutuhum" be an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) and "khawiyah" the predicate of "tilka." It is permissible that "khawiyah" be in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is empty," or as a substitute for "buyutuhum," because an indefinite noun may be a substitute for a definite noun.

(إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ. وَأَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا) ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know. And We saved those who believed﴾ in Salih (بِصَالِحٍ) (وَكانُوا يَتَّقُونَ) ﴿and were God-fearing﴾, fearing God and fearing His punishment. It has been said: about four thousand men believed in Salih. The rest went out with their bodies, according to Muqatil and others, as pustules like chickpeas (khurrajat mithl al-himmis). On the first day it was red, then on the next day it became yellow, then on the third day it became black. The slaughter of the she-camel was on Wednesday, and their destruction on Sunday. Muqatil said: Those pustules burst, and Jibril shouted at them during that a single cry, and they were extinguished, and that was in the forenoon. Salih went out with those who believed with him toward Hadramawt, and when he entered it, Salih died, so Hadramawt was named after him. Al-Dahhak said: Then the four thousand built a city called Hadur, as its explanation has preceded in the story of the People of the Rass.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 54–61:**

His the Exalted's words: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people﴾. That is, [We sent] Lot, or [mention] Lot. "When he said to his people," and they were the people of Sodom. And he said to his people: ﴿Do you commit an indecency﴾, the ugly and monstrous deed.

﴿While you see [it]﴾ that it is an indecency, and that is greater in your sins. It was said: some of you come upon others while you are looking at one another. They did not conceal themselves, out of their insolence and defiance.

﴿Indeed, you approach men in lust instead of women﴾. He repeated it because of its extreme ugliness and monstrousness.

﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾, either of the command of prohibition or of the punishment. As for the choice of al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) and Sibawayh, it is to soften the second hamza (glottal stop) in ﴿a-innakum﴾. As for the script, the proper way is to write it with two alifs in all its forms, because it is an initial hamza to which the interrogative alif has been prefixed.

His the Exalted's words: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your town; indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ That is, from the anuses of men. They said that mockingly, as Mujahid said. Qatadah said: By Allah, they found fault with them without any fault, [saying] that they keep themselves pure from evil deeds.

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We had decreed her to be among those who remained behind﴾. Ásim read ﴿qaddarna﴾ with a light pronunciation, and the meaning is the same. It is said: "qadtu al-shay'a qadran wa qadaran wa qaddartuhu."

﴿And We rained upon them a rain, and wretched was the rain of those who were warned﴾. That is, those who were warned but did not accept the warning. The explanation of this has already passed in [Surah] "al-A'raf" [See vol. 7, p. 247, first or second edition.] and [Surah] "Hud" [See vol. 9, p. 81 onward, first or second edition.].

His the Exalted's words: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Al-Farra' said, the people of meanings said: It was said to Lot, "Say, 'Praise be to Allah'," over their destruction. A group of scholars disagreed with al-Farra' on this and said: it is an address to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), that is, "Say, praise be to Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of the earlier nations." Al-Nahhas said: This is more appropriate, because the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and everything in it is addressed to him, peace be upon him, except what cannot have its meaning apply except to someone else. It was also said: the meaning is, "Say," O Muhammad, "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen," meaning his community (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi said: Allah chose them through knowing Him and obeying Him. Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan said: they are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to recite these verses, which bear proofs of His oneness, His power over everything, and His wisdom, and to begin by praising Him and sending peace upon His prophets and the chosen ones among His servants. In this there is a fine instruction, a directive to a beautiful manner, an encouragement to seek blessing and auspiciousness by mentioning these two, and to rely on their status for the acceptance of what is conveyed to the listeners, for their attentiveness to it, and for placing it in their hearts in the position that the listener desires. The scholars, preachers and admonishers have inherited this manner from generation to generation: they praise Allah and send blessings upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before every beneficial lesson, before every exhortation, and at the opening of every sermon. The careful writers followed them, placing it at the beginning of their letters concerning conquests and congratulations, and other events of importance.

His the Exalted's words: ﴿Those whom He has chosen﴾, meaning He selected them for His message, and they are the prophets, peace be upon them. The evidence is His the Exalted's words: ﴿And peace upon the messengers﴾.

﴿Is Allah best?﴾ Abu Hatim permitted "a-Allahu khayr" with two hamzas. Al-Nahhas said: We do not know of anyone who followed him in that, because this lengthening was only introduced to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative, and this is the alif of inquiry. "Khayr" here does not mean "better than you," but is like the saying of the poet [He is Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him]: "Do you satirize him, while you are not his equal? So the worse of you two is a ransom for the better." The meaning is: the one among you two in whom there is evil is a ransom for the one in whom there is good. It cannot mean "min" (than), because if you say, "So-and-so is worse than so-and-so," then each of them has some evil. It was also said: the meaning is, "Is the good in this [i.e., Allah] or in this which you associate with Him in worship?" Sibawayh related: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" while he knows that happiness is more beloved to him. It was also said: it is on its own basis of comparison, and the meaning is: "Is Allah better, or what you associate?" That is, is His reward better, or the punishment of what you associate? It was also said: He said that to them because they believed that there was good in worshipping idols, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed them according to their belief. It was also said: the wording is that of a question, but its meaning is a statement. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read ﴿yushrikun﴾ with a ya' as a statement. The rest read it with a ta' as address, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he recited this verse, would say: "Rather, Allah is better, more enduring, more exalted and more generous."

His the Exalted's words: ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth?﴾ Abu Hatim said: its implied sense is, "Are your gods better, or He who created the heavens and the earth?" and this has already been mentioned. Its meaning is: He had power over their creation. It was also said: the meaning is, "Is the worship of what you worship of your idols better, or the worship of Him who created the heavens and the earth?" This is referred back to what preceded it in meaning, and in it there is a rebuke to them and an alert to the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the helplessness of their gods.

﴿And caused to grow thereby gardens of delightful beauty﴾. The ḥadīqah (garden) is an orchard enclosed by a wall. And al-bahjah is a fine sight. Al-Farra' said: the ḥadīqah is an orchard enclosed by a wall; if there is no wall on it, then it is an orchard but not a ḥadīqah. Qatadah and Ikrimah said: the ḥadā'iq are palm trees, dhāt bahjah; and al-bahjah is adornment and beauty, by which whoever sees it is delighted.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. "Mā" here is for negation. Its meaning is prohibition and prevention from doing this, that is, it was not for humans, nor within their capacity, to cause its trees to grow, since they are incapable of the like of it, for that is bringing a thing from non-existence into existence. I say: this may be used as evidence for forbidding the depiction of anything, whether or not it has a soul, and this is the view of Mujahid. It is reinforced by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: And who is more unjust than one who goes about to create a creation like My creation? Let them create an atom, or let them create a grain, or let them create a barleycorn." Muslim related it in his Sahih from the ḥadīth of Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says," and he mentioned it. So it generally condemns, threatens and denounces everyone who undertakes to depict anything that Allah created and who imitates His creation in what is exclusive to Him, glorified is He, of creating and originating. This is clear. But the majority held that depicting what has no soul is permissible, and so is earning by it. Ibn 'Abbas said to the one who asked to make pictures: "If you must do it, then make the trees and what has no soul." Muslim also related this. The prohibition is more appropriate, and Allah knows best, for the reasons we have mentioned. More detailed explanation of this will come in [Surah] "Saba'," if Allah wills. Then He said, as a rebuke: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, that is, is there a worshipped one besides Allah who helps Him in that?

﴿Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals [to Allah]﴾, equating others with Allah. It was also said: ﴿ya'dilun﴾ means they deviate from the truth and the right path, that is, they disbelieve. It was also said: "ilāh" is in the nominative case governed by "ma'a," its implied sense being: "Ama'a Allahi waylakum ilāh" (Is there a god with Allah, woe to you?). And stopping at "ma'a Allah" is acceptable.

His the Exalted's words: ﴿Or who made the earth a stable place﴾, that is, a fixed resting place.

﴿And made within it rivers﴾, that is, in its midst, like His saying: "And We caused to gush forth rivers within them."

﴿And placed within it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains that are stable, holding it and preventing it from moving.

﴿And placed between the two seas a barrier﴾, a prevention from His power, so that the salt water does not mix with the fresh. Ibn 'Abbas said: an authority from His power, so that neither this changes that nor that changes this. And al-ḥajz means prevention.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, that is, once it is established that none besides Him has power over this, then why do they worship what neither harms nor benefits?

﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾, meaning, as if they ignore Allah, so they do not know what is due to Him of oneness.

**Third chapter of the commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran), on surah 27, verses 62–64:**

There are three issues in this.

**The first issue** concerns His words: ﴿Who answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "He is the one in dire need who is overwhelmed." Al-Suddi said: "The one who has no power and no strength." Dhu al-Nun said: "He is the one who has cut off his attachments to anything other than Allah." Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Uthman al-Naysaburi said: "He is the destitute." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: "He is the one who, when he raises his hands to Allah in supplication, has no means of nearness through any act of obedience that he has sent ahead." A man came to Malik ibn Dinar and said: "I ask you by Allah to pray for me, for I am in distress." He said: "Then ask Him, for He answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him."

The poet said:

"I call upon Allah while the matter is tight upon me,
and it does not cease that it is relieved.
How many a brother whose faces were closed to him
found an exit when he called upon Allah."

**The second issue:** In the Musnad of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Abu Bakra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning the supplication of the one in distress: "O Allah, Your mercy I hope for, so do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye, and set right for me all my affairs. There is no god but You."

**The third issue:** Allah, exalted is He, guaranteed the answering of the one in distress when he calls upon Him, and He informed of this concerning Himself. The reason for this is that the need for Him that arises through seeking refuge comes from sincerity and from the heart being severed from all else. Sincerity has a station and a weight with Him, glorified is He, whether it comes from a believer or a disbeliever, an obedient person or a wicked one, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice in it, there comes upon it a violent wind, and the waves come to them from everywhere, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You save us from this, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ And His words: ﴿But when He saves them to the land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ So He answered them at the time of their distress and the occurrence of their sincerity, although He knew that they would return to their polytheism and their disbelief. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion.﴾ Thus He answers the one in distress because of the place of his distress and his sincerity.

There is a hadith: "Three supplications are answered, there is no doubt about them: the supplication of the one who has been wronged, the supplication of the traveler, and the supplication of a parent against his child." This was mentioned by the author of al-Shihab, and it is a sound hadith. In Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said to Mu'adh when he sent him to the land of Yemen: "Beware of the supplication of the one who has been wronged, for there is no barrier between it and Allah."
