I say: For this reason, Allah knows best, some of the later exegetes said: The closer view is that this beast is a speaking human being who debates the people of innovation and disbelief and argues with them so that they are silenced, so that whoever perishes perishes by clear evidence, and whoever lives lives by clear evidence. Our shaykh, the Imam Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Umar al-Qurtubi, said in his book al-Mufhim: The reason this speaker held the view that it is closer is His saying, the Exalted: "it will speak to them." On this view, there is no extraordinary sign specific to this beast, and it would not be among the ten signs mentioned in the hadith, because the existence of debaters and those who argue against the people of innovation is common, so there is no sign specific to it, and it should not be mentioned with the ten. Its unique existence is also lifted when the word is fulfilled. Moreover, it involves a departure from naming this virtuous, learned debater, whom the people of the earth should call a human, a scholar, or an imam, by the name of a beast. This is a departure from the custom of eloquent speakers and from the honouring of scholars, and it is not the practice of sensible people. So the better view is what the people of tafsir have said, and Allah knows best the realities of matters.

I say: The difficulty concerning this beast has been removed by what we have mentioned from the hadith of Hudhayfah, so let it be relied upon. It has been disputed from which place it will emerge. Abdullah ibn Umar said: It will emerge from Mount Safa in Makkah, splitting open, and it will come out of it. Abdullah ibn Amr said something similar and said: "If I wished to place my foot upon the place of its emergence, I would do so." It was also reported in a report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The earth will split open for the beast, while Isa, peace be upon him, is circling the House, and with him are the Muslims from the direction of al-Masa'. It will emerge from al-Safa and will mark between the eyes of the believer, 'this is a believer,' with a mark like a shining star, and will mark between the eyes of the disbeliever with a black spot, 'this is a disbeliever.'" It is also mentioned in the report that it has fur and feathers, as al-Mahdawi mentioned.

From Ibn Abbas: it will emerge from a mountain pass, its head touching the clouds while its feet are still in the earth, not yet emerged. It will come out with the staff of Musa and the ring of Sulayman, peace be upon them both.

From Hudhayfah: it will emerge three times: one emergence in some of the deserts, then it will remain hidden; and an emergence in the towns, where the rulers will fight one another until much blood is shed; and an emergence from the greatest, most honoured, noblest and most excellent of the mosques. Al-Zamakhshari said: it will emerge from between the Corner, opposite the house of Banu Makhzum, on the right of one leaving the mosque. Some people will flee, and some will stand watching.

It was reported from Qatadah that it will emerge in Tihamah. It was also reported that it will emerge from the mosque of Kufah, from the place where the oven of Nuh, peace be upon him, boiled over. It was also said: from the land of al-Ta'if. Abu Qabil said: Abdullah ibn Amr struck the land of al-Ta'if with his foot and said: "From here the beast will emerge which speaks to the people." It was also said: from some valleys of Tihamah, said by Ibn Abbas. It was said: from a rock in the valley of Ajyad, said by Abdullah ibn Amr. It was said: from the Sea of Sodom (Sadum), said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. Al-Mawardi mentioned these last three sayings in his book.

Al-Baghawi Abu al-Qasim Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz mentioned: Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated to us, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq al-Raqqashi al-Aghar (about whom Yahya ibn Ma'in was asked, and he said: "trustworthy"), from Atiyyah al-Awfi, from Ibn Umar, who said: "The beast will emerge from a crack in the Ka'bah, running like a horse for three days, and a third of it will not emerge."

I say: These are the sayings of the Companions and the Successor regarding the emergence of the beast and its description. They refute the view of those exegetes who said that the beast is merely a speaking human being who debates the people of innovation and disbelief. Abu Umamah narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The beast will emerge and mark people on their noses." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

"تُكَلِّمُهُمْ" with a ḍammah

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 27, verses 82–86 (part 2 of 2):

The reading of the common readers (qira'ah, recitation) is *tukallimuhum* (تُكَلِّمُهُمْ) with a *tā'* and a doubled *lām* that is karsa, from *al-kalam* (speech). Evidence for it is the reading of Ubayy, "tunabbi'uhum" (تُنَبِّئُهُمْ). Al-Suddi said: "It speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions other than the religion of Islam." It was also said: "It speaks to them with what distresses them." It was also said: "It speaks to them in an eloquent tongue, saying in a voice that is heard by those near and far: *'Inna al-nasa kanu bi-ayatina la yuqinun'* (that people did not have certainty in Our signs)," meaning in My coming out, because its coming out is one of the signs. And it says: "Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers."

Abu Zur'ah, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read *takulimuhum* (تَكْلِمُهُمْ) with a fatha on the *tā'*, from *al-kalm*, which is the wound. Ikrimah said: that is, it brands them. Abu al-Jawza' said: I asked Ibn Abbas about this verse, "*tukallimuhum*" or "*takulimuhum*"? He said: "By Allah, it is both: it speaks to the believer, and it wounds the disbeliever and the wicked," that is, it wounds him. Abu Hatim said: "*tukallimuhum*" is like saying "*tujarrihuhum*" (it wounds them); he holds that it is an intensive form of "*takulimuhum*."

*Anna al-nasa kanu bi-ayatina la yuqinun* (أَنَّ النَّاسَ كانُوا بِآياتِنا لَا يُوقِنُونَ): The Kufans, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yahya read *anna* (أَنَّ) with a fatha. The people of the two Holy Cities, the people of Syria and the people of Basra read *inna* (إِنَّ) with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: regarding the fatha-form there are two opinions, and likewise the kasra-form. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is *bi-anna* (بِأَنَّ), and Ibn Mas'ud also read *bi-anna*. Abu Ubaydah said: its position is in the accusative by the verb falling upon it, meaning: it informs them that the people [...]. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' read *inna al-nas* (إِنَّ النَّاسَ) with a kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf). Al-Akhfash said: it has the meaning of "you say, *inna al-nas*," meaning the disbelievers. "*Bi-ayatina la yuqinun*" means: with the Qur'an and with Muhammad (ﷺ), and that is when Allah will not accept faith from a disbeliever, and only believers and disbelievers remain in Allah's knowledge before its coming out. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the Day when We shall gather from every nation a troop﴾: that is, a group and a company.

(*Min man yukadhdhibu bi-ayatina*, "of those who deny Our signs"): meaning with the Qur'an and with Our clear indications that point to the truth.

(*Fahum yuza'un*, "then they will be driven"): that is, they will be pushed and driven to the place of reckoning. Al-Shammakh said:

"How many a host of a massive army have we driven back,
and how many a chief, vigorous and sharp, have we bestowed."

Qatadah said: "*yuza'un*" means that their first is held back until their last joins them.

(*Hatta idha ja'u qala*, "until, when they come, He will say"): that is, Allah says: (*Akadhdhabtum bi-ayati*, "Did you deny My signs") which I sent down upon My messengers, and the signs which I established as proof of My oneness?

(*Wa lam tuhituu biha 'ilman*, "while you did not encompass them in knowledge"): that is, you did not know their falsehood so that you would turn away from them; rather, you denied them in ignorance, without seeking evidence.

(*Amma dha kuntum ta'maluna*, "or what were you doing?"): this is rebuke and reproach. That is: what were you doing when you did not investigate them and did not reflect on what is in them?

(*Wa waqa'a al-qawlu 'alayhim bima zalamu*, "and the word will fall upon them because of what they wronged"): that is, the punishment becomes due upon them because of their wrongdoing, that is, their polytheism.

(*Fahum la yantiqun*, "so they will not speak"): that is, they have no excuse and no proof. It was said: their mouths will be sealed so they do not speak. This is what most of the exegetes said.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not see that We made the night for them to rest therein﴾: that is, that they may settle and sleep.

(*Wa al-nahara mubsiran*, "and the day as something to see by"): that is, it is seen by, for the pursuit of provision.

(*Inna fi dhalika la-ayatin li-qawmin yu'minun*, "Surely in that are signs for a people who believe"): in Allah. He mentioned the proof of His divinity and His power, meaning: have they not known the completeness of Our power so that they would believe?

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 87–90 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾. That is, "Remember the Day when the Trumpet is blown," or "Remind them of the Day when the Trumpet is blown." The view of al-Farra' (the grammarian) is that the meaning is "That is the Day when the Trumpet is blown," and he permitted an ellipsis (hadhf) here. The sound position regarding the Trumpet (al-Sur) is that it is a horn of light into which Israfil (the angel Israfil) blows. Mujahid said: "It is like the shape of a horn (al-buq)." It was also said: "It is al-buq in the dialect of the people of Yemen." Its explanation and what the scholars have said about it has already passed in "al-An'am" (see vol. 7, p. 20 of the first or second edition).

﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾. Abu Hurayra said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had finished creating the heavens, He created the Trumpet and gave it to Israfil. He places it at his mouth, fixing his gaze on the Throne, waiting for when he will be commanded to blow." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said: "A horn, by Allah, a great one. By the One who sent me with the truth, the circumference of its opening is as wide as the heavens and the earth. He will blow into it three blasts. The first blast is the blast of terror (faza'), the second is the blast of swooning (sa'q), and the third is the blast of resurrection and standing before the Lord of the worlds." And he mentioned the hadith. It was related by Ali ibn Ma'bad, al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi and others, and Ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it. I have mentioned it in my book "al-Tadhkira," and we discussed it there. The correct view regarding the blowing into the Trumpet is that there are two blasts, not three. The blast of terror refers back to the blast of swooning, because the two matters have no duration of their own; that is, they become terrified with a terror by which they die. Or it refers to the blast of resurrection. This is the choice of al-Qushayri and others, for he said in his commentary on this verse: "The intended one is the second blast, meaning they will be brought to life terrified, saying: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ and they will witness matters that overwhelm and frighten them. This blowing is like the sound of a horn, so that the creation gathers in the land of recompense." This was said by Qatadah. Al-Mawardi said: "﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ is the Day of Rising from the graves." He said: Regarding this terror there are two views. One: it is haste and responsiveness to the call, from the expression "fazi'tu ilayka fi kadha" (I hastened to you concerning such-and-such) when one quickly answers your call for help. The second view: the terror here is the familiar terror of fear and grief, because they are driven out of their graves and fear. This is more fitting of the two views. I say: The established Sunnah from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr indicates that there are two blasts, not three. Muslim recorded them, and we have mentioned them in "al-Tadhkira." This is the correct view, if Allah wills, that there are two blasts. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills﴾. He made an exception here just as He made an exception in the blast of terror, which indicates that they are one (blast). Ibn al-Mubarak related from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts there are forty years. With the first, Allah causes every living thing to die, and with the second, Allah brings every dead thing to life."

If it is said: Allah's saying: ﴿On the Day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, until He said: ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ (79:6–13), outwardly indicates that there are three. It is said in reply: This is not so. The "shout" (zajra) here means the second blast, by which people come out of their graves. Thus said Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata', Ibn Zayd and others. Mujahid said: "They are two cries. The first causes everything to die by Allah's permission, and the second causes everything to live by Allah's permission." Ata' said: "al-Raajifa" is the Judgment (al-Qiyama), and "al-Radifa" is the Resurrection (al-Ba'th). Ibn Zayd said: "al-Raajifa" is death, and "al-Radifa" is the Hour (al-Sa'a). And Allah knows best.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾. Then the scholars differed about who this exception is. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra, they are the martyrs with their Lord, who are provided for, since terror only reaches the living. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that they are the martyrs wearing swords around the Throne. Al-Qushayri said: The prophets are included among them, because they have martyrdom along with prophethood. It was also said: they are the angels. Al-Hasan said: He excepted groups of angels who die between the two blasts. Muqatil said: He means Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and the Angel of Death. It was also said: they are the dark-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). And it was said: they are the believers, because Allah the Exalted said after this: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from terror on that Day﴾ (27:89). Some of our scholars said: The correct view is that no sound report has come concerning specifying them, and all (possibilities) are open. I say: The hadith of Abu Hurayra escaped his notice, and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it, so let one rely upon it, for it is explicit in specifying them, while the others are ijtihad (personal reasoning). And Allah knows best. Other views have been stated apart from this, which will come in "al-Zumar" (see vol. 15, p. 277 onward).

His saying ﴿So whoever is in the heavens … will be terrified﴾: "fazi'a" is a past tense verb, while "yunfakhu" is a present/future verb. So it is asked: how is a past verb conjoined to a future one? Al-Farra' claimed that this is understood according to the meaning, because the meaning is: "When the Trumpet is blown, they will be terrified." The phrase ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾ is in the accusative as an exception.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾. Abu Amr, Asim, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Ibn Amir and Ibn Kathir read "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) with the present-future form, treating it as a verb in the future. Al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza, and Hafs from Asim read "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) with the past tense, restricted to the past verb. Ibn Mas'ud also read it thus. And from Qatadah: "wa-kullun ataahu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ دَاخِرِينَ). Al-Nahhas said: In my book on the readings from Abu Ishaq, whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) makes it singular according to the wording of "kull," and whoever reads "ātūhu" (أَتُوهُ) makes it plural according to its meaning. This view is a gross error, because if he says "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) it is not singular but plural. If it were singular, he would say "ataahu" (أَتَاهُ). But whoever says "ataw-hu" (أَتَوْهُ) has made the verb plural according to meaning, and he brought it in the past tense because he referred it back to "fazaʿ" (terror). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ) has also taken it according to meaning and said "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) because it is a separate clause from the first. Ibn Nasr said: What is reported from Abu Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on him, is what he did not say. The actual text of Abu Ishaq is: "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin," and it is read "ātūhu." Whoever makes it singular does so according to the wording of "kull," and whoever makes it plural does so according to its meaning. He means that whatever comes in the Qur'an or elsewhere of the predicate of "kull" being singular is according to the wording, or plural is according to the meaning. Abu Ja'far did not take this meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is a verb from "ityan" (coming), and it is taken according to the meaning of "kull" not its wording. Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is the active participle from "atā." What indicates this is Allah's saying: ﴿And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾ (19:95). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataahu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ) takes it according to the wording of "kull" and not its meaning, and takes "dakhirin" according to the meaning. Its meaning is "humbled" (saghirin), according to Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. It has already passed in "al-Nahl" (see vol. 10, p. 111, first or second edition).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾. Ibn Abbas said: That is, standing, while they are moving at a rapid pace. Al-Qutaybi said: That is because the mountains are gathered and set in motion, so in the sight of the eye they appear as standing while they move. Likewise, every great thing and vast multitude whose extent the eye falls short of, due to its vastness and the distance between its extremities, appears to the observer as standing while it moves. Al-Nabigha said describing an army:

*With a host like a mountain, you think them*
*Standing still for a pilgrimage, while the mounts are pacing.*

Al-Qushayri said: This is the Day of Resurrection, meaning they, because of their great number, appear as if solid, that is, standing in the sight of the eye, though in themselves they move like the clouds. Piled-up clouds are thought to be standing while they move. "They pass as the clouds pass" until nothing of them remains. Then Allah says: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ (78:20). It is said that Allah the Exalted described the mountains with various attributes, all of which return to emptying the earth of them and revealing what they had concealed. The first attribute is crumbling (indikak), which happens before the quaking. Then they become like carded wool (al-'ihn al-manfush). This happens when the sky becomes like molten brass (al-muhl). Allah joined the two when He said: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ (70:8–9). The third state is that they become like scattered dust (al-habaʾ), because they are cut off after having been like carded wool. The fourth state is that they are blown away (nasf), because with the previous states they are still fixed in their places while the earth beneath them is not exposed, so they are blown away from it to be exposed. When they are blown away, it is by sending winds upon them. The fifth state is that the winds lift them above the surface of the earth, making them appear as rays in the air like dust, so that whoever looks at them from afar thinks them solid bodies because of their density, while in reality they are passing, except that their passing is from behind the winds, as though they are crumbled and scattered. The sixth state is that they become a mirage, so whoever looks at their places finds nothing of them, like a mirage. Muqatil said: They fall upon the earth and are levelled with it. Then it is said: this is an illustration (mathal). Al-Mawardi said: Regarding what it illustrates there are three views. One: it is a parable Allah struck for this world, in which the observer thinks it is standing like the mountains, while it is in fact taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn Abd Allah. The second: it is a parable Allah struck for faith, which you think is firmly established in the heart, while its deeds rise to heaven. The third: it is a parable Allah struck for the soul at the moment of its departure, when the spirit moves toward the Throne.

﴿The handiwork of Allah, who has perfected everything﴾. That is, this is from the act of Allah, and whatever is an act from Him is perfected. "Tara" (تَرَى) is from sight with the eye; if it were from sight with the heart, it would take two objects. The original form is "turʾā" (تُرْأَى), so the vowel of the hamza was moved onto the rāʾ, the rāʾ became vowelled and the hamza was dropped. This is the way of easing the hamza when a consonant precedes it, except that the easing is obligatory in "tara." The people of Kufa read "taḥsabuhā" (تَحْسَبُها) with a fatha on the sīn, which is the analogical form, since it comes from "ḥasiba yaḥsibu." However, it has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) a contrary reading, that he recited with a kasra in the imperfect, so it is of the pattern "fa'ila yaf'alu," like "ni'ima yan'amu" and "bi's yab'asu," and it is reported "yi'isa yay'isu" from the sound verbs. Nothing is known in the speech of the Arabs other than these letters. "Wa-hiya tamurru marra al-saḥāb" (وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحابِ): its implied meaning is "a passing like the passing of the clouds." So the attribute has been put in the place of the thing described, and the annexed noun in place of the noun it is annexed to. The mountains are removed from their places on the surface of the earth, gathered and set in motion as clouds are set in motion, then they are broken into pieces and return to the earth, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crushed to powder﴾ (56:5).

(The sawing of God's handiwork) — according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, (صُنْعَ اللَّهِ) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), since when He said, "and it passes as the clouds pass" (27:88), this indicates that He made that happen as a making (ṣun'an). The accusative is also permissible as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: "Look at God's handiwork." On this reading one stops at "the clouds" (al-sahab), but one does not stop there on the first interpretation. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: "That is God's handiwork." "Who perfected everything" (alladhi atqana kulla shay'): that is, He made it firm (ahkamahu). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "May God have mercy on the one who does a deed and perfects it." Qatadah said: its meaning is "He made everything good." Al-itqan is al-ihkam (firmness). It is said: "rajul tiqn," meaning a man who is skilled in things. Al-Zuhri said: its origin is from Ibn Tiqn, who was a man from 'Ad, for whom no arrow would miss its target, so he became a proverb. It is said: "More accurate in shooting than Ibn Tiqn," and then every person skilled in things is called tiqn.

(Indeed, He is Aware of what you do) — reading with the "ta'" (second person address) is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read it with the "ya'" (third person).

The words of the Exalted: (Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it) — Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: the good deed is "There is no god but God." Abu Ma'shar said: Ibrahim used to swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, without making an exception, that the good deed is "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them, said: a man went out to fight, and whenever he was alone in a place he would say, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." Then, while he was in the land of the Romans, in the land of Julfa and Baradi, he raised his voice and said, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." A man came out to him on a horse, wearing white clothes, and said to him: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is the word of which God the Exalted said, 'Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it.'" Abu Dharr narrated: I said, "O Messenger of God, advise me." He said: "Fear God, and when you do an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out." I said: "O Messenger of God, is 'There is no god but God' among the good deeds?" He said: "It is among the best of good deeds." In another narration he said: "Yes, it is the best of good deeds." Related by al-Bayhaqi. Qatadah said: "Whoever comes with a good deed" means with sincerity and monotheism. It was also said: it means performing all the obligatory duties.

I say: when one comes with "There is no god but God" in its true reality and what is required by it, as explained earlier in Surah Ibrahim, then he has come with monotheism, sincerity and the obligations.

"Then he will have better than it": Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, the good reached him from it. Mujahid also said this. It was said: then for him is a beautiful reward, which is Paradise. And "khayr" here is not comparative. 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jurayj said: as for it being that he has better than it, meaning better than faith, that is not so, for nothing is better than one who says "There is no god but God"; rather, he has good from it. It was also said: "Then he will have better than it" is comparative, meaning God's reward is better than the servant's deed, his saying and his remembrance of Him; likewise God's good pleasure is better for the servant than the servant's action. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: this returns to multiplication, for God gives ten for one, and for faith in a brief period the eternal reward; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

(And they will be secure from the terror of that Day) — 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "faza'i yawma'idhin" with the genitive construction (idafah). Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations: that the security is from all the terror of that Day. When He says "min fazi'in yawma'idhin," it becomes as if it were a terror rather than the terror. Al-Qushayri said: it is also read "min fazi'in" with tanwin; then it is said that it means one single terror, as He said: "The Greatest Terror will not grieve them." It was also said: it means plurality, since it is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun is suitable for plurality. I say: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "min fazi'in yawma'idhin" with tanwin, "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative by the verbal noun "fazi'" itself; it may also be an attribute of "fazi'," and it would be connected to an elided element, since verbal nouns may be described by time-nouns and described by them; it may also be connected to the active participle "amanun." The idafah is by way of broadening in time-adverbs. Whoever omits the tanwin and makes the mim fathah builds it, because it is a time-adverb, and the case-ending in a time-adverb is not fully inflected; when it was attached to something that is neither fully inflected nor case-marked, it was built. Sibawayh recited:

"At a time when most of their concerns distracted the people, / Zurayq, seize the wealth, seizing as foxes seize."

[[Zurayq: the name of a tribe, and it is a vocative. "Nadal" here means taking with both hands; "nadal" also means swiftness in movement. "Nadal al-tha'alib" (the foxes' seizing): it is said in a proverb, "He is more gainful than a fox," because it stores for itself and attacks whatever animal it can reach. The verse describes merchants, and it is also said it describes thieves; before it is:
"They pass by al-Dahna lightly burdened in their saddlebags, / and return from Darin with heavy bags."]]

The words of the Exalted: (And whoever comes with an evil deed) — that is, with polytheism. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Abu Hurayrah, Mujahid, Qays ibn Sa'd and al-Hasan, and it is a consensus among the people of interpretation that the good deed is "There is no god but God," and that the evil deed in this verse is polytheism.

(Their faces will be thrown into the Fire) — Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be cast down. Al-Dahhak said: they will be thrown. It is said "kababtu al-inā'" meaning I turned the vessel over onto its face; the intransitive form is "akabba," and this rarely occurs in Arabic speech.

(Are you being recompensed) — that is, it will be said to them: "Are you being recompensed?" Then it may be from the speech of God, and it may be from the speech of the angels.

(Except for what you used to do) — that is, nothing but the recompense of your deeds.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 87–90 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾. That is, "Remember the Day when the Trumpet is blown," or "Remind them of the Day when the Trumpet is blown." The view of al-Farra' (the grammarian) is that the meaning is "That is the Day when the Trumpet is blown," and he permitted an ellipsis (hadhf) here. The sound position regarding the Trumpet (al-Sur) is that it is a horn of light into which Israfil (the angel Israfil) blows. Mujahid said: "It is like the shape of a horn (al-buq)." It was also said: "It is al-buq in the dialect of the people of Yemen." Its explanation and what the scholars have said about it has already passed in "al-An'am" (see vol. 7, p. 20 of the first or second edition).

﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾. Abu Hurayra said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had finished creating the heavens, He created the Trumpet and gave it to Israfil. He places it at his mouth, fixing his gaze on the Throne, waiting for when he will be commanded to blow." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said: "A horn, by Allah, a great one. By the One who sent me with the truth, the circumference of its opening is as wide as the heavens and the earth. He will blow into it three blasts. The first blast is the blast of terror (faza'), the second is the blast of swooning (sa'q), and the third is the blast of resurrection and standing before the Lord of the worlds." And he mentioned the hadith. It was related by Ali ibn Ma'bad, al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi and others, and Ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it. I have mentioned it in my book "al-Tadhkira," and we discussed it there. The correct view regarding the blowing into the Trumpet is that there are two blasts, not three. The blast of terror refers back to the blast of swooning, because the two matters have no duration of their own; that is, they become terrified with a terror by which they die. Or it refers to the blast of resurrection. This is the choice of al-Qushayri and others, for he said in his commentary on this verse: "The intended one is the second blast, meaning they will be brought to life terrified, saying: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ and they will witness matters that overwhelm and frighten them. This blowing is like the sound of a horn, so that the creation gathers in the land of recompense." This was said by Qatadah. Al-Mawardi said: "﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ is the Day of Rising from the graves." He said: Regarding this terror there are two views. One: it is haste and responsiveness to the call, from the expression "fazi'tu ilayka fi kadha" (I hastened to you concerning such-and-such) when one quickly answers your call for help. The second view: the terror here is the familiar terror of fear and grief, because they are driven out of their graves and fear. This is more fitting of the two views. I say: The established Sunnah from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr indicates that there are two blasts, not three. Muslim recorded them, and we have mentioned them in "al-Tadhkira." This is the correct view, if Allah wills, that there are two blasts. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills﴾. He made an exception here just as He made an exception in the blast of terror, which indicates that they are one (blast). Ibn al-Mubarak related from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts there are forty years. With the first, Allah causes every living thing to die, and with the second, Allah brings every dead thing to life."

If it is said: Allah's saying: ﴿On the Day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, until He said: ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ (79:6–13), outwardly indicates that there are three. It is said in reply: This is not so. The "shout" (zajra) here means the second blast, by which people come out of their graves. Thus said Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata', Ibn Zayd and others. Mujahid said: "They are two cries. The first causes everything to die by Allah's permission, and the second causes everything to live by Allah's permission." Ata' said: "al-Raajifa" is the Judgment (al-Qiyama), and "al-Radifa" is the Resurrection (al-Ba'th). Ibn Zayd said: "al-Raajifa" is death, and "al-Radifa" is the Hour (al-Sa'a). And Allah knows best.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾. Then the scholars differed about who this exception is. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra, they are the martyrs with their Lord, who are provided for, since terror only reaches the living. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that they are the martyrs wearing swords around the Throne. Al-Qushayri said: The prophets are included among them, because they have martyrdom along with prophethood. It was also said: they are the angels. Al-Hasan said: He excepted groups of angels who die between the two blasts. Muqatil said: He means Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and the Angel of Death. It was also said: they are the dark-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). And it was said: they are the believers, because Allah the Exalted said after this: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from terror on that Day﴾ (27:89). Some of our scholars said: The correct view is that no sound report has come concerning specifying them, and all (possibilities) are open. I say: The hadith of Abu Hurayra escaped his notice, and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it, so let one rely upon it, for it is explicit in specifying them, while the others are ijtihad (personal reasoning). And Allah knows best. Other views have been stated apart from this, which will come in "al-Zumar" (see vol. 15, p. 277 onward).

His saying ﴿So whoever is in the heavens … will be terrified﴾: "fazi'a" is a past tense verb, while "yunfakhu" is a present/future verb. So it is asked: how is a past verb conjoined to a future one? Al-Farra' claimed that this is understood according to the meaning, because the meaning is: "When the Trumpet is blown, they will be terrified." The phrase ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾ is in the accusative as an exception.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾. Abu Amr, Asim, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Ibn Amir and Ibn Kathir read "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) with the present-future form, treating it as a verb in the future. Al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza, and Hafs from Asim read "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) with the past tense, restricted to the past verb. Ibn Mas'ud also read it thus. And from Qatadah: "wa-kullun ataahu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ دَاخِرِينَ). Al-Nahhas said: In my book on the readings from Abu Ishaq, whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) makes it singular according to the wording of "kull," and whoever reads "ātūhu" (أَتُوهُ) makes it plural according to its meaning. This view is a gross error, because if he says "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) it is not singular but plural. If it were singular, he would say "ataahu" (أَتَاهُ). But whoever says "ataw-hu" (أَتَوْهُ) has made the verb plural according to meaning, and he brought it in the past tense because he referred it back to "fazaʿ" (terror). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ) has also taken it according to meaning and said "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) because it is a separate clause from the first. Ibn Nasr said: What is reported from Abu Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on him, is what he did not say. The actual text of Abu Ishaq is: "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin," and it is read "ātūhu." Whoever makes it singular does so according to the wording of "kull," and whoever makes it plural does so according to its meaning. He means that whatever comes in the Qur'an or elsewhere of the predicate of "kull" being singular is according to the wording, or plural is according to the meaning. Abu Ja'far did not take this meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is a verb from "ityan" (coming), and it is taken according to the meaning of "kull" not its wording. Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is the active participle from "atā." What indicates this is Allah's saying: ﴿And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾ (19:95). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataahu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ) takes it according to the wording of "kull" and not its meaning, and takes "dakhirin" according to the meaning. Its meaning is "humbled" (saghirin), according to Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. It has already passed in "al-Nahl" (see vol. 10, p. 111, first or second edition).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾. Ibn Abbas said: That is, standing, while they are moving at a rapid pace. Al-Qutaybi said: That is because the mountains are gathered and set in motion, so in the sight of the eye they appear as standing while they move. Likewise, every great thing and vast multitude whose extent the eye falls short of, due to its vastness and the distance between its extremities, appears to the observer as standing while it moves. Al-Nabigha said describing an army:

*With a host like a mountain, you think them*
*Standing still for a pilgrimage, while the mounts are pacing.*

Al-Qushayri said: This is the Day of Resurrection, meaning they, because of their great number, appear as if solid, that is, standing in the sight of the eye, though in themselves they move like the clouds. Piled-up clouds are thought to be standing while they move. "They pass as the clouds pass" until nothing of them remains. Then Allah says: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ (78:20). It is said that Allah the Exalted described the mountains with various attributes, all of which return to emptying the earth of them and revealing what they had concealed. The first attribute is crumbling (indikak), which happens before the quaking. Then they become like carded wool (al-'ihn al-manfush). This happens when the sky becomes like molten brass (al-muhl). Allah joined the two when He said: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ (70:8–9). The third state is that they become like scattered dust (al-habaʾ), because they are cut off after having been like carded wool. The fourth state is that they are blown away (nasf), because with the previous states they are still fixed in their places while the earth beneath them is not exposed, so they are blown away from it to be exposed. When they are blown away, it is by sending winds upon them. The fifth state is that the winds lift them above the surface of the earth, making them appear as rays in the air like dust, so that whoever looks at them from afar thinks them solid bodies because of their density, while in reality they are passing, except that their passing is from behind the winds, as though they are crumbled and scattered. The sixth state is that they become a mirage, so whoever looks at their places finds nothing of them, like a mirage. Muqatil said: They fall upon the earth and are levelled with it. Then it is said: this is an illustration (mathal). Al-Mawardi said: Regarding what it illustrates there are three views. One: it is a parable Allah struck for this world, in which the observer thinks it is standing like the mountains, while it is in fact taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn Abd Allah. The second: it is a parable Allah struck for faith, which you think is firmly established in the heart, while its deeds rise to heaven. The third: it is a parable Allah struck for the soul at the moment of its departure, when the spirit moves toward the Throne.

﴿The handiwork of Allah, who has perfected everything﴾. That is, this is from the act of Allah, and whatever is an act from Him is perfected. "Tara" (تَرَى) is from sight with the eye; if it were from sight with the heart, it would take two objects. The original form is "turʾā" (تُرْأَى), so the vowel of the hamza was moved onto the rāʾ, the rāʾ became vowelled and the hamza was dropped. This is the way of easing the hamza when a consonant precedes it, except that the easing is obligatory in "tara." The people of Kufa read "taḥsabuhā" (تَحْسَبُها) with a fatha on the sīn, which is the analogical form, since it comes from "ḥasiba yaḥsibu." However, it has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) a contrary reading, that he recited with a kasra in the imperfect, so it is of the pattern "fa'ila yaf'alu," like "ni'ima yan'amu" and "bi's yab'asu," and it is reported "yi'isa yay'isu" from the sound verbs. Nothing is known in the speech of the Arabs other than these letters. "Wa-hiya tamurru marra al-saḥāb" (وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحابِ): its implied meaning is "a passing like the passing of the clouds." So the attribute has been put in the place of the thing described, and the annexed noun in place of the noun it is annexed to. The mountains are removed from their places on the surface of the earth, gathered and set in motion as clouds are set in motion, then they are broken into pieces and return to the earth, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crushed to powder﴾ (56:5).

(The sawing of God's handiwork) — according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, (صُنْعَ اللَّهِ) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), since when He said, "and it passes as the clouds pass" (27:88), this indicates that He made that happen as a making (ṣun'an). The accusative is also permissible as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: "Look at God's handiwork." On this reading one stops at "the clouds" (al-sahab), but one does not stop there on the first interpretation. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: "That is God's handiwork." "Who perfected everything" (alladhi atqana kulla shay'): that is, He made it firm (ahkamahu). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "May God have mercy on the one who does a deed and perfects it." Qatadah said: its meaning is "He made everything good." Al-itqan is al-ihkam (firmness). It is said: "rajul tiqn," meaning a man who is skilled in things. Al-Zuhri said: its origin is from Ibn Tiqn, who was a man from 'Ad, for whom no arrow would miss its target, so he became a proverb. It is said: "More accurate in shooting than Ibn Tiqn," and then every person skilled in things is called tiqn.

(Indeed, He is Aware of what you do) — reading with the "ta'" (second person address) is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read it with the "ya'" (third person).

The words of the Exalted: (Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it) — Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: the good deed is "There is no god but God." Abu Ma'shar said: Ibrahim used to swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, without making an exception, that the good deed is "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them, said: a man went out to fight, and whenever he was alone in a place he would say, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." Then, while he was in the land of the Romans, in the land of Julfa and Baradi, he raised his voice and said, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." A man came out to him on a horse, wearing white clothes, and said to him: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is the word of which God the Exalted said, 'Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it.'" Abu Dharr narrated: I said, "O Messenger of God, advise me." He said: "Fear God, and when you do an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out." I said: "O Messenger of God, is 'There is no god but God' among the good deeds?" He said: "It is among the best of good deeds." In another narration he said: "Yes, it is the best of good deeds." Related by al-Bayhaqi. Qatadah said: "Whoever comes with a good deed" means with sincerity and monotheism. It was also said: it means performing all the obligatory duties.

I say: when one comes with "There is no god but God" in its true reality and what is required by it, as explained earlier in Surah Ibrahim, then he has come with monotheism, sincerity and the obligations.

"Then he will have better than it": Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, the good reached him from it. Mujahid also said this. It was said: then for him is a beautiful reward, which is Paradise. And "khayr" here is not comparative. 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jurayj said: as for it being that he has better than it, meaning better than faith, that is not so, for nothing is better than one who says "There is no god but God"; rather, he has good from it. It was also said: "Then he will have better than it" is comparative, meaning God's reward is better than the servant's deed, his saying and his remembrance of Him; likewise God's good pleasure is better for the servant than the servant's action. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: this returns to multiplication, for God gives ten for one, and for faith in a brief period the eternal reward; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

(And they will be secure from the terror of that Day) — 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "faza'i yawma'idhin" with the genitive construction (idafah). Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations: that the security is from all the terror of that Day. When He says "min fazi'in yawma'idhin," it becomes as if it were a terror rather than the terror. Al-Qushayri said: it is also read "min fazi'in" with tanwin; then it is said that it means one single terror, as He said: "The Greatest Terror will not grieve them." It was also said: it means plurality, since it is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun is suitable for plurality. I say: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "min fazi'in yawma'idhin" with tanwin, "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative by the verbal noun "fazi'" itself; it may also be an attribute of "fazi'," and it would be connected to an elided element, since verbal nouns may be described by time-nouns and described by them; it may also be connected to the active participle "amanun." The idafah is by way of broadening in time-adverbs. Whoever omits the tanwin and makes the mim fathah builds it, because it is a time-adverb, and the case-ending in a time-adverb is not fully inflected; when it was attached to something that is neither fully inflected nor case-marked, it was built. Sibawayh recited:

"At a time when most of their concerns distracted the people, / Zurayq, seize the wealth, seizing as foxes seize."

[[Zurayq: the name of a tribe, and it is a vocative. "Nadal" here means taking with both hands; "nadal" also means swiftness in movement. "Nadal al-tha'alib" (the foxes' seizing): it is said in a proverb, "He is more gainful than a fox," because it stores for itself and attacks whatever animal it can reach. The verse describes merchants, and it is also said it describes thieves; before it is:
"They pass by al-Dahna lightly burdened in their saddlebags, / and return from Darin with heavy bags."]]

The words of the Exalted: (And whoever comes with an evil deed) — that is, with polytheism. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Abu Hurayrah, Mujahid, Qays ibn Sa'd and al-Hasan, and it is a consensus among the people of interpretation that the good deed is "There is no god but God," and that the evil deed in this verse is polytheism.

(Their faces will be thrown into the Fire) — Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be cast down. Al-Dahhak said: they will be thrown. It is said "kababtu al-inā'" meaning I turned the vessel over onto its face; the intransitive form is "akabba," and this rarely occurs in Arabic speech.

(Are you being recompensed) — that is, it will be said to them: "Are you being recompensed?" Then it may be from the speech of God, and it may be from the speech of the angels.

(Except for what you used to do) — that is, nothing but the recompense of your deeds.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 87–90 (part 1 of 2)**

He made an exception here just as He made an exception in the blast of terror, which indicates that they are one (blast). With the first, Allah causes every living thing to die, and with the second, Allah brings every dead thing to life."

Mujahid said: "They are two cries. The first causes everything to die by Allah's permission, and the second causes everything to live by Allah's permission." Ata' said: "al-Raajifa" is the Judgment (al-Qiyama), and "al-Radifa" is the Resurrection (al-Ba'th). Ibn Zayd said: "al-Raajifa" is death, and "al-Radifa" is the Hour (al-Sa'a). And Allah knows best.

﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾. Then the scholars differed about who this exception is. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra, they are the martyrs with their Lord, who are provided for, since terror only reaches the living. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that they are the martyrs wearing swords around the Throne. Al-Qushayri said: The prophets are included among them, because they have martyrdom along with prophethood. It was also said: they are the angels. Al-Hasan said: He excepted groups of angels who die between the two blasts. Muqatil said: He means Jibril, Mikail, Israfil and the Angel of Death. It was also said: they are the dark-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in). And it was said: they are the believers, because Allah the Exalted said after this: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from terror on that Day﴾ (27:89). Some of our scholars said: The correct view is that no sound report has come concerning specifying them, and all (possibilities) are open. I say: The hadith of Abu Hurayra escaped his notice, and Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it, so let one rely upon it, for it is explicit in specifying them, while the others are ijtihad (personal reasoning). And Allah knows best. Other views have been stated apart from this, which will come in "al-Zumar" (see vol. 15, p. 277 onward).

His saying ﴿So whoever is in the heavens … will be terrified﴾: "fazi'a" is a past tense verb, while "yunfakhu" is a present/future verb. So it is asked: how is a past verb conjoined to a future one? Al-Farra' claimed that this is understood according to the meaning, because the meaning is: "When the Trumpet is blown, they will be terrified." The phrase ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾ is in the accusative as an exception.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾. Abu Amr, Asim, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Ibn Amir and Ibn Kathir read "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) with the present-future form, treating it as a verb in the future. Al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza, and Hafs from Asim read "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) with the past tense, restricted to the past verb. Ibn Mas'ud also read it thus. And from Qatadah: "wa-kullun ataahu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ دَاخِرِينَ). Al-Nahhas said: In my book on the readings from Abu Ishaq, whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) makes it singular according to the wording of "kull," and whoever reads "ātūhu" (أَتُوهُ) makes it plural according to its meaning. This view is a gross error, because if he says "wa-kullun ataw-hu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ) it is not singular but plural. If it were singular, he would say "ataahu" (أَتَاهُ). But whoever says "ataw-hu" (أَتَوْهُ) has made the verb plural according to meaning, and he brought it in the past tense because he referred it back to "fazaʿ" (terror). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ) has also taken it according to meaning and said "ātūhu" (آتُوهُ) because it is a separate clause from the first. Ibn Nasr said: What is reported from Abu Ishaq, may Allah have mercy on him, is what he did not say. The actual text of Abu Ishaq is: "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin," and it is read "ātūhu." Whoever makes it singular does so according to the wording of "kull," and whoever makes it plural does so according to its meaning. He means that whatever comes in the Qur'an or elsewhere of the predicate of "kull" being singular is according to the wording, or plural is according to the meaning. Abu Ja'far did not take this meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataw-hu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is a verb from "ityan" (coming), and it is taken according to the meaning of "kull" not its wording. Whoever reads "wa-kullun ātūhu dakhirin" (وَكُلٌّ آتُوهُ دَاخِرِينَ) it is the active participle from "atā." What indicates this is Allah's saying: ﴿And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾ (19:95). Whoever reads "wa-kullun ataahu" (وَكُلٌّ أَتَاهُ) takes it according to the wording of "kull" and not its meaning, and takes "dakhirin" according to the meaning. Its meaning is "humbled" (saghirin), according to Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. It has already passed in "al-Nahl" (see vol. 10, p. 111, first or second edition).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by as the clouds pass﴾. Ibn Abbas said: That is, standing, while they are moving at a rapid pace. Al-Qutaybi said: That is because the mountains are gathered and set in motion, so in the sight of the eye they appear as standing while they move. Likewise, every great thing and vast multitude whose extent the eye falls short of, due to its vastness and the distance between its extremities, appears to the observer as standing while it moves. Al-Nabigha said describing an army:

*With a host like a mountain, you think them*
*Standing still for a pilgrimage, while the mounts are pacing.*

Al-Qushayri said: This is the Day of Resurrection, meaning they, because of their great number, appear as if solid, that is, standing in the sight of the eye, though in themselves they move like the clouds. Piled-up clouds are thought to be standing while they move. "They pass as the clouds pass" until nothing of them remains. Then Allah says: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ (78:20). It is said that Allah the Exalted described the mountains with various attributes, all of which return to emptying the earth of them and revealing what they had concealed. The first attribute is crumbling (indikak), which happens before the quaking. Then they become like carded wool (al-'ihn al-manfush). This happens when the sky becomes like molten brass (al-muhl). Allah joined the two when He said: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ (70:8–9). The third state is that they become like scattered dust (al-habaʾ), because they are cut off after having been like carded wool. The fourth state is that they are blown away (nasf), because with the previous states they are still fixed in their places while the earth beneath them is not exposed, so they are blown away from it to be exposed. When they are blown away, it is by sending winds upon them. The fifth state is that the winds lift them above the surface of the earth, making them appear as rays in the air like dust, so that whoever looks at them from afar thinks them solid bodies because of their density, while in reality they are passing, except that their passing is from behind the winds, as though they are crumbled and scattered. The sixth state is that they become a mirage, so whoever looks at their places finds nothing of them, like a mirage. Muqatil said: They fall upon the earth and are levelled with it. Then it is said: this is an illustration (mathal). Al-Mawardi said: Regarding what it illustrates there are three views. One: it is a parable Allah struck for this world, in which the observer thinks it is standing like the mountains, while it is in fact taking its share of passing away like the clouds. This was said by Sahl ibn Abd Allah. The second: it is a parable Allah struck for faith, which you think is firmly established in the heart, while its deeds rise to heaven. The third: it is a parable Allah struck for the soul at the moment of its departure, when the spirit moves toward the Throne.

﴿The handiwork of Allah, who has perfected everything﴾. That is, this is from the act of Allah, and whatever is an act from Him is perfected. "Tara" (تَرَى) is from sight with the eye; if it were from sight with the heart, it would take two objects. The original form is "turʾā" (تُرْأَى), so the vowel of the hamza was moved onto the rāʾ, the rāʾ became vowelled and the hamza was dropped. This is the way of easing the hamza when a consonant precedes it, except that the easing is obligatory in "tara." The people of Kufa read "taḥsabuhā" (تَحْسَبُها) with a fatha on the sīn, which is the analogical form, since it comes from "ḥasiba yaḥsibu." However, it has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) a contrary reading, that he recited with a kasra in the imperfect, so it is of the pattern "fa'ila yaf'alu," like "ni'ima yan'amu" and "bi's yab'asu," and it is reported "yi'isa yay'isu" from the sound verbs. Nothing is known in the speech of the Arabs other than these letters. "Wa-hiya tamurru marra al-saḥāb" (وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحابِ): its implied meaning is "a passing like the passing of the clouds." So the attribute has been put in the place of the thing described, and the annexed noun in place of the noun it is annexed to. The mountains are removed from their places on the surface of the earth, gathered and set in motion as clouds are set in motion, then they are broken into pieces and return to the earth, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crushed to powder﴾ (56:5).

(The sawing of God's handiwork) — according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, (صُنْعَ اللَّهِ) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), since when He said, "and it passes as the clouds pass" (27:88), this indicates that He made that happen as a making (ṣun'an). The accusative is also permissible as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: "Look at God's handiwork." On this reading one stops at "the clouds" (al-sahab), but one does not stop there on the first interpretation. It is also permissible to read it in the nominative, meaning: "That is God's handiwork." "Who perfected everything" (alladhi atqana kulla shay'): that is, He made it firm (ahkamahu). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "May God have mercy on the one who does a deed and perfects it." Qatadah said: its meaning is "He made everything good." Al-itqan is al-ihkam (firmness). It is said: "rajul tiqn," meaning a man who is skilled in things. Al-Zuhri said: its origin is from Ibn Tiqn, who was a man from 'Ad, for whom no arrow would miss its target, so he became a proverb. It is said: "More accurate in shooting than Ibn Tiqn," and then every person skilled in things is called tiqn.

(Indeed, He is Aware of what you do) — reading with the "ta'" (second person address) is the reading of the majority. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read it with the "ya'" (third person).

The words of the Exalted: (Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it) — Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: the good deed is "There is no god but God." Abu Ma'shar said: Ibrahim used to swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, without making an exception, that the good deed is "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God." 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them, said: a man went out to fight, and whenever he was alone in a place he would say, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." Then, while he was in the land of the Romans, in the land of Julfa and Baradi, he raised his voice and said, "There is no god but God alone, He has no partner." A man came out to him on a horse, wearing white clothes, and said to him: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is the word of which God the Exalted said, 'Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it.'" Abu Dharr narrated: I said, "O Messenger of God, advise me." He said: "Fear God, and when you do an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will wipe it out." I said: "O Messenger of God, is 'There is no god but God' among the good deeds?" He said: "It is among the best of good deeds." In another narration he said: "Yes, it is the best of good deeds." Related by al-Bayhaqi. Qatadah said: "Whoever comes with a good deed" means with sincerity and monotheism. It was also said: it means performing all the obligatory duties.

I say: when one comes with "There is no god but God" in its true reality and what is required by it, as explained earlier in Surah Ibrahim, then he has come with monotheism, sincerity and the obligations.

"Then he will have better than it": Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, the good reached him from it. Mujahid also said this. It was said: then for him is a beautiful reward, which is Paradise. And "khayr" here is not comparative. 'Ikrimah and Ibn Jurayj said: as for it being that he has better than it, meaning better than faith, that is not so, for nothing is better than one who says "There is no god but God"; rather, he has good from it. It was also said: "Then he will have better than it" is comparative, meaning God's reward is better than the servant's deed, his saying and his remembrance of Him; likewise God's good pleasure is better for the servant than the servant's action. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: this returns to multiplication, for God gives ten for one, and for faith in a brief period the eternal reward; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

(And they will be secure from the terror of that Day) — 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "faza'i yawma'idhin" with the genitive construction (idafah). Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations: that the security is from all the terror of that Day. When He says "min fazi'in yawma'idhin," it becomes as if it were a terror rather than the terror. Al-Qushayri said: it is also read "min fazi'in" with tanwin; then it is said that it means one single terror, as He said: "The Greatest Terror will not grieve them." It was also said: it means plurality, since it is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun is suitable for plurality. I say: according to this, the two readings have the same meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "min fazi'in yawma'idhin" with tanwin, "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative by the verbal noun "fazi'" itself; it may also be an attribute of "fazi'," and it would be connected to an elided element, since verbal nouns may be described by time-nouns and described by them; it may also be connected to the active participle "amanun." The idafah is by way of broadening in time-adverbs. Whoever omits the tanwin and makes the mim fathah builds it, because it is a time-adverb, and the case-ending in a time-adverb is not fully inflected; when it was attached to something that is neither fully inflected nor case-marked, it was built. Sibawayh recited:

"At a time when most of their concerns distracted the people, / Zurayq, seize the wealth, seizing as foxes seize."

[[Zurayq: the name of a tribe, and it is a vocative. "Nadal" here means taking with both hands; "nadal" also means swiftness in movement. "Nadal al-tha'alib" (the foxes' seizing): it is said in a proverb, "He is more gainful than a fox," because it stores for itself and attacks whatever animal it can reach. The verse describes merchants, and it is also said it describes thieves; before it is:
"They pass by al-Dahna lightly burdened in their saddlebags, / and return from Darin with heavy bags."]]

The words of the Exalted: (And whoever comes with an evil deed) — that is, with polytheism. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Abu Hurayrah, Mujahid, Qays ibn Sa'd and al-Hasan, and it is a consensus among the people of interpretation that the good deed is "There is no god but God," and that the evil deed in this verse is polytheism.

(Their faces will be thrown into the Fire) — Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be cast down. Al-Dahhak said: they will be thrown. It is said "kababtu al-inā'" meaning I turned the vessel over onto its face; the intransitive form is "akabba," and this rarely occurs in Arabic speech.

(Are you being recompensed) — that is, it will be said to them: "Are you being recompensed?" Then it may be from the speech of God, and it may be from the speech of the angels.

(Except for what you used to do) — that is, nothing but the recompense of your deeds.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 27, verses 87–90 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾. That is, "Remember the Day when the Trumpet is blown," or "Remind them of the Day when the Trumpet is blown." The view of al-Farra' (the grammarian) is that the meaning is "That is the Day when the Trumpet is blown," and he permitted an ellipsis (hadhf) here. The sound position regarding the Trumpet (al-Sur) is that it is a horn of light into which Israfil (the angel Israfil) blows. Mujahid said: "It is like the shape of a horn (al-buq)." It was also said: "It is al-buq in the dialect of the people of Yemen." Its explanation and what the scholars have said about it has already passed in "al-An'am" (see vol. 7, p. 20 of the first or second edition).

﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾. Abu Hurayra said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had finished creating the heavens, He created the Trumpet and gave it to Israfil. He places it at his mouth, fixing his gaze on the Throne, waiting for when he will be commanded to blow." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said: "A horn, by Allah, a great one. By the One who sent me with the truth, the circumference of its opening is as wide as the heavens and the earth. He will blow into it three blasts. The first blast is the blast of terror (faza'), the second is the blast of swooning (sa'q), and the third is the blast of resurrection and standing before the Lord of the worlds." And he mentioned the hadith. It was related by Ali ibn Ma'bad, al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi and others, and Ibn al-'Arabi authenticated it. I have mentioned it in my book "al-Tadhkira," and we discussed it there. The correct view regarding the blowing into the Trumpet is that there are two blasts, not three. The blast of terror refers back to the blast of swooning, because the two matters have no duration of their own; that is, they become terrified with a terror by which they die. Or it refers to the blast of resurrection. This is the choice of al-Qushayri and others, for he said in his commentary on this verse: "The intended one is the second blast, meaning they will be brought to life terrified, saying: ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ and they will witness matters that overwhelm and frighten them. This blowing is like the sound of a horn, so that the creation gathers in the land of recompense." This was said by Qatadah. Al-Mawardi said: "﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ is the Day of Rising from the graves." He said: Regarding this terror there are two views. One: it is haste and responsiveness to the call, from the expression "fazi'tu ilayka fi kadha" (I hastened to you concerning such-and-such) when one quickly answers your call for help. The second view: the terror here is the familiar terror of fear and grief, because they are driven out of their graves and fear. This is more fitting of the two views. I say: The established Sunnah from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr indicates that there are two blasts, not three. Muslim recorded them, and we have mentioned them in "al-Tadhkira." This is the correct view, if Allah wills, that there are two blasts. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills﴾. He made an exception here just as He made an exception in the blast of terror, which indicates that they are one (blast). Ibn al-Mubarak related from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between the two blasts there are forty years. With the first, Allah causes every living thing to die, and with the second, Allah brings every dead thing to life."

If it is said: Allah's saying: ﴿On the Day when the quaking one quakes, followed by the following one﴾, until He said: ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ (79:6–13), outwardly indicates that there are three. It is said in reply: This is not so. The "shout" (zajra) here means the second blast, by which people come out of their graves. Thus said Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata', Ibn Zayd and others. Mujahid said: "They are two cries. The first causes everything to die by Allah's permission, and the second causes everything to live by Allah's permission." Ata' said: "al-Raajifa" is the Judgment (al-Qiyama), and "al-Radifa" is the Resurrection (al-Ba'th). Ibn Zayd said: "al-Raajifa" is death, and "al-Radifa" is the Hour (al-Sa'a). And Allah knows best.
